items.title: ChatGPT in Pakistani Higher Education:  Transforming Teaching, Learning, Assessment,  Research, and Academic Ethics

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education in Pakistan has created both opportunities and concerns for educators, researchers, and policymakers. ChatGPT, a generative AI tool developed by OpenAI, can support teaching, learning, assessment, research, and academic work. This study examined how experienced academicians view its benefits, limitations, and ethical implications in Pakistani higher education. A qualitative exploratory design was used in this study. Twelve experienced academicians from different higher education institutions in Pakistan were selected purposively and interviewed through a semi-structured guide. The interviews were transcribed and analysed through familiarization, coding, development and review of themes. ChatGPT was used only to help organize provisional codes; the researchers checked its suggestions against the transcripts and made the final analytical decisions. Five themes were identified: teaching, learning, assessment, research, and ethics. Participants reported that ChatGPT supported lesson planning, content preparation, student engagement, idea generation, academic writing, and research productivity. They also noted that it enables students to understand difficult topics, improve their writing skills, and obtain immediate academic support. Main concerns were identified as plagiarism, over-reliance on AI-generated content, weaker critical thinking, and the absence of clear institutional policies. The findings show that ChatGPT may be useful in higher education when its use is guided by academic judgment and clear rules. Universities should redesign assessment, prepare ethical guidelines, train faculty, and strengthen AI literacy. The study offers practical information for teachers, administrators, and policymakers planning the responsible use of generative AI in Pakistan.

items.abstract_text: Why can similarly configured AI agents amplify engagement in some communities yet mainly redirect it in others? We deployed two autonomous AI agents in separate Farcaster channels (January–February 2026) across two incentive phases: Phase 1 with $Degen token rewards and Phase 2 with social recognition through agent follow-backs and mutual-follow encouragement. In /replyors (71 daily replies at baseline, Attention Saturation Ratio 1.17), the difference-in-differences (DiD)-adjusted engagement lift was [Formula: see text]228% in Phase 1 and [Formula: see text]118% in Phase 2, consistent with engagement amplification, although the seven-day baseline does not establish parallel pre-treatment trends cleanly. In /degen (244 daily replies, ASR 2.17), the channel-level DiD estimate was [Formula: see text]18% ([Formula: see text]) and not statistically distinguishable from zero despite strong topic-level participation. Because the available /degen–/base control is poorly matched on baseline scale and ASR, that comparison is treated as suggestive rather than a clean causal estimate. Phase 1 generated 967 participant reply messages from 61 unique individuals and 101,980 $Degen distributed. Using historical DEGEN/USD closes at the beginning and end of the 9–22 January reward phase as a broad valuation bracket, the aggregate token budget was on the order of US$111–152; this is not a transaction-time weighted valuation. After token removal, participant reply volume within agent-initiated threads fell by approximately 82–90% and Phase 1 participant retention was 27–34%. We introduce the Contextual Amplification Framework (CAF) and Attention Saturation Ratio (ASR) as provisional, exploratory constructs derived from two treated channels. The evidence is consistent with the possibility that pre-existing attention saturation moderates agent effects, but the ASR is not a validated screening rule and requires multi-site replication. The findings carry implications for platform economics, AI governance, and token incentive design.

items.title: Between AI usage and academic procrastination among college students through anxiety, self-control, and ai guilt

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of AI tools in higher education has raised questions about how AI usage is associated with students’ academic behaviors. While AI can enhance efficiency, it may also be associated with greater academic procrastination. Existing studies have explored AI use and learning outcomes, but the psychological pathways underlying this association remain underexamined. Drawing on Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Moral Emotion Theory, this study examined the indirect roles of academic anxiety and self-control in the relationship between AI usage and academic procrastination, while also assessing whether AI guilt moderated these associations. In this cross-sectional survey, 782 students were recruited from two public universities in Guangxi, China, which were selected based on accessibility. Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were performed using PROCESS Models 4 and 7 in SPSS. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with academic procrastination. Academic anxiety and self-control both showed significant indirect associations, with completely standardized estimates of 0.129 and 0.119, respectively. Together, these indirect associations accounted for approximately 54.87% of the total association. In addition, AI guilt moderated the associations between AI usage and academic anxiety and self-control. Specifically, the positive association between AI usage and academic anxiety was weaker at higher levels of AI guilt, as was the negative association between AI usage and self-control. Within the scope of the variables examined, these findings provide context-specific evidence concerning selected emotional, behavioral, and moral-evaluative processes relevant to the associations among AI usage, academic anxiety, self-control, and academic procrastination among students at the participating universities.

items.title: Designing AI at the Rural Edge: A Micro-Social Venture Framework for Community-Led Digital Innovation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative and other AI-enabled technologies are accessible to small organisations, yet human–AI interaction (HAI) design guidance focuses on relatively direct user–system interaction. Rural HCI, community-centred design, participatory AI, digital inclusion, and social-enterprise research show that AI use is socially and organisationally situated. This late-breaking work develops the Micro-Social Venture (MSV) Framework through integrative conceptual synthesis of 55 selected sources. The framework connects six dimensions: Place, Community Agency, Organisational Mediation, Digital and AI Capability, Resource Conditions, and Governance and Social Outcomes. Its distinctive contribution is to treat the social venture as part of HAI itself: a community-embedded socio-technical intermediary through which AI is encountered, adapted, governed, and potentially refused. Five design propositions address place, collective agency, resource asymmetry, negotiated trust, and community stewardship. The framework is generative rather than predictive, offering HCI a diagnostic lens for examining community-embedded AI at geographic, organisational, infrastructural, and participatory edges.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Challenges and Managerial Risks

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become a near-universal part of students’ academic practice, confronting universities with challenges that reach beyond technology to the core of teaching and assessment. This article is an integrative narrative review of peer-reviewed studies, preprints and policy documents published mainly between 2023 and 2026. It examines the crisis in the validity of knowledge assessment and the unreliability of AI detectors; cognitive dependence, metacognitive laziness and the erosion of critical thinking; digital inequality; the meta-analytic evidence on learning effects; and the regulatory framework set by UNESCO, the OECD and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. The cross-cutting theme is the “performance–learning gap”: GenAI reliably improves task performance, but genuine learning gains depend on teacher support, pedagogical guardrails and the way students use the tool, and they often disappear when knowledge is assessed without AI. Particular attention is given to Georgia, where AI uptake is already high while the institutional response remains fragmented. The article proposes structural reform of assessment, a five-stage institutional pilot model for Georgian universities, a practical formula for students (“think first, ask AI, then evaluate critically”) and a research agenda of six priority directions.

analysis.discussion: Two positions in the literature both oppose and complement each other. A clear example of the restrictive (conservative) position is Ali [9] , who, after reviewing the benefits and risks of AI, sets out the author's personal view: AI should be avoided in schools and, in higher education, by undergraduate and master's students in the process of learning and completing assignments, while in research its use is acceptable only with critical verification of the accuracy and appropriateness of the results. The logic of this position is partly supported by the negative effect of use "without guardrails" [21, 22*] and by the fact that in many cases the gains disappear when knowledge is assessed without AI [38* ]. The integrative position [2, 4, 5, 28] argues that a ban is unrealistic when 95% of students already use the technology, and that the university's task is to teach its responsible use, which is also essential for graduates' employability. This position is supported empirically by evidence that pedagogically structured AI significantly improves learning outcomes [40, 41] and that gains are particularly large with teacher support [32] . Guardrails neutralise the negative effect, although they do not in themselves improve learning [21] . The latest experiments give this position an additional argument: practical training in AI use changes the student's own behaviour, and behaviour changes the learning effect ([45*]; [42*]; see Section 5.4). Both positions rest on a common premise: learning requires mental effort. The decisive difference lies not in a choice between being "for or against AI" but in how the technology is used: as a substitute for thinking or as its enrichment. In practice this means a differentiated approach: restricting AI at the stage of forming basic skills and in secured assessment, and integrating it in a structured, critical and transparent way at more advanced stages. This tension reflects well the central thesis of this article on the "performance-learning gap" and explains why pedagogical design is decisive. The integration of artificial intelligence into education is inevitable: by 2026 it has become a near-universal, everyday practice among students. In the approach set out in Gagnidze's lecture course, routine and standard tasks should be delegated to technology, while responsibility for conclusions, decisions and acquired knowledge must remain with the human being. Universities should assess not only the finished assignment but also the reasoning and process behind it. The best strategy is not prohibition (as New York City public schools attempted in 2023, only to reverse course within a few months) but teaching students to make the technology an intellectual assistant and interlocutor that stimulates mental activity and broadens the range of ideas, rather than a replacement for the brain. The latest evidence refines this position. Meta-analytic studies show an on-average positive effect of AI use, but this effect depends largely on teacher support and pedagogical design. When knowledge is assessed without AI, the gains often disappear, and use without guardrails may even harm learning. Moreover, the impact of AI is not only cognitive: it changes students' relationships, their sense of fairness and their psychosocial wellbeing, and its benefits and harms are unequally distributed. Three practical principles follow: structural reform of assessment (validity, oral defence and process assessment); institutionally governed AI (equal access, pedagogical guardrails and clear rules); and AI literacy as a new form of critical thinking, understood not as one-off information but as practical training in specific behaviours for working with AI (attempt, verify and correct), whose effect is already visible in early experiments but has yet to be confirmed in higher education. For Georgia these principles are particularly relevant: AI uptake is already high but the institutional response is fragmented, so evidence-based institutional pilots and local research are a necessary precondition for forming a national framework. The potential of AI will be realised only when the student remains the active subject of the thinking process.

items.title: Utilizing a GPT-based exam assistant to support practice and assessment in higher education: an exploratory study on learner engagement and perceptions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Instructors increasingly use chatbots to reduce their workload and to support students with individualized learning opportunities. However, there is still limited knowledge about how students engage with chatbot-based formats for practice and assessment compared to similar human-authored formats. This study examines whether chatbot-supported instruction can achieve similar outcomes with respect to students’ engagement, perceived fairness and perceived usefulness while reducing the workload associated with creating practice and assessment activities. We developed an Exam Assistant (EA) that delivers exam-like open-ended questions, including short case studies, provides immediate feedback, and supports automated scoring with instructor review (human-in-the-loop). The EA was implemented in a real classroom setting with N = 30 undergraduate business students at a German university. Students used the EA for practice and for a graded assignment in the first course phase, while in the second course phase, these activities were delivered via conventional Moodle quizzes. This ensured alignment between practice activities and assessment across both instructional formats . Using learning analytics, chatbot interaction logs from 224 sessions with the EA, and post-assessment surveys, we conducted a descriptive, exploratory comparison of students’ engagement patterns and fairness perceptions. Results show comparably high levels of practice intensity and perceived fairness across both instructional modes. Students demonstrated greater engagement with EA than has typically been reported in prior research on educational chatbots. Nevertheless, students perceived Moodle quizzes as more suitable for future graded assessments, a difference that appears to be driven by question format rather than by fairness concerns. Overall, the findings suggest that thoughtfully chatbot-supported practice and assessment may offer a promising pathway to reduce instructors’ workload without evident disadvantages in student engagement or perceived fairness.

analysis.discussion: This study examined how students engage with chatbot-supported practice and assessment across different instructional formats implemented in consecutive course phases. Practice intensity (RQ1) was comparable across the chatbot-supported and conventional Moodlebased modes and overall, relatively high. On average, students practiced with the EA about seven to eight times during the first course phase, with a large share of practice occurring on the day before the graded exam. About 40% of all practice attempts were fully completed. This finding contrasts with prior research showing that approximately onethird of students did not use the chatbot-based learning mode at all, and that those who did engage with the chatbot typically did so only for a few minutes across several days, exhibiting an initial peak followed by a gradual decline (Hellas et al., 2024; Martins et al., 2024) . One possible explanation is that, unlike the chatbot deployments examined in prior work, the EA was not introduced as an optional learning tool but was closely aligned with the graded assessment, which may have motivated students to engage more seriously with the EA during self-study. Interestingly, despite offering virtually unlimited practice opportunities and immediate feedback, students did not make markedly more practice attempts than in the Moodle condition. This suggests that practice intensity may be constrained by overall workload and competing study demands rather than by the availability of additional exercises. From an instructional perspective, however, achieving comparable practice intensity with substantially less authoring effort is itself a relevant benefit. This advantage may be greater than indicated by the estimates in Sect. "Instructor workload for authoring practice and assessment activities", because the EA also provided immediate individualized feedback on open-ended and case-based responses, which would be costly to deliver manually at scale. Regarding students' perceptions of fairness, the EA-based and Moodle-based assessments performed very well and at similarly high levels in both informational and procedural fairness evaluations by students. This also suggests that including the course reader as a domain-specific knowledge base in the EA setup, as suggested by earlier research, may have supported good alignment between AI-generated tasks and course content, as students did not report major issues related to hallucinations, off-topic content, or subjective bias. Overall, our results suggest that the AI-supported assessment format did not compromise students' perceptions of fairness compared to traditional, human-authored Moodle quizzes. In contrast to previous studies, which found a reluctance toward automated grading among as many as half of the students (Schei et al., 2024) , reluctance toward the EA appeared to be less pronounced in our context. As suggested before, the reasons for these differences are likely attributable to the general design of the instruction, which led to a very tight integration of the EA within the course. Students were invited to point out caveats with respect to the EA, which even led to major reconfigurations of the tool after an in-class introductory EA session. The participatory implementation process may have fostered a general atmosphere of trust and fairness with regard to the EA, including assessment practices. A notable difference between the two modes was that more students experienced time pressure when completing the tasks and questions presented by the EA during the graded exam, as compared to the Moodle quiz. First of all, students may have experienced additional stress due to technical issues encountered during the EA-based assessment. Moreover, the EA required free-text responses to all questions presented, whereas in the Moodle mode, this question type only made up about one-fifth of the questions, and the remaining questions used closed-response and interactive item formats. Because free-text answers typically take longer to formulate than closed-format questions, this likely resulted in increased time pressure, especially for slower writers. The differences in question formats may also provide a plausible explanation for the somewhat counterintuitive finding that, although students considered both modes to be equally fair, most students favored Moodle quizzes over the EA when asked about their preferences for future courses, particularly with respect to graded assessments. Apart from considerations of fairness, students may simply prefer a mix of predominantly clickable question formats with only a small proportion of open-ended responses over fully text-based question-answer interactions with a chatbot-especially in graded exams that must be completed under strict time constraints. Although this initial exploratory study has several limitations that should be addressed in future research on chatbot-supported practice and assessment, the absence of marked differences in student engagement and perceived fairness between the EA and Moodle formats provides an important starting point. The findings suggest that chatbot-supported practice and assessment can be integrated into higher education without evident disadvantages in these outcomes while reducing instructor workload associated with authoring. An important insight is that chatbot-supported practice seems to be particularly promising when closely aligned with assessment procedures, purposefully integrated into the course structure, and linked to graded assessments. This suggests that alignment-a well-established principle of instructional design-should also be a key consideration when designing educational technologies, rather than offering them as an optional add-on. Practically speaking, the finding that chatbot-based formats were perceived as comparable to traditional, human-authored Moodle-based practice and assessment in terms of learning experience suggests that the choice between these formats primarily becomes a workload decision. In our study, we showed that chatbot-based tools for practice, feedback, and assessment, such as the EA, can be implemented using off-the-shelf tools and without technical expertise. The primary challenge for instructors lies in developing a structured system prompt that incorporates conceptual design considerations, such as task logic, rubrics, and feedback principles. However, instructors have to take into account these issues also when creating quiz questions and interactive tasks manually in Moodle or other learning management systems. When large numbers of practice and assessment questions are required, or when course content changes, creating such items entirely manually results in a high workload on the instructor side. In contrast, once a chatbot-based setup is stable, updating or extending the practice and assessment based on changes to the course content is as simple as replacing the domain-specific knowledge base. This implies that the same EA-like tool can be reused across courses with different content, requiring only minor adjustments. At the same time, it should not be overlooked that students were somewhat less comfortable with EA-based graded assessments than with conventional Moodle quizzes, even if they perceived them as similarly fair. analysis.limitations: A first set of limitations concerns the study design. Blended-learning formats like ours make it difficult to disentangle the effects of the two practice modes from those of other parallel instructional activities, such as lectures. Moreover, the two formats were implemented in a fixed sequence and covered different topics (Organizational Behavior vs. Human Resource Management). The lack of counterbalancing may have introduced order effects, although greater familiarity with the course and assessment procedures in the later Moodle phase would arguably have favored Moodle. Conversely, because prior knowledge and topic familiarity were not controlled, the potentially greater accessibility of the Organizational Behavior content may have favored the EA phase independently of the instructional format. These differences, together with the lack of formally established reliability and validity of the assessments, prevented a meaningful direct comparison of learning outcomes. At the same time, a coarse review of assignment scores and pre-post self-assessments during data analysis did not raise concerns that the use of the EA was associated with any noticeable negative effects on learning outcomes. Finally, because all participants shared the same classroom experience, their responses may not have been fully independent, further limiting the interpretation of individual-level comparisons. Additional limitations affect the comparability and precision of the available evidence. The system failure required an unplanned switch to a different LLM and platform during the graded EA assessment. As a result, data from both systems were analyzed together without formally testing their comparability. Second, detailed information about usage patterns was only available for the EA mode, but not for the Moodle mode. As a result, we were not able to directly compare how students actually practiced in the respective modes, for example how far they progressed through the questions, how extensively they responded, and where they discontinued practice. Still, the detailed insights into students' use of the EA made it possible to compare the observed usage patterns with those of prior evaluation research on educational chatbots, suggesting a higher level of active use for practice than is commonly reported. Finally, workload estimates in Sect. "Instructor workload for authoring practice and assessment activities" for authoring both formats were retrospective and should be interpreted as approximate. Moreover, the study's small, context-specific sample and the particular instructional setting limit the generalizability of the findings. As the study was carried out in a single undergraduate business course, students in other disciplines or learning environments may respond differently to the EA and Moodle activities. In addition, the extensive support offered by instructors, the cooperative, open atmosphere between instructors and students and students' involvement in testing and refining the EA may not be replicable in largerscale teaching contexts and may partly explain the favorable perceptions of the EA phase. Lastly, although one of the main promises of chatbot-based teaching tools is individualized feedback at scale, this study did not look at how students used or perceived the EA's feedback. Conclusions about how AI-generated feedback affected subsequent learning or practice behavior cannot be drawn from the data currently available, indicating a crucial area for further study.

verified_article_review.provenance: Original paraphrases from the checked HTML article
verified_article_review.methods: Thirty business undergraduates at a German university practiced organizational behavior with a GPT tutor. It asked four questions and then presented a case. In one example, students had to explain how they would handle conflict in a newly reorganized team. The tutor gave written feedback after each response. In the next unit, the same class studied human resources with instructor-written Moodle quizzes, including an exercise on calculating wages. The researchers examined practice records and surveyed students after each unit.
verified_article_review.results: The first question appeared in 224 chatbot sessions. Students typed an answer in 118 sessions (52.7%). The final case appeared in 146 sessions and drew an answer in 91 (40.6% of all launches). Students could practice repeatedly, so these counts describe sessions. Most survey respondents reported 30 minutes to two hours of weekly practice with either tool. Among the 23 who took the second survey, over half preferred the chatbot for practice or considered either format suitable. Most preferred Moodle for graded work.
verified_article_review.discussion: A teacher looking only at the 224 launches would count opening the exercise and working through the case in exactly the same way. The written answers let the authors distinguish those actions. They suggest that students may have returned to rehearse the kind of question they expected on the exam. The logs cannot show how much students learned from reading the tutor’s feedback.
verified_article_review.limitations: All students used the chatbot first and Moodle second. The subject changed between units, and the chatbot exam was supervised while the Moodle exam was taken at home. Moodle recorded 181 practice attempts without showing which questions students actually answered. The researchers could compare reported practice time, but could not tell which tool produced more active practice or better learning.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology
items.abstract_text: In this study, we adopted a holistic approach by integrating bibliometric analysis and systematic review methods to thoroughly evaluate the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education and its research trends. The study aims to understand the current state of the field and provide strategic direction for future research by assessing general trends, intellectual contributions, and application potential in AI-focused mathematics education research from a multidimensional perspective. In the first phase, we conducted a content analysis of 363 articles published in high-quality journals indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database, focusing on dimensions such as publishers, method types, research designs, study groups, theoretical or conceptual frameworks, data collection techniques, preferred technologies, purposes of use, and roles. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of scientific productivity, citation performance, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, thematic maps, and intellectual transformations. During this process, we followed the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA). The findings indicate that AI technologies have been increasingly utilized in mathematics education, with significant growth observed since 2015. AI-focused mathematics education research has been predominantly concentrated in countries like the USA, China, and Germany, delving into areas such as personalized learning, assessment, feedback, and pedagogical innovations. Most studies have employed quantitative and mixed methods, with middle school and undergraduate students being the primary target groups. Bibliometric analyses reveal a rapid expansion in scientific productivity and collaboration networks, while thematic trends primarily focus on personalized learning and the integration of digital tools.

items.title: When the Tool Reshapes the Practitioner: A Futures-Oriented Analysis of Risks Associated with AI Applications in Psychotherapy

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence is entering psychotherapy at almost every point of clinical work: therapist training, screening and detection, risk prediction, diagnostic support and treatment planning, patient education, chatbot-delivered session content, between-session tracking, supervision, and documentation. Discussion of the associated dangers to this process has so far been overwhelmingly patient directed. This narrative review addresses these questions from a futures-oriented perspective: what AI may do to psychotherapists as professionals. We first map current and emerging applications across the phases of therapy. We then distinguish four forms of competence loss reported in the wider clinical literature, namely deskilling, never-skilling, mis-skilling, and moral deskilling, and use them to structure a function-by-function analysis of nine clinical tasks. The risks we identify, most of which rest on extrapolation from medicine and education and are therefore best read as hypotheses, extend beyond technical skill. Algorithmic flags may redistribute clinical attention, and accountability may shift from the quality of judgement to adherence to procedure. Case formulation may close prematurely, and theoretical pluralism may narrow toward the traditions best represented in training data. Findings that chatbots are rated as more empathic than clinicians may threaten professional identity, while supervision may lose its relational and formative functions. We then set out four possible trajectories for the field: AI as a support to professional judgement, gradual dependency, standardized AI-mediated practice, and systems designed explicitly to preserve and cultivate expertise, together with the drivers that may lead toward each. Implications are drawn for training, clinical governance, and professional ethics.

items.title: ThoughtPaths: Navigating Persistent, Multi-Perspective AI Trajectories in Collaborative Knowledge Work

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Most generative AI interfaces organise interaction as a linear conversational thread. However, open-ended collaborative knowledge work often requires comparing alternatives, revisiting ideas, and negotiating direction over time. We designed and studied ThoughtPaths, a multi-branch generative AI interface that produces three parallel response trajectories—balanced, critical, and provocative—and maintains them as persistent, navigable structures. Through a qualitative study with five groups (three dyads, two triads; N = 12), we examine how knowledge workers use these branches to expand and redirect exploration, surface assumptions through contrast, and coordinate decisions by revisiting earlier trajectories. We found that persistent divergence supported negotiated interaction while introducing challenges in managing cognitive load. This work contributes an open-source prototype, an empirical account of collaborative practices, and design implications for generative AI interfaces that support knowledge work.

reading.findings: We report three themes describing how groups worked with persistent AI-generated trajectories: navigating and revisiting divergent directions, coordinating attention and direction through discussion, and interpreting ambiguous or potentially biased outputs. Across these themes, persistent branching expanded the material available for exploration, while also requiring participants to compare, prioritise, and make sense of the trajectories they developed. Participants did not treat the three branches as equivalent responses to be read in sequence. Instead, they moved laterally across neighbouring outputs, compared their differences, and decided which trajectories warranted further attention. The persistent structure kept explored and unexplored directions visible, but it did not determine which alternatives were meaningful or worth extending. Participants therefore had to prioritise some trajectories while leaving others aside. One participant described this flexibility as being able to "go in different directions, like starting from one branch and then shifting to another, exploring multiple trajectories simultaneously." Rather than requiring an immediate commitment to a single direction, the visible branches allowed groups to keep alternatives available while deciding how their inquiry should develop. In one session, participants initially extended a critical branch, but later paused to compare it with the balanced and provocative alternatives. After discussing how the responses framed the issue differently, they returned to the earlier node and extended another trajectory, shifting the focus of their inquiry. Returning to the earlier node reopened a choice that had initially been set aside, allowing the group to reconsider it in light of what they had subsequently discussed. The persistent structure also allowed participants to inspect how a trajectory had developed over time and where its framing began to diverge from earlier directions. As one participant explained, "I like the way that it operates almost like a chain of ideas. . . to see at which point trajectories diverged from the initial direction." reading.interpretation: This study examined how small groups used persistent AI-generated trajectories during synchronous, open-ended exploration. Keeping divergent directions visible expanded collective inquiry but left groups to decide which trajectories mattered, how to interpret them, and when to narrow focus. Persistent divergence therefore shifted, rather than removed, the work of comparison, prioritisation, and coordination. We discuss three related issues: trajectories as shared resources and coordination burdens; the articulation work needed to turn alternatives into collective direction; and participants' responsibility for judging whether trajectories were distinct, credible, and productive. Prior research has shown that collaborative work depends on maintaining common ground and coordinating attention through shared representations [27, 28] . In our study, persistent trajectories supported this by keeping earlier prompts, outputs, and branching points jointly visible -reference points participants returned to when comparing alternatives or reconsidering how their inquiry had developed. Rewinding was central to this as returning to an earlier node let groups recover a shared point of reference, inspect where a trajectory had begun to diverge, and reopen alternatives previously set aside, a form of collaborative repair when a direction became less useful. This same persistence, however, increased the material requiring attention, because alternatives were not automatically merged or discarded, groups had to compare outputs and leave some trajectories unexplored, making verbal summarisation and informal pruning necessary rather than peripheral. reading.limitations: This study focuses on the emerging practices of a novel AI interface for knowledge work, following an established approach in HCI/CSCW and research-through-design prior to summative studies of user performance and task efficiency [9, 44] . Future work could explore longer-term engagement and how knowledge work teams appropriate these multi-branch interfaces in their own practice and domain. The study involved five groups with prior experience using generative AI in their work, exploring open-ended, value-laden questions during synchronous sessions. These findings apply to earlystage collaborative sensemaking; future work should validate them in longer-term, asynchronous settings, for example, by isolating the effects of persistent branching or behavioural stance. Across sessions, groups typically extended three to five branching steps, producing approximately 9 to 15 sub-branches. They managed this growth by slowing their pace, verbally summarising trajectories, narrowing attention to a smaller set of branches, and leaving some alternatives unexplored. These practices made continued exploration manageable, while also showing that preserving divergence introduced ongoing comparison and informal pruning work for the group. Making multiple trajectories visible did not produce a shared direction on its own. Participants still had to negotiate which outputs deserved attention, how alternatives should be evaluated, and when to continue along a particular path. Branches were treated as candidate directions: participants read them aloud, compared them, and debated which to pursue. In one triad, one participant proposed extending the provocative branch, while another argued that the critical branch better addressed potential risks. The group compared both before selecting the critical branch to challenge their existing framing. Similar proposing and countering occurred across groups, although some reached agreement quickly while others spent longer comparing divergent responses. The three branches provided a bounded set of options without fully determining the inquiry. Participants could associate new ideas with the closest branch or develop them through follow-up prompts. Because trajectories remained visible, groups could refer to several directions within the same shared view. One participant said the interface "allows you to see the multiple directions as steps, " while another described it as providing "more clarity. . . showing that there are multiple perspectives. " Interpretation and selection occurred largely through discussion. Participants described the AI as a "critique engine" and a "vehicle to explore 'what if' scenarios, " positioning it as a source of candidate directions rather than a decision-maker. Persistent trajectories provided shared reference points, while collective direction emerged through participants' coordination. While participants valued multiple perspectives, they also identified friction in how responses were framed, passive or hedged language made some outputs difficult to interpret, as when one response stated that "certain actions may be considered problematic in some contexts" without specifying who should act or what should be done. Concerns about bias arose similarly in how trajectories were extended: repeatedly following a branch could reinforce a narrow framing, as one participant cautioned, "If we engineer it to a rabbit hole, we are going to get that rabbit hole response. " These moments of directional drift often led groups to reconsider whether to continue along a trajectory or return to earlier branches to broaden exploration. These observations highlight a tension between making multiple trajectories available and the interpretive work required to evaluate them. Participants remained responsible for assessing whether branches expressed substantively different perspectives, how ambiguous language should be understood, and when repeated extension narrowed rather than developed a direction.
analysis.discussion: This study examined how small groups used persistent AI-generated trajectories during synchronous, open-ended exploration. Keeping divergent directions visible expanded collective inquiry but left groups to decide which trajectories mattered, how to interpret them, and when to narrow focus. Persistent divergence therefore shifted, rather than removed, the work of comparison, prioritisation, and coordination. We discuss three related issues: trajectories as shared resources and coordination burdens; the articulation work needed to turn alternatives into collective direction; and participants' responsibility for judging whether trajectories were distinct, credible, and productive. Prior research has shown that collaborative work depends on maintaining common ground and coordinating attention through shared representations [27, 28] . In our study, persistent trajectories supported this by keeping earlier prompts, outputs, and branching points jointly visible -reference points participants returned to when comparing alternatives or reconsidering how their inquiry had developed. Rewinding was central to this as returning to an earlier node let groups recover a shared point of reference, inspect where a trajectory had begun to diverge, and reopen alternatives previously set aside, a form of collaborative repair when a direction became less useful. This same persistence, however, increased the material requiring attention, because alternatives were not automatically merged or discarded, groups had to compare outputs and leave some trajectories unexplored, making verbal summarisation and informal pruning necessary rather than peripheral. This reveals an inherent tension in multi-trajectory interaction: preserving divergence supports common ground by externalising alternatives and maintaining a shared history, but also creates coordination work by keeping unresolved possibilities present. The exploratory value and cognitive cost of persistent branching are therefore closely connected -the system enables reconsideration precisely by postponing decisions about what should be prioritised, abandoned, or brought forward. Making alternative trajectories jointly visible did not by itself produce a collective direction. Although the interface preserved the available branches and the paths already taken, it did not represent why participants preferred one trajectory, how they evaluated differences between outputs, or where members disagreed. Groups therefore relied on verbal coordination to transform visible alternatives into a shared course of action. This work can be understood as articulation work: the ongoing effort required to organise distributed contributions, align interpretations, and coordinate how collaborative activity should proceed [34] . In our study, participants performed this work by reading branches aloud, explaining why particular outputs mattered, questioning one another's preferences, and negotiating when to extend, redirect, or leave a trajectory unexplored. Parallel trajectories provided shared objects of attention, but their significance was established through participants' discussion rather than by the branching structure alone. Off-interface discussion was therefore not separate from interaction with the AI, but part of how the generated trajectories became usable in collaboration. The interface externalised possible directions, while participants supplied the evaluative criteria and selection rationales needed to act on them. This distinction is important because the persistence of multiple branches can support deliberation without resolving it: the system can make disagreement and alternatives visible, but it cannot determine which differences are relevant to the group's evolving purpose. Figure 3 illustrates how groups used rewinding and verbal coordination to support this process. We presented ThoughtPaths, a multi-branch generative AI interface for knowledge work. Departing from the linear, closure-oriented structure of mainstream AI interfaces, it prioritises divergence through three contrasting responses to every prompt-balanced, critical, and provocative-preserved as persistent, navigable trajectories. Through a qualitative study with five groups (𝑁 = 12), we show that persistent divergence did not remove convergence work; it shifted comparison, interpretation, prioritisation, and coordination towards the group. Groups compared, revisited, and selectively extended trajectories, while questioning whether the branches were meaningfully distinct. This work contributes ThoughtPaths as an open-source prototype, an empirical account of these practices, and design implications for generative AI interfaces that support knowledge work without premature closure.
analysis.limitations: This study focuses on the emerging practices of a novel AI interface for knowledge work, following an established approach in HCI/CSCW and research-through-design prior to summative studies of user performance and task efficiency [9, 44] . Future work could explore longer-term engagement and how knowledge work teams appropriate these multi-branch interfaces in their own practice and domain. The study involved five groups with prior experience using generative AI in their work, exploring open-ended, value-laden questions during synchronous sessions. These findings apply to earlystage collaborative sensemaking; future work should validate them in longer-term, asynchronous settings, for example, by isolating the effects of persistent branching or behavioural stance. Branch distinctness across topics and interaction depth could also be systematically evaluated; as noted in Section 6.3, this open opportunities to examine how divergence should scale over longer or more varied use. Further work could also examine mechanisms such as multimodal summarisation or grouping that help manage divergence, context, and knowledge retention.

items.title: AI for Spiritual Growth: A Collaborative Ethnography with Professing Christians

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Spiritual AI is a nascent area of HCI research exploring how generative AI can augment spiritual experiences. Research to date has focused on speculative design, but actual AI use for spiritual purposes remains unexplored. To address this gap, this research explored how AI is used in daily life, specifically for spiritual growth in a Christian tradition. This research was inspired by and based on the first author’s experience, as well as collaborative ethnographic research with 20 participants who publicly identify as Christians. Our findings show how AI was used for spiritual practices across three areas – growth in knowledge, faith, and godliness – and how AI both supported and conflicted with practices such as Bible study and prayer. Based on these findings, we propose a revised notion of spiritual AI that is grounded in lived spiritual practice, rather than augmented experience, and present an agenda for future HCI research.

items.title: Motivational gain trumps cognitive offloading: a MASEM study on the net positive effect of AI use on critical thinking

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The application of artificial intelligence technology in education is becoming increasingly widespread, but there is no consensus yet on its impact on learners’ critical thinking. To gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between the two, this study adopted the meta-analysis structural equation modeling method and systematically integrated data from 31 empirical studies worldwide in this field. The results show that the use of artificial intelligence is not directly associated with the improvement or decline of critical thinking, but rather appears to operate through two different psychological mechanisms. On the one hand, frequent use of artificial intelligence can easily lead to technological dependence, and this tendency of dependence can harm the development of critical thinking. On the other hand, the proper use of artificial intelligence tools can stimulate learning motivation, thereby promoting the cultivation of critical thinking skills. These two opposite indirect effects coexist and nearly offset each other; the net indirect effect was not statistically significant, whereas the direct association of AI use with critical thinking remained positive and significant. Further analysis suggests that this dual effect may vary across groups: the motivational pathway appeared especially pronounced among college students, whereas the group difference in the inhibition pathway was not statistically significant. This study, from a theoretical perspective, reveals the dual paths through which artificial intelligence influences critical thinking, providing an important reference for how to effectively utilize artificial intelligence tools in educational practice and also offering new directions for future related research. However, causal interpretations are limited by the predominantly cross-sectional nature of the included studies.

items.title: Influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on learners’ critical thinking and academic performance: Basis for AI-driven instructional toolkit

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Research Studies in Education
items.abstract_text: This study aimed to determine the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on learners’ critical thinking and academic performance as a basis for developing an AI-Driven Instructional Toolkit for San Carlos Elementary School, Caba, La Union. Specifically, it examined learners’ awareness and experiences in using AI tools, their level of critical thinking, academic performance in Mathematics, Science, and English, and the relationship among these variables. The study employed a quantitative research design involving twenty-six (26) learner-respondents who answered a validated and reliable survey questionnaire. The findings revealed that learners had a high level of awareness of AI tools, including ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, and Jenni AI, while their learning and collaborative experiences were very high. Their overall level of critical thinking was high, with a median of 4.17, particularly in reasoning, problem-solving, and collaborative skills. Likewise, their academic performance in Mathematics, Science, and English was very high, with grades ranging from 91 to 95. Statistical analysis further revealed a significant but weak positive correlation between awareness of AI tools and critical thinking (r = .300), as well as a significant positive correlation with academic performance in Mathematics (r = .343). These findings suggest that AI tools can support learners’ critical thinking and academic performance when integrated meaningfully and responsibly into instruction. The developed AI-Driven Instructional Toolkit obtained a very high level of validity, indicating its suitability for instructional use. The study recommends the guided integration of AI tools to promote responsible technology use, independent thinking, collaborative learning, and improved academic outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming traditional productivity and task management systems by enabling intelligent assistance for task planning, prioritization, scheduling, collaboration, and decision-making. This paper presents a survey of AI-driven personal and collaborative productivity systems, focusing on intelligent task management, scheduling, meeting management, large language models (LLMs), AI agents, multi-agent systems, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Existing research is reviewed and classified according to the AI techniques employed, application areas, system capabilities, and limitations. The survey examines how these technologies support individual productivity as well as collaborative workflows involving tasks, calendars, meetings, communication, and shared knowledge. A comparative analysis is presented to identify the strengths and limitations of existing approaches. The study further highlights key research gaps, including fragmented productivity tools, limited contextual awareness and personalization, challenges in autonomous task execution and multi-agent coordination, and concerns related to privacy, security, reliability, and human oversight. Finally, emerging trends and future research directions are discussed toward developing more integrated, adaptive, trustworthy, and context-aware AI-driven productivity systems. This survey provides a structured understanding of the current research landscape and identifies opportunities for advancing intelligent productivity and task management systems. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Productivity Management, Task Management, Intelligent Scheduling, Large Language Models, AI Agents, Multi-Agent Systems, Human-AI Collaboration, Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

items.title: Retrospective analysis of nursing interventions using artificial intelligence multimodal emotion recognition for perioperative depression in head and neck tumors

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND Perioperative depression is prevalent among head and neck tumor patients, while traditional emotional assessment methods lag and fail to meet clinical nursing needs. AIM To investigate artificial intelligence (AI) multimodal emotion recognition's effects on enhancing individualized nursing care for depression patients during perioperative head and neck tumor surgeries, focusing on emotional fluctuations, nursing response efficiency, and postoperative recovery outcomes. METHODS Sixty patients with perioperative depression associated with head and neck tumors admitted to our hospital between January 2023 and December 2025 were selected and divided into two groups: The conventional care group (27 patients.) and the AI individualized care group (33 patients). We compared the baseline data, perioperative emotional indicators, postoperative outcomes, emotional recognition, and nursing responses between the two groups while simultaneously evaluating the recognition performance of the multimodal model. RESULTS There were no significant baseline differences between the groups. During observation, the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD) score, emotional score, Emotional Mood Index (EMI), and proportion of positive emotions showed dynamic changes with significant group-time interaction. The AI-individualized care group demonstrated lower HAMD and EMI scores, higher comprehensive emotional scores, and a greater proportion of positive emotions, postoperatively. Additionally, hospital stay length was reduced, complications decreased, and Physical Component Summary, Mental Component Summary, and Emotional Recovery Score improved significantly. The AI group outperformed the conventional nursing group in recognizing negative emotions, intervention matching, and emotional improvement within 24 hours. The time for initial recognition and nursing responses was much shorter. The area under the curve, sensitivity, and specificity of the multimodal fusion model were 0.894, 86.364%, and 83.871%, respectively, indicating its superiority over the single-modal model. CONCLUSION AI-informed individualized nursing can facilitate earlier identification of abnormal emotions in patients with head and neck tumors perioperatively, enhance nursing efficiency, and positively influence perioperative emotions and recovery.

items.abstract_text: Modern children are growing up in a digital world that offers immense potential, with many beginning to use technology from an early age. This digital environment presents countless opportunities for learning and development, but it also necessitates a balanced, thoughtful approach to raising children as informed, open-minded citizens. Industry 4.0, driven by artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and the Internet of Things (IoT), is reshaping how children think, learn, and interact with the world. The integration of AI into children's lives is a complex issue, bringing both significant benefits and notable risks. On the positive side, AI can power educational tools, interactive games, and personalized learning experiences, fostering cognitive development and creativity. However, it also introduces serious concerns, such as exposure to cyber threats, potential manipulation, privacy violations through data collection, and increased access to harmful content. This study explores the dual impact of information technologies on children's digital development. It examines the primary cybersecurity challenges children face and assesses how AI can both enhance and jeopardize their well-being. By analyzing these multifaceted dynamics, the research aims to offer recommendations for maximizing the advantages of the digital age while ensuring a safer and more supportive online environment for children.

items.venue: International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology
items.abstract_text: Having been studied for centuries, mathematical modelling is an important perspective in mathematics education; however, teachers often face difficulties in accessing appropriate and high-quality modelling activities for classroom use. This study investigates the capacity of ChatGPT and its customised version, the Mathematical Modelling Problem Generator (MMPG), to produce mathematically and pedagogically meaningful modelling problems. Four AI-generated model-eliciting activities were comparatively analysed: three produced in independent ChatGPT-4 sessions and one produced by MMPG, all focusing on ratios and proportions. The problem scenarios were evaluated using five characteristics from established frameworks, focusing on context (non-routine and real-life relevance) and complexity (multiple steps, uncertain solution paths, and multiple solutions). The results show that ChatGPT failed to produce MEAs that met key modelling characteristics, whereas MMPG successfully generated non-routine, multi-step MEAs with unclear solution paths and multiple valid solutions. Therefore, MMPG can be considered an effective tool for supporting pedagogical practice by improving teachers’ access to and design of content-aligned, high-quality modelling activities.

items.abstract_text: This research seeks to analyze the connection between perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being of employees through a quantitative correlational approach. The emergence of artificial intelligence in the working environment raises worries in regard to job security and the threat of unemployment. Thus, there may be a rise in employment worries and a decrease in employees' mental well-being. The methodology to collect data on employees levels of perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being is based on surveying them using conventional self-reported questionnaires. Descriptive statistics will be used to analyze the levels of these factors in terms of their means (M) and standard deviations (SD). The reliability analysis is going to be done for checking internal reliability of a research tool using Cronbach's alpha. To measure the relationships between these three variables, a Pearson product-moment correlation will be used. Additionally, a simple linear regression will be run in order to see if perceived threat from AI can predict unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being and if unemployment anxiety can predict psychological well-being. The measurement of psychological well-being is going to be based on the six dimensions introduced by Ryff: autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations with others, purpose in life, and self-acceptance. The results of this study will allow understanding how the way employees view AI being a threat to their jobs relates to worries about unemployment and psychological well-being. All in all, the results of this research can be helpful for realizing the significance of recognizing employees’ concerns in the course of technological changes and encourage businesses to provide adequate support to employees for mitigating job-related uncertainty and reaching psychological well-being.

analysis.discussion: The research investigated how perceived threat from artificial intelligence (AI) correlates with unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being of employees in the IT industry. The results showed that there is a positive correlation between perceived threat from AI and unemployment anxiety. It turns out that people who see the threat of losing their job to AI experience more anxiety about it. Moreover, the findings demonstrated that perceived threat from AI is negatively correlated with psychological well-being. Therefore, higher threat perception results in lower psychological well-being. On the other hand, the correlation analysis indicates that unemployment anxiety is not related to psychological well-being. Therefore, it can be concluded that perceived threat from AI is one of the main psychological issues of employees whose work The positive association of the perceived AI threat with anxiety over unemployment follows the ideas laid out in the STARA awareness model developed by Brougham and Haar (2018), where employees' worries related to intelligent technologies and AI in general can result in negative job- and wellness-related effects. As AI systems take over the tasks previously performed by people, workers may become more anxious about the prospects of their jobs and employment as a whole. The current discovery implies that those employees who believe there is a higher chance of AI replacing them are also more anxious about unemployment. This finding also coincides with the job insecurity theories, which describe job insecurity as the feeling of uncertainty regarding possible job loss (Greenhalgh & Rosenblatt, 1984; Sverke et al., 2002). Therefore, the idea of being replaced by AI can be an important factor influencing job insecurity even in those cases when an employee remains employed. The fact that there is a negative link between the perceived AI threats and psychological well- being highlights the idea that problems associated with technological efficacy affect the psychological state of workers. Brougham and Haar (2018) noted that having the relevant knowledge about STARA had an impact on career satisfaction and well-being parameters of employees. Ryff (1989) described psychological well-being as something that involves functionality in terms of having autonomy, personal development, mastery of the environment, goals in life, and positivity in relationships. The worries about the job replacement and prospects of getting a job in the future possibly decrease the perceived controllability, safety, and meaning of life of individuals. The negative links in this case can indicate that people experience psychological discomfort due to technological uncertainties. It is curious that anxiety over unemployment showed no statistically significant correlation with psychological well-being in the correlation analysis. This suggests that while employees’ perceptions of the threat of AI were linked with increased anxiety over unemployment as well as decreased psychological well-being, anxiety over unemployment itself did not correlate significantly with psychological well-being. The present pattern implies that the threat of AI may involve wider issues related to technological change, professional identity, skills and career prospects that may affect psychological well-being regardless of unemployment anxiety. Prior studies have argued that there is a difference between cognitive perceptions of job insecurity and emotional reaction to insecurity, thus suggesting that the two can lead to distinct psychological consequences (Jiang & Lavaysse, 2018). However, this interpretation should be treated with caution and needs further elaboration using advanced analytical techniques and proper measures In short, this research contributes to existing studies on AI-related employment issues, because it combines in a single investigation perceived threat of AI technology, anxiety regarding job loss and psychological well-being of IT specialists. The existing body of studies reveals the worries of employees in relation to the possibility of technological substitution and confirms the association of awareness of STARA with other aspects in the workplace and well-being (Brougham & Haar, 2018). The literature related to job insecurity points to the significance of perception of job insecurity by employees for their mental and professional functioning (Sverke et al., 2002). The current study undertakes the analysis of the relationship between perceived threat of AI and job loss anxiety and psychological well-being of the employees in Pakistan. The results of the current study show the significance of organizational actions aimed at creating conditions under which it is easier for employees to deal with their concerns about the future job The current study investigated the connection between the perception of AI threat, unemployment anxiety, and psychological well-being among IT workers. It has been found out that the perception of AI threat was positively connected with unemployment anxiety and negatively connected with psychological well-being, but the association between unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being was insignificant during the correlation analysis. This means that perceptions of employees about the AI-related employment threats may have an impact on psychological experiences and may be related to the issues concerning future employment and well-being of employees. It can be seen that the psychological experience of employees should be considered in addition to the advancement of technology. The organization may gain certain benefits through the creation of an opportunity for the development of skills, communication, and adaptation of employees to AI-related changes in work.
analysis.limitations: The current research presents several limitations which ought to be taken into consideration while interpreting the results. First of all, the cross-sectional correlational method is incapable of establishing causal conclusions concerning the relationship between perceived AI threat, unemployment anxiety, and psychological well-being. Although a significant relationship has been found, the question of whether the participants see AI as a threat to their job due to their unemployment anxiety or people are anxious about losing their jobs because they are low in psychological well-being cannot be answered. Secondly, the research utilized a convenience sample, which might limit the representativity of the sample and extent to which the results can be generalized across IT population. The sample consisted of 150 respondents whereby the majority were male aged between 20-40. Furthermore, it can be seen that the respondents belong to the private sector which makes the application of the results on employees from other sectors less feasible. Third, all variables were measured using self-report methods. Thus, answers could have been subject to respondents' interpretations of the questionnaire items and influenced by social desirability and various response tendencies. Apparently, application of the self-report measurement tool for all variables also creates the chance for prevalence of common method Fourth, the measurement of unemployment anxiety needs to be clarified in regards to its origins and construct validation. It is noted that the measure in the study includes seven questions and has good internal consistency, but its original authorship, psychometric properties, and precise assessment of unemployment anxiety should be confirmed. Furthermore, the psychological well- being measure must be defined to ensure the relevance of the measure used and obtained results. Finally, the study was limited by the specific occupational and national context. The employees of the IT sector can experience different exposure to AI technologies and concerns about employment as compared to workers in other fields. Therefore, the results may not be fully generalizable to other occupations and countries. Further research on the topic should focus on using longitudinal or multiple wave research designs in order to study how the constructs of perceived AI threat, employment anxiety, and psychological well-being may be influenced over time by the exposure of the workers to AI technologies in their work environment. Probability-based sampling method, where possible, and increased sample sizes from both public and private sector organizations should be employed in future studies on the topic. Increased gender, age, education, and experience heterogeneity of the samples studied would contribute to the generalizability of results obtained. Comparison of employees working in IT and non-IT professions could uncover whether the direct contact with AI technology results in specific psychological concerns for the employees. In future research, one might also look at other constructs like self-efficacy regarding AI, perceived organizational support, job insecurity, career adaptability, technological skills, and coping to determine the reasons for increased levels of psychological issues experienced by workers due to changes resulting from the use of AI in the workplace. Lastly, future research can be conducted on organizational interventions, including training related to AI, career development, supportive leadership, and open communication on AI. items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Steatotic liver disease (SLD) is highly prevalent, and noninvasive identification of patients with significant fibrosis remains a clinical challenge. Objective We conducted an exploratory evaluation of explainable machine learning models for predicting significant fibrosis in a US-based cohort of adults with SLD, with particular attention to sensitivity, false-negative risk, and the limitations of using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) alone to assess screening suitability. Methods We evaluated explainable machine learning models for predicting significant fibrosis in a US population–based dataset. A total of 43 routinely available clinical, demographic, anthropometric, laboratory, and lifestyle variables were included. After preprocessing and imputation, data were split into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets. The synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) was used to address class imbalance in the training set. Logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), k-nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, an artificial neural network, and a stacked ensemble were trained and evaluated. Performance metrics included accuracy, precision, recall, F 1 -score, Cohen κ, and the AUROC. Because the intended use case was screening or triage, sensitivity was given particular interpretive importance. In addition to overall discrimination, a primary analytical objective was to examine sensitivity trade-offs, false-negative classifications, and the implications of model performance for screening suitability. Global and local model interpretability were assessed using feature importance, Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values, individual conditional expectation (ICE) plots, and individualized explanations. Results Among 7056 participants, 716 (10.1%) had significant fibrosis. XGBoost achieved the highest discrimination (AUROC 0.79), followed by random forest (AUROC 0.78) and logistic regression (AUROC 0.77); however, XGBoost had low sensitivity (0.17), indicating limited utility for screening at the evaluated threshold. Logistic regression and naive Bayes demonstrated the highest sensitivity (0.65 and 0.55, respectively), suggesting that models with slightly lower discrimination may be more appropriate for triage-oriented use. Across models, waist circumference, BMI, cardiovascular comorbidity, sex, hemoglobin A 1c (HbA 1c ), and liver enzymes were the most influential predictors. Conclusions In this exploratory model development study, moderate discrimination did not necessarily translate into clinically meaningful screening performance. The model with the highest AUROC showed poor sensitivity, indicating a substantial risk of false-negative classifications and limiting its usefulness for screening in its current form. Because imputation was performed before the train-test split, the reported performance estimates may be optimistic and should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of clinical readiness. Leakage-free preprocessing, threshold optimization, calibration assessment, decision curve analysis, external validation, and prospective evaluation are needed before clinical application.

Accordingly, the purpose of the comparative analysis was not simply to identify the model with the highest AUROC but also to determine which models may be clinically unsuitable or potentially unsafe for screening because of the high number of false-negative classifications. Although ensemble methods such as XGBoost demonstrated higher overall discrimination, they were notably less effective at identifying individuals with significant fibrosis at the evaluated threshold than simpler probabilistic models, such as logistic regression and naive Bayes, which showed higher sensitivity. This finding should not be interpreted as support for using the model with the highest AUROC for screening; rather, it illustrates that models with favorable discrimination may still be unsuitable for triage if they miss a large proportion of true cases. This distinction is important because a model intended for screening or triage should prioritize the identification of true cases rather than rely on discrimination alone. Anthropometric measures related to central adiposity, specifically waist circumference and BMI, were the most influential predictors, showing a strong positive correlation with increased predicted risk. A total of 43 prespecified predictors were used, including age (years), sex (female), race, BMI (kg/m²), waist circumference (cm), hip circumference (cm), alanine aminotransferase (ALT; U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (AST; U/L), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT; U/L), alkaline phosphatase (ALP; U/L), albumin (g/dL), total bilirubin (mg/dL), total protein (g/dL), hemoglobin A 1c (HbA 1c ; %), fasting glucose (mg/dL), triglycerides (mg/dL), total cholesterol (mg/dL), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (mg/dL), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol (mg/dL), average systolic blood pressure (mm Hg), systolic blood pressure (first oscillometric), diastolic blood pressure (first oscillometric), alcohol consumption (g/day), Healthy Eating Index (HEI), smoking status, statin use, cardiovascular comorbidity, new diagnosis of hypertension, and hip-to-waist anthropometric measures. Missing data were addressed using single imputation to create a complete analytic dataset. In the original analytic workflow, imputation was performed before the data were divided into training and test subsets. We acknowledge that this approach may have introduced data leakage because information from the held-out test set could have influenced the imputed values used during model development. Consequently, the reported performance metrics may be optimistic and should be interpreted as exploratory rather than definitive estimates of out-of-sample performance. A leakage-free pipeline, in which imputation and any other learned preprocessing steps are fitted exclusively to the training data and subsequently applied to the held-out test set, is required for future validation and clinical translation. Within the training set, we applied the synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) to address class imbalance [ 20 ]. SMOTE generates synthetic minority class observations by interpolating between existing minority class samples in feature space. In this study, SMOTE was applied only to the training set after data partitioning; the held-out test set was not oversampled and retained the original class distribution. After SMOTE, the training data included 10,142 observations, with equal numbers of participants with and without significant fibrosis. However, the absence of sensitivity-focused threshold optimization limits conclusions about deployment-ready screening performance. Calibration analysis and decision curve analysis were not performed in the current exploratory analysis.
