The SHAP summary analysis showed that high values of waist circumference, BMI, and HbA 1c were strongly associated with positive impact on model output, indicating increased likelihood of significant fibrosis. Elevated levels of GGT and AST demonstrated a positive correlation with predicted risk. Female sex generally exerted a more negative influence on model output than male sex. Older age and higher alcohol consumption also contributed positively to the risk assessment. Other factors, such as cardiovascular comorbidity, smoking status, and lipid profiles, showed more moderate or individualized effects across the study population ( Figure 1 ). Local interpretability was assessed for 2 participants: one with fibrosis (ie, test index 30) and one without fibrosis (ie, test index 0). The model generated a predicted probability of 0.0220 for the individual with fibrosis and a predicted probability of 0.0891 for the individual without fibrosis. Patient-level model behavior was further examined using SHAP waterfall plots for the individual with fibrosis and the individual without fibrosis ( Multimedia Appendices 1 and 2 ). ICE analysis of the predicted probability of significant fibrosis across the 6 most influential features (ie, waist circumference, BMI, cardiovascular comorbidity, sex (female), HbA 1c , and hip circumference) showed that the average predicted probability remained low at lower values of waist circumference and BMI but demonstrated a marked increase as these values rose, particularly beyond the standardized mean. Similar patterns were observed for HbA 1c , where higher levels were associated with an elevated probability of fibrosis. Hip circumference exhibited a gradual positive relationship. Of note, cardiovascular comorbidity and female sex were associated with stable, stratified effects on predicted probability patterns across their respective categories ( Figure 2 ). SHAP dependence analysis demonstrated distinct nonlinear relationships for waist circumference and BMI. Both features exhibited a strong positive, nearly linear relationship with predicted risk. In addition, cardiovascular comorbidity exerted a positive impact on the model’s predictions across all observed values, with interactions often mediated by average systolic blood pressure. Moreover, female sex generally resulted in lower SHAP values, and the magnitude of this effect was influenced by waist circumference. Of note, HbA 1c displayed a steep increase in its contributions to predicted risk at lower concentrations, followed by a leveling off as values increased; this pattern often interacted with BMI. In contrast, hip circumference showed a more complex, U-shaped relationship with significant fibrosis, with its contribution to predicted risk influenced by age ( Figure 3 ).
analysis.discussion: In this exploratory, population-based model development study, machine learning models for predicting significant fibrosis demonstrated a clinically important trade-off between discrimination and sensitivity, although all performance estimates should be interpreted cautiously because imputation before the train-test split may have introduced data leakage. Accordingly, the purpose of the comparative analysis was not simply to identify the model with the highest AUROC but also to determine which models may be clinically unsuitable or potentially unsafe for screening because of the high number of false-negative classifications. Although ensemble methods such as XGBoost demonstrated higher overall discrimination, they were notably less effective at identifying individuals with significant fibrosis at the evaluated threshold than simpler probabilistic models, such as logistic regression and naive Bayes, which showed higher sensitivity. This finding should not be interpreted as support for using the model with the highest AUROC for screening; rather, it illustrates that models with favorable discrimination may still be unsuitable for triage if they miss a large proportion of true cases. This distinction is important because a model intended for screening or triage should prioritize the identification of true cases rather than rely on discrimination alone. Anthropometric measures related to central adiposity, specifically waist circumference and BMI, were the most influential predictors, showing a strong positive correlation with increased predicted risk. Interpretability analyses further showed that metabolic indicators, liver enzymes, cardiovascular comorbidities, and lifestyle factors, such as alcohol consumption, also contributed meaningfully to model predictions. These explainability analyses should be interpreted as an application of established methods for examining model behavior and error patterns rather than as a methodological advance in XAI. These findings highlight the multifactorial clinical risk profile underlying advanced liver stiffness. Furthermore, the findings should be interpreted in light of the study’s internal validity limitations, particularly the risk of data leakage introduced by performing imputation before the train-test split, which may have inflated discrimination and classification metrics [ 22 ]. The principal finding was a clear trade-off between discrimination and sensitivity across algorithms. These results highlight the importance of selecting both model families and operating points that align with clinical priorities, particularly in a screening or triage context, where missed disease may delay further evaluation. In such settings, a model with a modestly lower AUROC but higher sensitivity may be more clinically appropriate than a model with superior discrimination but a substantial false-negative burden. The performance profile observed across models likely reflects the characteristics of the underlying predictive signals in SLD. Anthropometric and metabolic predictors consistently dominated global importance rankings and SHAP summaries, reinforcing the central role of adiposity and glycemic dysregulation in fibrosis risk [ 23 - 26 ]. From an implementation perspective, the contrast between high-AUROC, low-sensitivity models and simpler, more sensitive alternatives is clinically relevant. In many care pathways, initial risk assessment must favor sensitivity to avoid false reassurance, with subsequent specialized testing (eg, VCTE) reserved for individuals most likely to benefit. This concern was reinforced by the local SHAP example of a false-negative prediction, in which a participant with confirmed fibrosis was assigned a predicted probability of only 2.2%, illustrating how an apparently interpretable model may still generate clinically misleading reassurance at the individual level. In our analysis, logistic regression and naive Bayes identified more fibrosis cases than complex ensembles. Although these models had higher false-positive rates, such trade-offs may be acceptable in stepped triage strategies, particularly when downstream tests are noninvasive, and the baseline disease prevalence is modest. The use of SMOTE-balanced training data may also have influenced precision-recall behavior when models were evaluated on the naturally imbalanced test set, contributing to lower PPV and higher false-positive counts in models with greater sensitivity. Explainability may add value by illuminating model behavior, identifying influential predictors, and exposing error patterns. However, explainability does not, by itself, establish reliability or clinical usefulness. The local explanation showing that a participant with confirmed fibrosis received a very low predicted probability illustrates that interpretable outputs may still be clinically misleading when probability estimates are poorly calibrated or when minority class cases are missed [ 27 ]. The clinical implications are pragmatic. In health care systems seeking to expand noninvasive fibrosis detection, a sensitive, explainable model could serve as a front-end screening tool to prioritize elastography, specialist referral, and targeted lifestyle or metabolic interventions [ 28 - 31 ]. Although the framework suggests potential utility for noninvasive fibrosis risk stratification, its current performance and methodological limitations preclude clinical deployment at this stage. Any implementation-oriented interpretation should await reanalysis using a leakage-free pipeline, sensitivity-focused threshold optimization, probability calibration, decision curve analysis, and external validation. We specifically note the importance of validating and adapting models across geographies and health care settings, where population risk profiles, measurement pathways, and access constraints differ. Embedding explainability throughout the workflow can help ensure transparency, support clinician trust, and identify context-specific biases at an early stage. This study has several limitations. The most important limitation is that missing data imputation was performed on the full dataset before the train-test split. This creates a risk of data leakage because information from the held-out test set may have influenced the imputation process used during model development. Consequently, the reported discrimination and classification metrics may be optimistic, and comparisons across models should be interpreted cautiously. This limitation weakens internal validity and means that the results should be viewed as exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Future work must use a leakage-free pipeline in which imputation, scaling, encoding, and other learned preprocessing steps are fitted exclusively to the training data and then applied to the held-out test set. items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND High rates of psychological distress among university students, together with persistently low use of professional mental health services, have become a notable public health issue. AIM To examine how help-seeking attitudes, stigma and individual psychological characteristics jointly shape university students’ preferences for different counseling formats. METHODS A cross-sectional survey was conducted which included 313 university students. Latent profile analysis was applied to identify distinct subgroups based on help-seeking attitudes and perceived stigma. Differences in psychological symptoms and preferences for artificial intelligence (AI) counseling were then compared across these subgroups. RESULTS The following three subgroups were identified: “Low willingness-high stigma” (36.4%), “moderate willingness-moderate stigma” (43.8%), and “high willingness-low stigma” (19.8%). Interestingly, the “low willingness-high stigma” group showed the most severe depression and anxiety symptoms, and reported the highest prior use of AI-based support and the strongest preference for AI counseling. CONCLUSION AI and human counselors play complementary roles: AI offers advantages in accessibility and anonymity, while human counselors remain irreplaceable in terms of empathy, complex problem-solving, and long-term therapeutic relationships.

items.venue: Interdisciplinary Journal of Research and Development

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into modern justice systems, influencing decision-making in criminal justice, hiring, surveillance, healthcare, and public administration. Although AI promises efficiency and consistency, a growing body of research documents risks of algorithmic bias and unequal performance across demographic groups. This paper examines the relationship between artificial intelligence, gender bias, and human rights within contemporary justice systems through a qualitative, interdisciplinary analysis combining a narrative review of scholarly literature with doctrinal analysis of relevant international and European legal and ethical frameworks. It considers how biased datasets, discriminatory or uneven algorithmic outcomes, and unequal technological representation may affect fairness, equality, privacy, due process, and access to justice. Particular attention is given to documented evidence on facial-analysis systems and automated recruitment, while broader claims concerning institutional legitimacy and human-centered justice are treated as normative implications rather than empirical findings. The paper also evaluates regulatory responses, including Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU Artificial Intelligence Act) and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. It concludes by identifying transparency, accountability, representative data, independent evaluation, and meaningful human oversight as central safeguards for rights-respecting AI governance. items.title: The boundaries of copyright law in regulating AI-generated content: lessons from the UK

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Intellectual Property Law & Practice
items.abstract_text: Abstract Section 9(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 attributes authorship of a computer-generated work to the person who undertakes the arrangements necessary for its creation. The rapid development of generative AI has renewed attention to this provision, yet its legal function remains uncertain. In particular, its relationship with the originality requirement is unresolved, and it is unclear whether section 9(3) should be understood as an authorship rule or as a mechanism for protecting investment in authorless outputs. This article reassesses section 9(3) through doctrinal and comparative analysis. It argues that AI-assisted works involving sufficient human creative contribution can be accommodated within the existing framework of human authorship and originality. Comparative experience from China and the United States supports this conclusion. The potential independent role of section 9(3) should therefore be confined to the genuinely authorless AI-generated outputs. Protection of such outputs, however, cannot be justified merely because copyright is unavailable. The article argues that the future of section 9(3) should depend on whether it continues to serve a distinct and defensible social or economic function. Until the legal position is clarified or changed, courts should first apply general copyright principles and avoid assuming that section 9(3) automatically displaces the originality requirement. If special protection for authorless outputs is retained in the future, its scope and duration should be designed in accordance with the specific policy objectives that such protection is intended to serve.

items.abstract_text: In spite of the fact that there is widespread agreement regarding the ethical principles that need to guide artificial intelligence, there is still a significant gap between these normative objectives and the operational realities of technical implementation. An investigation into how to operationalize a proactive, iterative AI governance paradigm is the focus of this study. The investigation is conducted via the prism of private law liabilities and constant technical verification. Both corporate compliance theater and opportunistic ethics shopping are the driving forces behind our inquiry. Both of these shortcomings in practice have occurred repeatedly. During the course of the study, a multi-layered methodological framework is utilized. This framework triangulates a comparative assessment of growing international regulatory frameworks and a "cross-sectoral typological mapping of auditing procedures from banking, data privacy, and environmental law." The findings reveal a systemic disconnect: corporate ethical commitments continue to be largely detached from operational audit systems, leaving data scientists frustrated by guidelines that are too abstract to act on. Furthermore, existing environmental, social, and governance standards do not provide any AI-specific tools for quantifying the hidden socio-technical harms that are embedded in global supply chains. rules that are abstract, whereas the existing ESG standards do not provide the AI-specific guidance that is required to assess the hidden socio-technical damages that are present throughout global supply chains.The purpose of this article is to offer a solution to this problem by advocating for the transition from voluntary soft law to an enforceable, longitudinal regulatory framework. We propose that corporate governance frameworks be merged with automated auditing pipelines, value-based engineering (also known as ethics-by-design), and independent third-party oversight. This would result in the transformation of abstract ethical concepts into private law duties that can be verified.

items.title: Higher education at the core of research on generative artificial intelligence referring to Ecuador: a systematic mapping review (2024–2026)

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can transform teaching, learning, assessment and research in higher education. In Ecuador, the adoption of ChatGPT, Gemini and other language models is driving academic interest, yet little is known about the scientific production that addresses it. This systematic mapping review, reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, maps the scientific production on generative artificial intelligence that explicitly refers to Ecuador, indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection between 2024 and 2026, in order to establish the weight that higher education holds within it. No disciplinary filter was applied to the query, so that this weight could be measured rather than assumed. The search, executed on 4 July 2026, retrieved 57 records (all 16 Web of Science records were also in Scopus, so the corpus comes in practice from Scopus; regional databases were not searched); after removing 16 duplicates and excluding 9 records, 32 documents were mapped with bibliometric indicators (Bibliometrix, VOSviewer), and the 18 higher education studies with primary data were subjected to a focused synthesis that included the appraisal of their methodological quality with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Higher education accounts for 20 of the 32 documents (63%); the other 12 are spread over political communication and journalism, legal and technical applications and four smaller domains. A sensitivity search with synonyms, Spanish terms and the year 2023, run on 15 October 2026, gave a similar share (44 of 73 documents, 60%). Within the higher education corpus, perceptions and acceptance of GAI are the most frequent outcome domain (16 of 18 studies); learning outcomes appear in six, but only two measure them directly. Eight studies use descriptive or cross-sectional designs, and none is randomised or longitudinal. ChatGPT is the most frequently examined tool (11 of 18). Sample representativeness and control of confounding were the most frequent methodological weaknesses. The findings highlight the need for experimental and longitudinal research evaluating the impact of GAI on Ecuadorian higher education.

To ensure methodological transparency and reproducibility in the document selection process, the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines were adopted. This review was designed and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement ( Page et al., 2021 ), which governs the identification, screening, eligibility and inclusion of records, and whose completed checklist is provided as Supplementary Table 2 . As a systematic mapping review, the study charts the extent, distribution and thematic composition of a defined body of literature; PRISMA 2020 is applied throughout, with the adaptations for mapping and scoping designs noted where relevant. Although critical appraisal is not a constitutive component of mapping reviews ( Grant and Booth, 2009 ; Munn et al., 2018 ), the methodological quality of the studies included in the focused synthesis was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), version 2018 ( Hong et al., 2018 ), because that corpus combines qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods designs that a single design-specific tool could not cover. The procedure is described in Section 3.6 and the results are reported in Section 4.7 . In addition, the methodological recommendations for conducting bibliometric analyses in the social sciences and education were followed, particularly those concerning the identification of research trends, intellectual structures, and patterns of scientific collaboration ( Aria and Cuccurullo, 2017 ). The review question was specified using the PICOS framework (population, intervention, comparators, outcomes and study designs), as required for systematic and mapping reviews. Because a mapping review charts the extent and thematic composition of a body of literature rather than estimating the effect of an intervention, the framework is applied here in its descriptive form: the intervention component is understood as the phenomenon of interest addressed by the included studies, and no comparator was required for eligibility. The review was organised in two sequential stages that share the same search strategy and information sources and differ only in the population to which they apply. Stage 1 mapped the whole body of peer-reviewed literature on GAI that explicitly refers to Ecuador, irrespective of the sector addressed. Applying no disciplinary restriction at this stage was deliberate: it allows the share of that output concentrated in higher education to be established empirically rather than assumed a priori , and it retains the adjacent domains — digital governance, political communication, business innovation and industrial applications — as the comparative background against which that concentration is measured. Stage 2 took the subset of documents addressing Ecuadorian higher education and subjected it to a focused synthesis, comprising the extraction of study characteristics and the appraisal of their methodological quality. The three research questions map onto this structure. RQ1 and RQ2, which concern the weight of higher education within the production on GAI that refers to Ecuador and the distribution of that production across authors, institutions and sources, are answered at Stage 1. RQ3, which concerns thematic areas, emerging trends and research gaps, draws on both stages: the thematic structure of the field at Stage 1, and the substantive findings and methodological profile of the higher education corpus at Stage 2. Records were eligible for Stage 1 if they met all of the following: indexed in Scopus (Elsevier) or the Web of Science Core Collection (Clarivate Analytics); published within the 2024–2026 window; containing the exact expression “generative artificial intelligence” in title, abstract or keywords; containing the terms “ecuador” or “ecuadorian” in the same fields; and constituting peer-reviewed output, namely journal articles, review articles, or full conference papers published in indexed proceedings or in book series such as Communications in Computer and Information Science, Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems and Lecture Notes in Educational Technology. analysis.discussion: The results show a small and recent body of research on generative artificial intelligence (GAI) that refers to Ecuador: 32 documents published between 2024 and July 2026. Recent bibliometric studies document a rapid growth of international research on GAI in higher education ( Ng and Ho, 2025 ; Xu and Thien, 2025 ). The production identified here has a limited scale and is concentrated in higher education. One of the most relevant findings is that higher education is the main object of the indexed research on GAI that refers to Ecuador. Because universities produce most indexed research in any field, this does not by itself show that adoption is more advanced in universities than in other sectors. The share was not compared with a baseline, such as the distribution of all indexed research on Ecuador across fields, so it shows where this research concentrates, not that higher education is over-represented relative to its weight in national research output. Rivadeneira et al. (2025) report that higher education institutions in Latin America have become scenarios for the adoption and evaluation of tools such as ChatGPT, with notable differences between countries in institutional policies, teacher training and levels of technological integration. The centrality of this theme is consistent with the approaches of Kasneci et al. (2023) , UNESCO (2023) and Chiu (2024) , who argue that GAI has the potential to significantly transform educational processes through the personalization of learning, the automation of academic tasks, and the strengthening of digital skills. Likewise, recent research carried out with teacher training students shows a growing interest in understanding the perceptions, opportunities, and challenges associated with the use of artificial intelligence in foreign language teaching and learning contexts ( Castillo-Cuesta et al., 2025 ). But in addition, there is evidence of a positive association between the adoption of GAI and business innovation ( Naranjo Vaca et al., 2025 ), while other researchers highlight its potential to strengthen entrepreneurship and complex thinking capacities ( George-Reyes et al., 2024 ). Outside higher education, the documents address political communication and journalism, legal, industrial and technical applications and, with one document each, digital governance, business innovation, digital communication and military professional education ( Table 7 ). Similarly, research is beginning to emerge in areas of specialized training that evaluates the potential of tools such as ChatGPT to support the learning of technical and professional skills in simulated teaching environments ( Briones-Zamora et al., 2026 ). Within the higher education corpus, most studies report favourable perceptions of generative AI (Section 4.6 ). The methodological profile reported in Section 4.6 and the appraisal reported in Section 4.7 nevertheless indicate that, within the higher education corpus, these favourable results rest mostly on self-reported perceptions gathered from non-representative samples, and that more robust designs are needed to assess these educational effects accurately ( Chiu, 2024 ). Beyond the corpus, the wider literature indicates that adopting GAI depends on technological infrastructure, the quality of connectivity, access to digital resources and the technological skills of the teaching staff. These constraints are long-standing problems of Latin American higher education systems, and where institutions do not put training and universal access strategies in place, the benefits of GAI end up unevenly distributed across institutions and user groups ( López-Vasco et al., 2025 ; Vasquez Blanco, 2026 ). According to Buele et al. (2025) , there are recent studies carried out with Ecuadorian university students that also highlight the importance of promoting principles of ethical and responsible use of generative artificial intelligence within academic environments, in addition to other studies that warn of risks associated with the protection of personal data, algorithmic discrimination, the spread of disinformation through automatically generated content, and the technological infrastructure limitations that still persist in different contexts of the country ( Farías, 2025 ; Meza et al., 2025 ; Montece Giler et al., 2023 ; Suing, 2025 ). Although interest in GAI has grown rapidly, important research gaps remain. The domain distribution reported in Section 4.6 shows that personalised learning is addressed by a single study, and that learning outcomes, although present in six studies, are measured directly in only two. Institutional governance appears in six studies, but always through participants' perceptions or the reported absence of policies rather than through the analysis of institutional policies themselves. Only a small proportion of studies explores adaptive learning environments, intelligent tutoring systems, or data-driven approaches for supporting personalized instruction (e.g., Ordoñez-Calero et al., 2026 ). Future research should prioritize rigorous empirical evaluation, interdisciplinary collaboration, responsible AI governance, faculty capacity building, and pedagogical models that support the sustainable integration of GAI into higher education ( Table 8 ). The findings describe a small and recent output on GAI that refers to Ecuador, spread across several domains. International projections likewise suggest that research on GAI will move towards greater thematic specialization and interdisciplinary integration ( Chiu, 2024 ). International co-authorship is limited to eight of the 32 documents (Section 4.1 ), and no author contributed more than two documents, so the corpus does not reveal stable collaboration networks. This scenario suggests the value of national and international academic alliances that favor the generation of specialized knowledge and the development of interdisciplinary projects of greater scope. Recent bibliometric studies have shown that scientific collaboration is one of the main factors associated with increased productivity, international visibility, and the impact of research in emerging technological fields ( Donthu et al., 2021 ; Ng and Ho, 2025 ). Overall, the dispersion of authorship and the small size of the corpus suggest that research on GAI referring to Ecuador is still at an early stage. Inter-institutional collaboration networks, specialized training programs and scientific policies aimed at promoting responsible innovation could help to consolidate it, so that higher education institutions not only adopt technologies developed in other contexts but also contribute knowledge, methodolo
analysis.limitations: This study has several limitations. It draws exclusively on Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection, which may have left out relevant publications. The corpus is also small, 32 documents, and very recent, since most works were published from 2024 onward and have accumulated few citations; citation-based mapping techniques such as co-citation and bibliographic coupling, together with long-term trend analyses, could not be applied reliably and were deliberately excluded. The search, restricted to the exact expression “generative artificial intelligence” combined with terms identifying the country, may also have missed records that refer only to particular tools or models. The national scope was operationalized through the mention of the country in the indexed fields rather than through author affiliation, so the corpus may omit work by Ecuadorian authors that does not name Ecuador and may include contributions authored outside the country that address the Ecuadorian context. The findings should therefore be read as describing research that explicitly refers to Ecuador, not the totality of nationally affiliated production. The full-counting approach used for institutional productivity may over-represent documents with multiple affiliations. The main search used English terms only, so records whose indexed fields are in another language were not retrieved; the sensitivity search added Spanish terms but not regional databases such as SciELO, Redalyc or Latindex. In practice the corpus comes from Scopus, since Web of Science added no unique records. The review was not registered and no protocol was published, and the primary-data criterion for Stage 2 was agreed after the Stage 1 search had been run. Screening and classification were decided by consensus, without independent double screening, and classification, extraction and appraisal were carried out by the same team without a prior calibration exercise. A further limitation concerns extraction and appraisal. The MMAT ratings reflect what the primary studies report, so a criterion rated can't tell may reflect incomplete reporting rather than a flawed procedure, and the classification of each study into an MMAT category involves judgement. For three conference chapters the full text could not be accessed, so their extraction relies on the abstract and the publisher's record, and none of them was appraised. Claims about the effectiveness of generative AI in Ecuadorian higher education should therefore be read in light of the quality profile reported in Section 4.7 rather than as validated by this review. Finally, the corpus reflects the search of 4 July 2026 and was not updated. When the query was repeated on 15 October 2026 it returned 11 new records from 2026, and eight corpus documents were no longer retrieved because the query no longer matched their indexed terms (Section 4.1 ); the expanded sensitivity search run on that date gave a similar share for higher education, but the counts reported here will change as the field grows. Future research could deepen the analysis of scientific collaboration networks, the impact of GAI on university learning processes and its applications in the other domains identified in Table 7 .

source_review.thesis: In Colorado classrooms, the choice of when to introduce AI shapes which parts of writing students still practice themselves.
source_review.reasoning: A finished essay can look equally polished after two very different kinds of work. One student may have interpreted a text and asked for feedback. Another may have handed the interpretation to a chatbot. Teachers describe changing where students write and what questions they answer to make those differences visible.
source_review.examples: Marissa Donjuan asked AI to compare an essay she had written with her teacher’s comments and rubric. At the University of Denver, Josh Wilson moved extended writing into class so he could see students develop their arguments.
source_review.tension: Wilson says that supervising writing across several class meetings costs time he could spend teaching political science.
source_review.implications: A teacher deciding where AI belongs can start with the particular skill students need to demonstrate. A revision exercise and an exercise in forming an original argument call for different decisions.
source_review.open_question: Which steps of a writing assignment does the instructor need to see to judge a student’s reasoning?
source_review.qualification: These classroom accounts establish what participants tried. Their effects on learning and attention remain unmeasured.

items.title: Co-Creating Value with Generative AI in Later Life: A Qualitative Diary Study of Older Adults’ Everyday Appropriation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents both opportunities and challenges for later life, with its benefits depending on how older adults appropriate, evaluate, and regulate its use rather than on technical capability alone. Existing research has focused primarily on technology acceptance, offering limited insight into how GenAI becomes valuable after adoption. Drawing on a socio-technical appropriation perspective, this study conducted a 14-day qualitative diary study with 16 community-dwelling older adults to examine everyday GenAI use. Thematic analysis identified four interconnected forms of appropriation: functional, creative, and relational appropriation, which co-created functional, experiential, and relational value; and critical appropriation, which regulated these forms of value while preserving human agency. We propose the GenAI Appropriation and Value Co-creation Framework (GAVC), explaining how older adults transform GenAI into a capability-expanding resource that supports later-life well-being. The framework advances appropriation theory and informs GenAI system design and literacy initiatives that foster active, productive aging.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The CIViC (Clinical Interpretations of Variants in Cancer) knowledgebase (https://civicdb.org) remains one of the few free, unrestricted knowledgebases for the distribution of somatic cancer variant interpretations. CIViC leverages public curation and expert moderation to address the bottleneck problem of cancer variant interpretation for patient care. As the curation platform for ClinGen Somatic Cancer, the CIViC knowledge model is informed by multiple experts across disparate fields in cancer and, in turn, acts as a model for cancer variant classification and representation. In order to capture a wider range of genomic variations, several updates to CIViC’s data and curation model have been made with a focus on maintaining familiar workflows and user interface layouts. A new top-level entity called the Feature represents Genes, Fusions, Regions for large-scale structural variations, and Factors for genome-wide biomarkers. Accompanying Variants capture information unique to each genomic event. Molecular Profiles enable the curation of complex combinations of these Variants. CIViC has also developed a system for approval and submission of Assertions to ClinVar, guidance for the use of AI in curation and moderation of content, and additional capabilities such as source retraction monitoring and an advanced query builder.

analysis.discussion: A landscape of variant knowledgebases currently exists, each with different strengths and specializations [ 44 ] , including resources like OncoKB [ 45 ] , GENOMENON's Cancer Knowledge Base (CKB) ( https://ckb.genomenon.com/ ), Personalized Cancer Therapy (PCT) knowledge base [ 46 ] , Molecular Oncology Almanac [ 47 ] , COSMIC [ 48 ] , and the Mitelman Database [ 49 ] for highly complex structural variation. As many of the valuable and highly used community resources have turned to more restrictive licensing models, limiting both access and community consensus ( Supplementary Table S4 ), we have argued that free and open community-curated resources for variant interpretation are a more optimal way to approach the bottleneck problem that arises from the use of next-generation sequencing in clinical cancer care [ 50 ] . The CIViC resource, in collaboration with ClinGen Somatic, has been fortunate to be able to adhere to the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable). Unique amongst somatic cancer resources, this has resulted in one of the largest and growing publicly available sets of humancurated variant interpretations in cancer. Following a unique structured data model, which ties to established guidelines in the field whenever possible [ 31 , 32 , 51 ] ( Supplementary Figs S21 and S22 ), CIViC leverages human curation to convert rel- evant publications into structured, clinically relevant data. Future plans include the incorporation of emerging guidelines [ 52 ] , including those being developed by SC-VCEPs. Since its inception, being "computationally accessible" has been a founding principle of CIViC [ 12 ] . Through the support of structured data elements tied to ontologies and clinical guidelines, CIViC has enabled the mapping of clinically relevant genomic data to publications. Initially demonstrated in 2019 by advances in natural language processing to produce CIViCmine [ 27 ] , we continue to expand on the utility of structured data, machine learning, and human interpretation to improve the availability and reliability of cancer variant interpretations. LLMs have emerged as a potentially useful tool for assisting variant curators in preparing variant interpretations, identifying curation candidates, identifying errors, and extracting knowledge from the literature. This is reflected by a marked acceleration of the use of LLMs in scientific writing between 2023 and 2024 [ 53 ] . LLMs can also assist researchers and clinicians in preparing clinical reports and aggregating variant knowledge. To that end, in addition to providing our own MCP server, CIViC has been included as a "featured connection" in Claude Science ( https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/ connectors-and-skills#featured-connectors ) positioning it as an important part of this ecosystem. While the use of these tools can help directly address the curation bottleneck issue and has proven to be useful in carefully targeted and trained environments, they have not been proven to replace human intervention. Human curated content remains crucial for the field of cancer variant interpretation. LLMs can, at times, provide incomplete or erroneous information (hallucination), or misunderstand the task being asked of them. They may sometimes fail with rare or harder-to-classify variants [ 54 ] , and fully relying on these models can result in a loss of skills among highly trained biomedical knowledge workers (de-skilling) [ 55 ] . Furthermore, future improvements of LLM models may rely on additional human curated content for training, finetuning, or validating [ 56 ] . Developing future data models and standards for variant interpretation is also best guided by human experts such as ClinGen SC-VCEPs. Together, these considerations have guided CIViC's focus on remaining human-curated while integrating AI-and LLM-assisted tools within a human-in-the-loop framework, in which AI can support tasks such as information retrieval, literature prioritization, and identification of potential curation issues, while curators retain responsibility for evaluating evidence and making final curation and moderation decisions (Fig. 3 ). The CIViC data and curation models have evolved over the decade since the first public release. The data model began with curated Evidence Items based on Gene-associated Variants. Assertions, which summarize collections of Evidence Items, were introduced to address emerging guidelines (e.g. AMP/ASCO/CAP for clinical significance [ 31 ] and Clin- Gen/CGC/VICC for oncogenicity [ 32 ] ) ( Supplementary Figs S21 and S22 ). The implementation of a GraphQL API was crucial to support this greater level of complexity. The re- build of the CIViC data model to include Features (Genes, Fusions, Factors, and Regions), along with Molecular Pro- files consisting of multiple Feature Variant pairs, uniquely equips CIViC with the ability to capture a large range of clin- ically impactful genomic variation in a highly structured way ( Supplementary Figs S23 and S24 ). In order to keep pace with the state of the field, CIViC has been under continuous development since its inception and there are already many additional features planned to support our community. Maintaining clinical relevance requires distinguishing the historical evidence captured by individual Evidence Items from the evolving interpretation of that evidence summarized in Assertions; publication age alone does not establish that a finding is outdated. CIViC's community model currently enables users to Flag items of concern, and propose revisions for editorial review. To complement this mechanism, we are developing a "Withdrawn" status that can be applied to Evidence Items and Assertions that accurately reflect their underlying Sources but whose interpretation or clinical relevance has changed because of subsequent evidence, retracted Sources, regulatory decisions, or updated guidelines. For example, the withdrawal of the previously FDA-approved tazemetostat for EZH2-mutant follicular lymphoma prompted revisions to the corresponding CIViC Assertions and demonstrates the need to capture such changes in a structured and consistent manner. This new status is intended to preserve the historical record while making altered relevance easily identifiable dur-ing both website and programmatic uses of the data. Additionally, applying a "Withdrawn" status to an Evidence Item or Assertion will automatically put any existing organizational approvals in an "under review" state. This will require Approvers to re-evaluate the Assertion before either reissuing or revoking the Approval. For Assertions written by Clin-Gen groups, review of existing content is part of the overall curation process and a plan for recuration must be established during step 4 of SC-VCEP approval. AI review of content will also likely play a future role in maintaining a growing knowledgebase of curation, and identifying Assertions for review. Automated ClinVar submissions are subject to a few limitations at present. Namely, ClinVar is actively working on representing fusion variants in their data model but while this development is ongoing, submissions are currently limited to only gene variants. Moreover, the current submission process does not support Complex Molecular Profiles or oncogenic assertions, both of which are active areas of development and we expect will be supported soon. items.title: AI Marketing Transparency and Brand Trust: How AI Literacy and Perceived Manipulative Intent Shape Consumer Responses in Pakistan

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: With AI’s increasing role in digital marketing, a brand’s transparency about its use of AI could act as an informational signal of accountability. However, the interpretation consumers make of such transparency might vary with their knowledge of AI and their perception of persuasive intent. This study examines the relationship between perceived AI marketing transparency, brand trust, and purchase intention and the role of perceived manipulative intent as a mechanism and AI literacy as a boundary condition. We surveyed 387 matched Pakistani consumers, in two waves. AI literacy was operationalised with the core 18-item AI literacy dimensions of the MAILS instrument (use and apply AI, know and understand AI, detect AI, and AI ethics), whereas the remaining MAILS dimensions were treated as separate constructs. We tested the hypotheses using regression-based simple mediation (PROCESS Model 4) and first-stage moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 7). Perceived AI marketing transparency was positively associated with brand trust (β = 0.24, p < 0.001). Brand trust carried a significant indirect association between perceived AI marketing transparency and purchase intention (indirect effect = 0.06, 95% CI [0.02, 0.11]); the direct association was not statistically significant (c′ = 0.10, p = 0.081). Perceived manipulative intent was negatively associated with brand trust (b = −0.25, p < 0.001). AI literacy positively moderated the association between perceived AI marketing transparency and perceived manipulative intent (B = 0.13, p = 0.031), such that this association was positive and significant only at high AI literacy (B = 0.25, p < 0.001). The conditional indirect association was statistically distinguishable from zero only at high AI literacy (effect = −0.06, 95% CI [−0.13, −0.01]). The index of moderated mediation was statistically significant at the 5% level (index = −0.03, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.001]) but the CI was close to the null value. The results are consistent with both theoretically opposite mechanisms suggested: an accountability-related association between perceived transparency and brand trust, and a conditional suspicion-related indirect association via perceived manipulative intent, which were analysed under the umbrella of two different empirical models. The interaction was small and the moderated-mediation evidence was statistically weak and should be considered a preliminary rather than a general finding of the negative effects on transparency. One of the contributions of the study is distinguishing perceived transparency from its interpretation, and examining core AI literacy competencies in addition to a focused measure of persuasion knowledge activation in the context of AI marketing and signaling research. Finally, practical implications highlight the importance of AI disclosure being credible and context-specific, not necessarily a strategy that builds trust.

items.title: Balancing Innovation and Compliance: The Impact of the EU AI Act on AI-Driven Cybersecurity Solutions in Healthcare
items.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on AI Research.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The focus of the study is on the impact of the EU AI Act on AI-based cybersecurity solutions in healthcare. Adopting AI in healthcare cybersecurity is expected to enhance threat identification, bolster operational stability, and safeguard against increasingly complex cyber threats. The European Union's AI Act mandates new regulatory requirements for AI systems utilised in high-risk settings, particularly in healthcare. This study investigates the EU AI Act's influence on the creation and implementation of AI-driven cybersecurity solutions, focusing on representative AI-based cybersecurity solutions used in healthcare environments. Qualitative research methods were employed via a literature review and policy analysis of the EU AI Act, healthcare cybersecurity regulations, and global AI governance systems. The research contrasts the EU's AI regulation with the NIST AI risk management framework and the OECD AI principles and evaluates how AI-enabled cybersecurity functions align with key regulatory criteria such as risk assessment, disclosure, human supervision, and system stability. The findings indicate that AI-driven cybersecurity tools can assist in regulatory adherence and enhance healthcare stability, contingent upon organisations establishing robust governance frameworks, detailed practices, and human supervision mechanisms. Additional actions are required to achieve full alignment with the new transparency and accountability mandates, though existing systems demonstrate robust support for operational security and decision-making. The investigation finds that the EU AI regulation should be considered not just as a requirement to comply with but also as a chance to enhance the reliability, transparency, and enduring viability of AI-driven healthcare security systems.

items.title: What Is the “Human” in Human-Centered AI? Restoring the Aesthetic Subject
items.venue: London Journal of Research In Humanities and Social Sciences

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Human-centered artificial intelligence (HCAI) seeks to orient AI toward human values, autonomy, oversight, safety, and meaningful control. Yet the term “human-centered” leaves a prior question unresolved: what conception of the human is being centered? Much HCAI discourse approaches the human as user, decision-maker, rights-holder, stakeholder, or bearer of preferences and values. These conceptions are indispensable but incomplete. This article argues that HCAI must also recognize the human as an aesthetic subject: a being whose perception, attention, imagination, interpretation, and judgment are formed through experience. As recommendation, personalization, generative AI, and predictive systems increasingly organize the conditions under which people encounter and evaluate the world, AI can participate in forming rather than merely serving human preferences. The article develops the concept of aesthetic agency to describe the human capacity to participate meaningfully in the formation of one’s perceptual, imaginative, interpretive, and evaluative relation to the world. It distinguishes choice from judgment, preference from taste, generation from imagination, and optimization from experience. On this basis, it proposes an aesthetically expanded HCAI organized around openness, plurality, reflectivity, and transformability. To center the human is not only to preserve control over AI, but to preserve the capacity to perceive, imagine, judge, and become otherwise.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering
items.abstract_text: Peer code review is widely used in programming and software engineering education, but its instructional value depends on the quality of student feedback rather than review completion alone. In large classes, instructors can readily monitor participation but lack scalable methods for assessing whether feedback is relevant, concrete, and constructive, limiting opportunities for timely instructional intervention. To address this gap, this study developed and evaluated the review engagement graph (REG), an instructor-focused learning analytics dashboard that integrates multilabel artificial intelligence classification of feedback quality with interactive network visualization. REG operationalizes feedback quality across three independent dimensions and translates five recurring visual patterns into corresponding pedagogical actions while preserving instructor judgment. The system was evaluated in two studies. Study 1 compared seven classification models spanning traditional machine learning, deep learning, fine-tuned transformers, and prompted large language models using 2,398 peer review comments independently annotated by two experts. Fine-tuned RoBERTa achieved the strongest overall performance, with a macro F1 score of 0.828. Study 2 evaluated REG with instructors and teaching assistants through scenario-based sessions. REG achieved a mean System Usability Scale score of 81.13, exceeding the benchmark of 68, and a mean perceived usefulness (PU) score of 4.31 out of 5. These findings demonstrate that AI-classified feedback quality indicators can be transformed into actionable visual evidence through a pattern-to-action framework that supports timely and informed instructor decision-making.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and the rebalanced hemostasis of chronic liver disease: From viscoelastic testing to digital twins

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Chronic liver disease, particularly cirrhosis, produces a fragile, rebalanced hemostatic state. Patients may develop bleeding or thrombosis. The international normalized ratio and platelet count incompletely reflect concurrent procoagulant and anticoagulant changes and poorly predict procedural bleeding. Viscoelastic testing and thrombin-generation assays assess hemostasis more broadly. Randomized trials support viscoelastic testing-guided reductions in blood product use, but these trials do not establish prediction of later bleeding or thrombosis. Machine-learning models address gastrointestinal bleeding outcomes, variceal hemorrhage, portal vein thrombosis (PVT), and transfusion requirements using clinical records, imaging, or elastography. Most cirrhosis models address one outcome, omit direct hemostatic measurements, and have limited external validation. Within the English-language eligibility criteria and focused queries of a PubMed update on July 29, 2026, no adult model jointly estimating future bleeding and PVT in cirrhosis was identified. This structured narrative minireview evaluates the evidence for both outcomes and specifies research requirements for paired-risk models and a possible digital twin of the coagulation-portal axis. Treatment-specific predictions would require additional causal validation.

items.title: Associations of managers’ AI literacy with innovative work behavior and work well-being through AI job crafting and psychological needs satisfaction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Learning to use AI is not the same as benefiting from it. As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in knowledge work, its implications are often discussed in contrasting terms—potential productivity gains and risks to well-being—raising the question of whether AI literacy is associated with both performance-related behavior and well-being. Conceptualizing AI literacy as a learnable competence, this study examines how AI literacy is associated with what managers achieve and how they experience their work. Managers here are examined as adult learners whose roles may provide opportunities to apply AI-related competence in their work. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources perspective and Self-Determination Theory, survey data from 322 managers experienced with generative AI were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI literacy was positively associated with AI job crafting, and AI job crafting was positively associated with psychological needs satisfaction (autonomy and competence satisfaction). AI literacy, AI job crafting, and psychological needs satisfaction were also significantly associated with innovative work behavior and work well-being, and the proposed indirect associations were statistically significant.

items.abstract_text: Poultry diseases and welfare issues can lead to significant production losses, compromise food safety, and create a need for ongoing farm monitoring. This narrative review summarises 81 peer-reviewed research papers published between 2016 and 2026 focusing on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for monitoring poultry diseases and health. The papers were grouped into the following categories, namely disease diagnosis, health and welfare monitoring, mortality and biosecurity surveillance, and post-harvest food safety, and are summarised in a study-level appendix by modality, technique and reported data details. Conventional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, YOLO-based object detection, transformer models, explainable AI, multimodal fusion, IoT, edge AI, federated learning, generative AI, and vision-language models are the focus of the reviewed literature. The most common methods are image and faecal-image analysis, complemented by audio, thermal, video, behavioural, and environmental sensing. The trend in recent work is to use lightweight models on local devices and to integrate multiple modalities. Some limitations to direct comparison of reported results include small sample sizes and the nature of the datasets in some studies, differences in class definitions, unbalanced classes, inconsistent validation protocols, and limited cross-farm testing. Cross-farm generalisation, standardised benchmarking, explainability, prospective veterinary validation, privacy-preserving collaboration features, and cost-effective edge deployment are highlighted as key priorities. Future work should involve creating multi-country and multi-breed benchmark datasets, developing commercially validated decision-support tools and poultry-specific foundation models, and implementing continual-learning systems and multimodal fusion frameworks. The review suggests that AI has the potential to enhance precision poultry production, but successful long-term implementation of AI in the field requires not only high accuracy but also robustness, interpretability, and affordability.

items.title: BlockKD3A: A Web3-Native Framework for Decentralized Collaborative AI and User-Generated Model Assets

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications
items.abstract_text: User-generated model assets in Web3 demand verifiable provenance, clear attribution, and dependable coordination across organizational boundaries without centralizing data. However, real-world deployments still face persistent challenges. Even algorithmically robust methods like KD3A often lack auditable coordination, failure resilience, and reproducible artifact lineage. These limitations make training brittle and results difficult to audit amidst node churn, adversarial behavior, and system heterogeneity. We introduce BlockKD3A, a hybrid on-chain/off-chain framework that operationalizes KD3A with three key system guarantees: (i) auditable coordination, achieved via smart contracts that record training state, model content identifiers (CIDs), and Consensus Focus (CF)-based attribution; (ii) reliability, through a transaction-safe client and failure-aware orchestration that applies nonnegative CF clipping, supports zero-CF fallback, and avoids blocking on stragglers; and (iii) reproducibility, enabled by content-addressable packaging and unified telemetry that couples machine learning metrics with blockchain events. In 9 end-to-end deployments (40 epochs per target), BlockKD3A delivered near-centralized performance, 96.74% macro-average accuracy on Office-Caltech10, and 89.40% on DigitFive—substantially outperforming representative federated baselines. Coordination remained efficient and predictable, with only 13 blockchain transactions across all 9 deployments, bounded gas costs per write (125,972–298,405), and stable epoch timings even under partial participation. By integrating KD3A’s algorithm-native attribution with on-chain provenance and robust execution, BlockKD3A closes the gap between decentralized learning algorithms and reliable system deployment, providing auditability, predictable cost envelopes, and transferable engineering patterns for verifiable user-generated model assets.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Clinical prediction models have historically relied on structured electronic health record data, leaving the rich prognostic signal embedded in free-text clinical documentation systematically underutilized. The proposed Clinical Multimodal Adaptive Clinical Prediction (CMACP) architecture — a dual-pathway prediction system integrating structured EHR features through gradient-boosted tree processing with unstructured clinical note embeddings through Clinical BERT encoding, unified by a cross-modal attention mechanism that weighs each modality's contribution by predictive confidence. The architecture is designed for geriatric acute care settings where clinical notes capture disease severity, symptom trajectory, and functional context unavailable from structured data alone. A federated fine-tuning protocol enables privacypreserving multi-institutional model development across health systems with different EHR platforms and patient populations. An attribution framework combining SHAP-based structured feature importance with Integrated Gradients note concept attribution provides role-differentiated clinical explanations, with a concordance quality badge signalling modality alignment. A governance framework specifies deployment standards, post-market performance monitoring, and equity evaluation protocols calibrated to multi-site clinical NLP systems. The CMACP framework addresses the technical and governance requirements for safe deployment of multimodal clinical AI in settings where older adult patients are most vulnerable to prediction errors. External validation across multiple health system types, equity stratification by race and documentation quality environment, and prospective evaluation of attribution quality are identified as priority research requirements.

items.title: Students' Knowledge of Personalised Learning: How AI Can Help?

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Personalised learning aims to align instruction with students' needs, interests, and motivation through responsive learning environments. However, many students demonstrate limited understanding of this concept, often associating it only with self‐paced learning or technology use. Such misconceptions weaken classroom implementation and may reduce student engagement and self‐regulation. This study aims to calibrate students' understanding of personalised learning and examine how artificial intelligence (AI) can be leveraged, directly and indirectly, to address key areas of misunderstanding and enhance effective implementation. The study involved 450 high school students aged 16–18 from selected schools in Kedah, Penang, and Perak, using a purposive sampling approach. Data were collected through a questionnaire administered during class after participants were briefed on the concept of personalised learning and the study purpose. Validity and reliability of the assessed constructs were evaluated using factor loadings ( λ ), average variance extracted (AVE), Cronbach's alpha ( α ), and composite reliability (CR), with acceptable thresholds of λ > 0.50, AVE > 0.50, α > 0.60, and CR > 0.60. Students' knowledge scores were analysed to identify aspects of personalised learning that were well understood and those requiring further clarification, providing an empirical basis for targeted instructional interventions. The findings indicate that the measurement model demonstrated adequate reliability and validity. Students strongly associated personalised learning with needs‐based differentiation, particularly in project‐based and mixed‐ability contexts, but showed weaker understanding of learner autonomy, self‐paced learning, and digital facilitation. These results reveal a conceptual gap between theory and practice. Practical AI‐based strategies are proposed to enhance learning effectiveness and support adaptive, self‐regulated learning environments.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming multiple sectors, including public health. Recent years have witnessed a substantial increase in research on integrating AI into public health systems, reflecting a growing interest in its potential to improve surveillance, diagnostics, policy development, and health outcomes. Objective This study aims to identify how AI has been applied in public health, examine its impact on the field, and determine future research directions at the intersection of AI and public health. Methods A systematic literature review was conducted to analyze existing scholarly research on AI applications in public health. Relevant studies were collected, screened, and categorized to identify dominant research themes and gaps in the literature. Results The analysis revealed five primary thematic clusters within the literature: (1) AI model development and performance, (2) public health threats and outbreak management, (3) systematic reviews and evidence synthesis, (4) social and ethical issues in public health, and (5) governance, policy, and innovation. The review also identified underexplored areas and inconsistencies across studies, highlighting significant research gaps. Conclusions AI has demonstrated substantial potential to enhance public health practice and research. However, further investigation is needed to address ethical, governance, and implementation challenges. Future research should focus on strengthening policy frameworks, improving transparency and accountability in AI systems, and promoting interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the responsible and equitable integration of AI into public health.

Unlike traditional literature reviews, SLRs offer enhanced replicability, reliability, and transparency [ 22 , 23 ]. SLRs have been utilized across a wide range of research domains, including IS and public health. In the realm of IS research, Anderson et al [ 24 ] adopted the SLR framework proposed by Vom Brocke et al [ 25 ] along with the content analysis to identify research themes from case-based learning and cybersecurity leadership education. Their goal was to understand how case-based learning could contribute to developing often overlooked elements in cybersecurity leadership education. Laine et al [ 26 ] applied the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework as developed by Moher et al [ 27 ] to analyze IS literature on AI auditing, focusing on the contributions of ethics-based AI auditing from the perspectives of various stakeholders. Additionally, Altrichter and Benoit [ 28 ] utilized the SLR procedure by Palmatier et al [ 29 ] to create a technology discontinuance framework that distinguishes technology discontinuance from related concepts and various types of technology discontinuance. SLRs have also proven effective for exploring numerous topics in public health research. For instance, Mustapha et al [ 30 ] followed the PRISMA framework [ 27 ] to evaluate the impact of Industry 4.0 on health care systems using cross-disciplinary literature. Khanra et al [ 31 ] employed a 3-stage SLR protocol [ 32 , 33 ] to investigate the applicability of big data analytics (BDA) in health care from 5 distinct perspectives. Furthermore, Pinto et al [ 34 ] applied the SLR framework by Kitchenham and Charters [ 35 ] and Petersen et al [ 36 ] to analyze variables and technologies relevant to the impact assessment of public health campaigns. Numerous methodological guidelines have been developed to conduct SLRs, including the Systematic Procedures and Rationales for Systematic Literature Reviews (SPAR-4-SLR) protocols [ 37 ], recommendations for literature searches by Vom Brocke et al [ 25 ], the PRISMA guidelines [ 27 ], Kitchenham [ 38 ] procedures for SLRs, and the SALSA (Search, Appraisal, Synthesis, and Analysis) framework [ 39 ]. For this study, we chose to follow the SPAR-4-SLR protocol because it provides comprehensive coverage of the entire SLR process. In contrast, frameworks such as Vom Brocke et al [ 25 ] and SALSA focus only on specific stages of the SLR process. Compared to other popular frameworks such as PRISMA, SPAR-4-SLR also offers more detailed requirements and justifications for each stage [ 37 , 40 ]. Additionally, it is applicable across multiple disciplines, unlike the Kitchenham [ 38 ] framework, which is primarily based in the software engineering context. SPAR-4-SLR consists of 3 major stages: assembling, arranging, and assessing. The assembling stage is further divided into 2 steps: identification and acquisition. In the identification step, SLR researchers must first define their research questions and then establish the scope of the SLR based on these questions. During the acquisition step, researchers create the literature search formula by specifying the time period, keywords, and databases to be used for the literature search. The next stage is arranging, which is also divided into 2 steps: organization and purification. In the organization step, reviewers code the retrieved papers based on various characteristics such as the number of citations, research methods, article types, and data types. This process is often guided by an organizing framework such as TCCM (Theory, Context, Characteristics, and Methodology) [ 37 ]. In the purification step, the initial set of literature is screened using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The final stage is assessing, which consists of evaluation and reporting. In the evaluation step, analysis methods such as bibliographic analysis, topic modeling, clustering, and meta-analytical analysis are defined according to the type of SLR and then applied to assess the review papers. In the reporting stage, SLR researchers identify research gaps in the domain that could inform future studies, as well as best practices for academic researchers, industry practitioners, and policymakers. This step highlights the practical and theoretical contributions of the SLR research. We followed the protocols outlined in SPAR-4-SLR. In the assembling stage, we utilized the Web of Science (WoS) database to search for papers on the intersection of AI and public health to address the research questions proposed earlier. It is worth noting that the broad terms “artificial intelligence” and “public health” were used in our search formula. This is due to the heterogeneous, dynamic, and cross-disciplinary nature of both concepts. For instance, the topic of AI includes discussions of traditional AI and generative AI. Some AI studies focus on the technical aspects of AI algorithm development, while others focus on the societal and ethical changes brought about by AI. Similar to AI, public health research spans a wide range of themes, including pandemic control and prevention, the design and implementation of public health policy, and health education. The use of broad rather than specific search terms ensured the unbiased and comprehensive coverage of literature relevant to the goal of this study. A general search using these terms returned 4273 papers. The search was restricted to the years 2021 to 2025. We restricted our search to these years because the use of AI surged after the release of generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, in 2022. Papers published before this time were not relevant to our study. A copy of the search terms used is provided in Multimedia Appendix 1 . The search resulted in 2122 papers. After discarding 51 papers that were not relevant to our study, we were left with 2071 papers. In the arranging stage, we restricted the WoS categories to those listed in the search query provided in Multimedia Appendix 1 . The search included all papers published until the end of August 2025. The search query resulted in 2071 relevant papers. Furthermore, we ranked authors, institutions, and countries based on their research productivity using the number of papers published under their names. During the performance analysis, we also identified the major research areas in this domain, which encompass the majority of the papers in our dataset.
