items.title: A Single-Center Retrospective Analysis of Artificial Intelligence-Based Emotion Recognition Systems for Attention-Regulation Training in Children with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Introduction: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often experience attention instability and emotion dysregulation. Existing interventions typically lack real-time responsiveness and ecological validity. This study retrospectively examined historical training records from an AI-assisted closed-loop system integrating emotion recognition and behavioral feedback for attention regulation in children with ADHD. Methods: This single-center retrospective analysis included historical training records from 60 children with ADHD who had completed either AI-assisted attention training or conventional attention training between 2021 and 2024. The AI-assisted training-record group comprised children whose archived records included 12 sessions of integrated cognitive training involving Go/No-Go, CPT, and Flanker tasks with real-time AI-generated feedback based on task performance and facial-emotion monitoring. The conventional training-record group completed the same attention tasks without AI-based feedback. Assessments included task performance, Conners Continuous Performance Test, 3rd Edition (CPT-3), teacher ratings, and emotion metrics, analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, linear growth modeling, and structural equation modeling (SEM). Results: Compared with conventional training records, AI-assisted training records showed greater pre-post changes in reaction time (RT), RT variability, and task accuracy, together with fewer commission errors in CPT-3. Post-feedback behavioral recovery was observed in 78.3% of feedback events. Teacher ratings showed consistent pre-post improvements across attention maintenance, emotional regulation, and task execution. Negative emotion labels decreased from 42.3% to 24.6% (p = 0.003). SEM supported an associative pathway linking emotion recognition frequency, feedback frequency, and RT reduction (95% CI: 0.15-0.38). Conclusions: The retrospective findings suggest that AI-assisted closed-loop training records were associated with favorable changes in attention and emotional-state indicators in children with ADHD. These exploratory results support further prospective, externally validated studies before broader clinical or educational implementation.

items.title: How Can Artificial Intelligence Explain its Thinking? A Review of Explainable AI
items.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on AI Research.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly shaping decision-making across industries such as healthcare, finance, e-commerce, education, and cybersecurity. Despite significant advances in machine learning and generative AI, many AI models continue to function as “black boxes,” producing outputs and recommendations without clearly communicating the reasoning behind them. This lack of transparency has raised growing concerns regarding trust, accountability, fairness, and ethical AI adoption. As organizations become more dependent on AI-driven systems, explainability has emerged as a critical factor influencing how users perceive, trust, and adopt artificial intelligence technologies. This literature review examines how Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) enables AI systems to communicate their reasoning in ways understandable to human users. The paper analyzes existing academic and industry research on explainability, transparency, and interpretability within AI systems, with a particular focus on how explanations influence human trust and organizational acceptance of AI technologies. The review evaluates major explainability approaches used in both traditional machine learning models and modern generative AI systems, including techniques such as Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), attention visualization, counterfactual explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning methods used in large language models (LLMs). In addition, the paper examines the distinctions between transparency, interpretability, and explainability, and how these concepts contribute to building trustworthy AI systems. The review further analyzes explainability from a human-centered perspective, including perceived fairness, ethical AI design, user confidence, and organizational adoption challenges. The paper also discusses the growing importance of explainability within responsible AI governance frameworks, particularly as regulatory initiatives such as the European Union AI Act increasingly emphasize transparency and accountable AI decision-making. This study contributes to the growing body of literature on explainable AI by consolidating fragmented research on transparency, trust, and human-centered AI adoption. The review identifies current research gaps, limitations of existing explainability approaches, and future opportunities for designing AI systems that are not only accurate and efficient but also understandable, trustworthy, and ethically aligned with human values.

items.title: AI-Based Rehabilitation System for Congenital Muscular Torticollis: Formative Usability Evaluation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Home-based exercise programs for congenital muscular torticollis (CMT) depend heavily on caregivers, yet adherence is often hindered by cognitive and emotional burdens. Objective This study conducted a formative usability evaluation of an AI-based CMT rehabilitation system comprising a clinician web interface and a caregiver mobile app to identify usability-related issues and preliminary design requirements during early development. Methods A formative usability evaluation was conducted with 8 clinical experts (rehabilitation physicians, nurses, and physical therapists). Participants engaged in focus group interviews (FGIs) following a demonstration of the system and completed the System Usability Scale (SUS) for the overall system, including a proxy evaluation of the caregiver mobile app. Qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis, and SUS scores were analyzed descriptively as a supplementary quantitative measure of perceived usability. Results The thematic analysis identified 2 core themes, “Usability Barriers of the CMT Rehabilitation System” and “Improvement Requirements,” encompassing 10 subthemes and 21 concepts. Key findings highlighted concerns regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated feedback and the need to simplify data visualization to reduce the potential cognitive burden on caregivers. The mean SUS score for the overall system was 73.44 (SD 18.01). This result was interpreted descriptively and considered supplementary to the qualitative findings. Conclusions The formative evaluation identified preliminary usability strengths and areas for improvement from clinicians’ perspectives, with particular concerns regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated feedback. The experts emphasized that the AI-based CMT rehabilitation system should function as a therapeutic bridge between clinicians and caregivers. As actual caregivers were not included in this evaluation, the findings represent preliminary formative design inputs based on clinicians’ proxy perspectives rather than evidence of usability for caregivers. Future iterations should incorporate the identified improvements and undergo evaluation with actual caregivers in home environments, along with separate technical verification of the accuracy of the AI feedback algorithm.

The qualitative findings identified usability-related concerns that were not adequately represented by the overall SUS score alone. These included the clarity of instructions, delineation of roles between clinicians and caregivers, feedback during exercise performance, and understanding of the system’s intended scope of use. These findings also suggest that usability issues in caregiver-delivered rehabilitation may extend beyond interface operability or functional arrangement to broader human factors considerations associated with the context in which caregivers perform therapeutic exercises with infants.

analysis.methods: This study used a formative usability evaluation that included FGIs and a survey with 8 clinical experts, including rehabilitation medicine physicians, nurses, and physical therapists. The evaluation was designed to identify usability-related issues, potential use errors, and areas for improvement in the prototype CMT rehabilitation system from the perspectives of clinical experts. Rehabilitation medicine physicians and nurses provided perspectives relevant to the clinician-facing web interface, while physical therapists contributed domain expertise in CMT rehabilitation. The caregiver-facing mobile app was evaluated from the clinical experts’ proxy perspectives, as actual caregivers were not included in this study. The findings were used to derive preliminary formative design inputs to guide subsequent iterations of the system rather than to establish the usability of the caregiver-facing app for actual caregivers. The CMT rehabilitation system used in this study was developed to facilitate the provision of rehabilitation exercises for infants under 12 months of age diagnosed with CMT. The system enables caregivers to perform rehabilitation interventions for their infants using a mobile app. The CMT rehabilitation system consists of a web interface for clinical staff and a mobile app for the infant and caregiver. The intended users of the web interface are health care professionals (physicians and nurses), while the mobile app is intended for caregivers. Health care professionals access the web interface to diagnose infants who require CMT rehabilitation, prescribe appropriate exercises, and manage or supervise the treatment process. Caregivers use the mobile app to follow guided exercise videos, enabling them to provide direct rehabilitation therapy to the infant. The treatment interface within the mobile app provides AI-based feedback intended to support caregivers during exercise performance. Furthermore, the app allows for the recording of participation and adherence upon completion of each session. The formative usability evaluation was designed with reference to the usability engineering process outlined in IEC 62366-1:2015+ AMD1:2020 [ 15 ]. For the focus group interviews, we aimed to recruit 5 to 8 clinical experts, including rehabilitation medicine physicians, nurses, and physical therapists involved in the diagnosis, treatment, or outpatient support of patients with CMT, to obtain multidisciplinary perspectives on the clinical workflow [ 16 ]. A total of 8 clinical experts participated in the study: 2 rehabilitation medicine physicians, 2 nurses, and 4 physical therapists. This formative evaluation was limited to clinical experts; caregivers, who are the intended users of the caregiver-facing mobile app, were not recruited. Accordingly, the clinicians evaluated the caregiver-facing app from a proxy clinical perspective, and the usability of the app from the perspective of actual caregivers was not assessed in this study. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) clinical experience in the diagnosis, treatment, or outpatient support of CMT; (2) sufficient proficiency in Korean and English to understand the terminology used in the system; and (3) provision of informed consent to participate in the evaluation. Individuals who did not meet the inclusion criteria or did not provide informed consent were excluded. Data saturation was not used as a criterion for determining the sample size because the number and composition of participants were predefined for this formative usability evaluation. The FGIs for the formative usability evaluation were conducted in a single session for each group. Participants were organized into 2 groups to capture complementary clinical perspectives based on their professional roles and experience with CMT care: group A consisted of 2 rehabilitation medicine physicians and 2 nurses involved in the clinical management and outpatient support of patients with CMT, and group B consisted of 4 physical therapists with expertise in CMT rehabilitation ( Figure 1 ). Both groups comprised clinical experts, and no caregivers participated in the evaluation. The formative evaluation procedure began with a briefing for participants regarding the purpose, overview, and methodology of the CMT rehabilitation system. Following the acquisition of informed consent, a preinterview survey was conducted to collect demographic and professional characteristics. The interviews were conducted based on a pre-established scenario and included a live demonstration of the system. Participants were provided with opportunities to interact directly with the product as necessary, while the evaluation facilitator observed and recorded the proceedings. Postinterview surveys were administered to gather additional feedback, and a standardized set of interview questions was applied to both focus groups ( Table 1 ). The question protocol was designed to explore usability-related issues and potential areas for improvement from the participating clinical experts’ perspectives, in accordance with the evaluation scenario. Each FGI session lasted approximately 100 minutes ( Table 2 ). FGIs are a qualitative research method designed to collect data through in-depth discussions with purposefully selected participants centered on specific topics [ 16 , 17 ]. Information gathered through FGIs is instrumental in identifying potential areas for further exploration or in clarifying themes that may be difficult to capture using other research instruments. The interactive and synergistic nature of focus groups allows participants to refine or elaborate on their thoughts by engaging with the opinions of others. This process often yields richer and more expansive insights than those typically obtained through one-on-one interviews [ 13 ]. In this study, FGIs were used to identify usability-related issues, potential use errors, and areas for improvement in the CMT rehabilitation system, thereby deriving preliminary formative design inputs to guide subsequent system development. The question protocol for the FGIs was structured to facilitate meaningful interaction among participants and to elicit comprehensive feedback based on the system’s operational scenarios. analysis.discussion: This formative evaluation identified several usability-related issues and preliminary design requirements for the prototype AI-based CMT rehabilitation system from the perspectives of clinical experts. The qualitative findings highlighted 3 main areas: the need to reduce the potential cognitive burden associated with caregiver-delivered rehabilitation, the need to improve the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated feedback, and the need to strengthen coordination between the clinician-facing web interface and caregiver-facing mobile app. The mean SUS score was 73.44 (SD 18.01); however, given the small sample size and variability in scores, this result was interpreted as a supplementary descriptive measure rather than as definitive evidence of overall system usability. Importantly, because caregivers did not participate in this study, findings concerning caregiver experience represent clinicians’ proxy perspectives and require confirmation through direct evaluation with actual caregivers. The qualitative findings identified usability-related concerns that were not adequately represented by the overall SUS score alone. These included the clarity of instructions, delineation of roles between clinicians and caregivers, feedback during exercise performance, and understanding of the system’s intended scope of use. Thus, the SUS findings should be regarded as supplementary to the qualitative findings rather than as evidence that the system has achieved an acceptable level of usability. These findings also suggest that usability issues in caregiver-delivered rehabilitation may extend beyond interface operability or functional arrangement to broader human factors considerations associated with the context in which caregivers perform therapeutic exercises with infants. The usability issues identified by the clinical experts were less related to basic interface elements, such as button placement, and more closely related to the potential cognitive demands placed on nonprofessional caregivers who are expected to perform therapeutic exercises in home settings. Unlike medical devices operated primarily by trained health care professionals, the caregiver-facing component of the CMT rehabilitation system requires caregivers to perform exercises with infants while simultaneously interpreting instructions and system feedback. From a human factors perspective, this dual role as both system user and provider of home-based exercises may create cognitive and emotional demands that should be considered during system design. Previous research has indicated that caregivers’ disease awareness, level of understanding, and trust in treatment can influence adherence [ 10 ]. Consistent with these findings, clinical experts in the present study anticipated that caregivers may experience fear or uncertainty when directly performing therapeutic exercises and may have difficulty simultaneously performing the exercises and interacting with the mobile app. Similarly, Stitt and Operacz [ 8 ] reported that caregivers of infants with torticollis may experience psychological stress during home exercise programs because of concerns about causing pain to the child, which may negatively affect adherence. However, the cognitive and emotional burdens identified in the present study were based on clinicians’ proxy perspectives and were not directly reported by caregivers. These findings suggest that the design of CMT rehabilitation software should consider not only basic operability but also the potential cognitive and emotional demands associated with caregiver-delivered rehabilitation. Clear visual materials, comprehensible safety information, and step-by-step guidance may help caregivers understand how exercises should be performed and when corrective action may be necessary. Rather than positioning caregivers as independent clinical decision-makers, the system should support them in performing clinician-prescribed exercises within clearly defined boundaries. From a human factors perspective, these considerations represent preliminary design inputs for reducing potential cognitive burden and use-related errors. Clear and interpretable feedback may be particularly important when caregivers are expected to determine whether an exercise is being performed appropriately. Subtle aspects of exercise performance, such as movement angle and direction, may be difficult for nonprofessional users to judge without adequate guidance. Clinical experts therefore emphasized the need for visual feedback that communicates exercise performance in an understandable manner. Such feedback may help reduce reliance on subjective judgment and support caregivers in identifying when an exercise requires correction. In addition, the clinical experts emphasized the importance of clearly defining conditions under which caregivers should discontinue an exercise or seek assistance from a clinician. Home-based rehabilitation requires caregivers to respond appropriately to changes in an infant’s condition during exercise. If warning signs, stopping criteria, or safety information are unclear, caregivers may have difficulty determining whether an observed response requires intervention. Accordingly, presenting concrete and observable safety information, including appropriate exercise discontinuation criteria, may represent an important human factors consideration for subsequent system development. A particularly important finding was the clinical experts’ concern regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated feedback. Participants questioned whether the feedback provided by the prototype could reliably distinguish appropriate from inappropriate exercise performance and whether caregivers would receive sufficient information to understand and correct inappropriate movements. These concerns are particularly relevant in infant rehabilitation, where inaccurate or insufficiently interpretable feedback could contribute to inappropriate exercise performance and potentially increase the risk of harm. These concerns are consistent with previous research emphasizing the importance of explainability and transparency in medical AI for supporting user understanding and trust [ 21 ]. Recent privacy-preserving and interpretable AI approaches for pose-based rehabilitation [ 22 ] also provide a useful framework for considering transparent and correction-oriented feedback. Future iterations of the CMT rehabilitation system could therefore explore feedback mechanisms that communicate not only whether a movement is considered appropriate but also why it was classified as such and how an inappropriate movement could be corrected. Importantly, the present study evaluated clinical experts’ perceptions of AI-generated feedback and did not assess the technical accuracy, reliability, or clinical validity of the underlying AI algorithm. Therefore, neither the SUS results nor the qualitative usability findings should be interpreted as evidence
analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study included only eight clinical experts, and actual caregivers—the intended users of the caregiver-facing mobile app—did not participate. Therefore, findings concerning caregiver-related usability issues reflect clinicians’ proxy perspectives and should not be interpreted as direct evidence of caregivers’ experiences or the usability of the caregiver-facing app. Future evaluations should directly involve caregivers to examine their actual interactions with the system, perceived cognitive and emotional demands, and use-related difficulties. Second, the small sample size and variability in SUS scores limit the precision and generalizability of the quantitative findings. Accordingly, the SUS results were interpreted descriptively and as supplementary to the qualitative findings rather than as a definitive assessment of overall system usability. Third, the prototype was evaluated in a controlled setting rather than in actual home environments. Consequently, contextual factors that may influence caregiver interaction with the system during home-based rehabilitation, including environmental distractions, simultaneous caregiving demands, and repeated use over time, were not directly assessed. Future studies should therefore evaluate the system with caregivers under realistic home-use conditions following iterative design refinement. Finally, this study examined clinical experts’ perceptions of AI-generated feedback but did not assess the technical accuracy, reliability, or clinical validity of the underlying AI algorithm. Separate technical verification of the AI feedback algorithm is therefore required before its performance can be established. Following iterative design refinement and technical verification, subsequent usability evaluations involving actual caregivers in representative use environments will be necessary to further assess the safety and usability of the system and to inform progression toward summative evaluation.

items.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
items.abstract_text: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become useful tools for analysing medical images because they can learn visual patterns associated with normal and abnormal tissue. In cancer screening and diagnosis, however, a high classification score alone is not sufficient: clinicians also need to understand which image regions influenced a model’s output. This paper proposes an explainable deep-learning framework that combines CNN-based image classification with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to support early cancer detection from histopathological images. The proposed workflow includes image collection, quality assessment, preprocessing, augmentation, CNN training, prediction, and explanation generation. Grad-CAM is used to produce class-specific heatmaps, while LIME and SHAP are considered for local image-region and feature-contribution explanations. The explanations are intended to help users inspect whether the model focuses on tissue regions that are relevant to the predicted class rather than irrelevant background patterns. Model performance can be assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, specificity, and area under the ROC curve. Explanation quality should additionally be examined through localization agreement, stability, and review by qualified domain experts. The framework is presented as a research proposal; its diagnostic performance and clinical usefulness must be established through controlled experiments and external validation. It is designed as a decision-support approach and is not intended to replace professional diagnosis.

items.abstract_text: Do you know what is in your beer? Increasingly, the answer depends not only on ingredients and fermentation, but on the integrity of the digital and physical systems that govern production. This paper examines commercial brewing as an underdeveloped cyberbiosecurity workforce problem intensified by AI. Brewing increasingly depends on digital networks, automated control, and connected supply chains. Yet the process remains a biologically active process shaped by human judgment, microbial control, and physical equipment. Although cyberbiosecurity research addresses biotechnology, biomanufacturing, food, and agriculture, commercial fermentation has received comparatively limited attention. Brewing is a useful case because cyber incidents can disrupt fermentation, sanitation, packaging, quality control, and operational decision-making even when finished beer remains inhospitable to many pathogens. Malicious use of AI to uplift novice actors, used in conjunction with generative phishing attacks, may further reduce informational barriers and support coordination across cyber, biological, and physical domains, although current evidence does not establish fully autonomous adversarial operations. Drawing on cyberbiosecurity, OT-security, workforce, and training frameworks, this paper identifies a socio-technical gap between brewing science and cybersecurity and proposes a competency model incorporating AI literacy, OT awareness, biological anomaly recognition, and scenario-based training. It argues that workforce preparedness should complement technical and governance controls in securing increasingly digitized brewing environments.

items.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

analysis.discussion: GenAI has not simply added one more tool to the educator's kit; it has unsettled the very hierarchies that underwrote models like Bloom's Taxonomy. By revising, inverting, or 'UnBlooming' those models, the approaches in this article argue for designs that foreground recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth as the real work of learning, especially in an age where GenAI is marketed as doing the 'thinking' for us. The future of learning is not arriving later. It is already here, unevenly distributed across classrooms, disciplines, and institutions. The educators who will shape that future are those willing to revise their most cherished frameworks, revisit their assessment practices, and keep asking questions about the kinds of thinkers, makers, and citizens we want our students to become. As we write, and as we advocate for this change, we are keenly aware that faculty at our Higher Education institutions already carry a heavy burden with teaching, researching, and public engagement. There are a finite number of hours in a day, and faculty do not have the time to stop and redesign courses almost weekly as GenAI changes and morphs. We make a point to call for change, but we know this change cannot happen overnight. It will require the dedicated commitment of administrators to find the funding and time for faculty to make these changes. Designing for recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth means little if only a subset of students and faculty have the material and institutional support to engage in that work. GenAI cannot be framed primarily as a compliance or efficiency problem because it is a fundamental change in the way teaching and learning happen. Right now, for example, many programs and professional standards have been rigidly structured to Bloom's Taxonomy, making authentic education suffer in the Age of AI (Gonsalves 2024) . Taken together, these post-AI frameworks reframe Bloom's Taxonomy not as a ladder to be climbed, but as a historical starting point-inviting educators to design learning that prioritizes metacognition, agency, and ethical judgment in a world where answers are instant but understanding is not. As Table 3 summarizes, Bloom's/Revised Bloom's, Fink's Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom's, and UnBlooms™ do not represent interchangeable models; rather, they mark a movement from hierarchical cognition, to relational learning, to AI-era inversion, and finally to recursive, judgment-centered pedagogy. Instructors and institutions must design new structures and assessment systems to account for the reality of GenAI. This does not mean being a full-on AI adopter, but it does mean that they will need to be 'AI aware' (Watkins 2024) . Ultimately, that is why we published this article: we needed to better understand how learning works in the Age of AI and build from there. In comparing selected pre-AI and post-AI pedagogical frameworks according to how they conceptualize the relationship among process, product, cognition, agency, and metacognitive reflection, we have demonstrated how learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks can be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning. Although Bloom's Taxonomy endures, we must see Bloom's as a point to begin the revision rather than an endpoint or script. If our institutions, educators, and students are to thrive in the Age of AI, we need to begin the inquiry into what pedagogy should look like with GenAI, what we are trying to accomplish, whose learning counts, who benefits, and who is left out of the future we are building. It is an ongoing conversation, one that we are privileged to be a part of, but also one we understand must move quickly into the future as our technology, institutions, and educational priorities change (hopefully) for the better.

items.venue: Journal of Economics, Finance And Management Studies
items.abstract_text: This study investigates how generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and business analytics capability shape strategic financial decision quality in emerging market SMEs, with particular attention to the moderating role of AI governance maturity. Grounded in organizational information processing theory and dynamic capabilities theory, the study argues that better financial decisions depend not simply on access to advanced technologies, but on how effectively firms turn AI generated forecasts and analytical information into useful financial judgment. AI governance maturity is expected to strengthen this process by providing appropriate oversight, accountability, validation, and control over the use of AI generated financial information. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 385 respondents who possessed relevant knowledge of SME financial management, business analytics, AI applications, or organizational decision making. Data were collected using a five-point Likert scale questionnaire and analyzed with IBM SPSS version 26. Reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and multiple linear regression were performed, while Hayes’ Process Macro Model 1 was used to test the moderating effect. The results show that generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability (β = 0.613) and business analytics capability (β = 0.487) both have significant positive effects on strategic financial decision quality. AI governance maturity also strengthens the relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality, with an interaction coefficient of 0.518. These findings suggest that emerging market SMEs gain greater value from generative AI when forecasting tools are supported by sound analytical capabilities and governance practices. Effective financial decision making therefore requires not only better technology, but also the organizational capacity to interpret, review, and responsibly use AI generated financial insights.

These results suggest that SMEs make better strategic financial decisions when they can generate for ward looking financial insights through generative AI and combine organizational data with effective analytical capabili ties. Generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability shows the larger standardized coefficient, highlighting the value of timely finan cial forecasts and prospective insights when managers assess risks, compare alternatives, and make financing, inve stment, liquidity, and resource allocation decisions. Business analytics capability also plays an important role by helping firms organize, inte rpret, and turn available data into evidence that can inform financial judgment. At the same time, AI governance maturity significantly strengthens the relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality. This moderating effect is reflected in the positive interaction coefficient of B = 0.518 and the c onfidence interval from 0.437 to 0.599, which does not include zero. The result indicates that AI generated financial forecasts become more useful for strateg ic decisions when SMEs have clearer responsibilities, appropriate oversight, validation procedures , monitoring mechanisms, and risk Overall, the empirical results support H1, H2, and H3 and are consistent with the proposed framework linking generative AI en abled financial forecasting capability, business analytics capability, AI governance maturity, and strategic financial decision qua lity. Regarding the first research question, the findings establish that generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability has a significant positive influence on strategic financial decision quality. The second research question is addressed by showi ng that business analytics capability also contributes positively to strategic financial decision quality, although its standardized coefficient is lower than that of generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability. For the third research question, the findings demonstrate that higher AI governance maturity strengthens the positive relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality. Taken together, the results suggest that emerging mar ket SMEs gain greater value from generative AI when forecasting capability is accompanied by broader analytical competence and sound governance arrangements. Improving strategic financial decision quality therefore involves not simply adopting advanced AI tools, but developing the organizational ability to interpret financial information, apply analytical insights, maintain appropriate human oversight, validate AI generated outputs, and establish clear responsibility for AI supported financial decisions. The empirical findings strongly support H1, as generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability significantly improves strategic financial decision quality with β = 0.613. This result strongly concurs with Metzger et al. (2025), who argue that genera tive AI can provide SMEs with accessible and timely financial diagnostics, and with Cheng et al. (2026), whose evidence demonstrates the predictive value of ChatGPT generated financial factors. It also reinforces Pelster & Val (2024), who associate ChatGPT based financial assessments with subsequent earnings and stock returns. However, the findings do not support an unqualified technological determinism in which stronger predictive capability automatically guarantees better decisions. Wasserbacher & Spindler (2022) caution that prediction cannot establish the causal knowledge required for planning, while Metzger et al. (2025) emphasize organizational readiness and managers’ ability to interpret AI outputs. The sizeable coefficient therefore suggests that forecasting capability matters, but not that managerial judgment becomes redundant. The findings strongly support H2, demonstrating that business analytics capability positively affects strategic financial dec ision quality with β = 0.487. This result strongly concurs with Awan et al. (2021), who associate big data analytics capability wit h higher decision-making quality, and supports Ashrafi et al. analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings. First, the cross-sectional design captures organizational perceptions at one point in time and therefore cannot establish how generative AI forecasting, analytics capability, governance maturity, and financial decision quality evolve together. Second, the reliance on self-reported assessments may introduce common method and perceptual bias, particularly because organizational capabilities and decision quality were evaluated by individual respondents. Third, purposive sampling improves access to knowledgeable participants but restricts statistical generalization to the broader population of emerging market SMEs. Although the study covers heterogeneous organizational contexts, institutional, technological, and financial conditions can differ substantially across emerging markets. Finally, strategic financial decision quality is perceptual rather than based on objective decision outcomes. The results should therefore be interpreted as evidence of theoretically specified associations rather than definitive causal effects. Future research should extend the framework longitudinally to determine whether improvements in generative AI forecasting capability precede sustained improvements in strategic financial decision quality. Multi respondent designs could combine assessments from owners, financial managers, and technology specialists to reduce single informant dependence. Researchers could also complement perceptual decision quality with objective indicators such as forecasting errors, financing costs, liqu idity outcomes, or investment performance. Cross country studies would be particularly valuable for examining whether institutional development, regulatory environments, digital infrastructure, or financial market conditions alter the relationships identifi ed here. Further work should also investigate whether AI governance has nonlinear effects, since increasingly formal governance may not generate proportionately greater decision benefits. Finally, extending the model to human AI collaboration, managerial financ ial literacy, data quality, and organizational readiness could clarify the mechanisms through which AI generated forecasts become strategically useful financial knowledge.

items.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on AI Research.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: AI-driven beauty filters are now embedded in adolescents' everyday digital self-presentation, yet their ethical implications for marketing communication have received limited attention within management and consumer research. Existing studies largely rely on exposure-based quantitative designs that assess outcomes such as body dissatisfaction, offering limited insight into how young users actively interpret digitally altered imagery. This study contributes to this literature by examining how early adolescent girls aged 10–14 make sense of AI-filtered and unfiltered facial images and how their side-by-side visual contrast shapes evaluations of beauty and postability. The study employs a three-stage qualitative visual elicitation design that mirrors naturalistic social media engagement. In Stage 1, participants are presented with five variations of the same face, ranging from unfiltered to differently filtered versions, and select their preferred image for beauty and posting suitability, providing baseline judgements for the analysis. Stage 2 introduces paired filtered and unfiltered images presented side by side, creating visual contrast that renders digital modification perceptually salient and functions as a brief visual micro-intervention. Stage 3 reintroduces the same facial images presented in Stage 1 to examine whether participants’ evaluative judgements shift following the contrast exposure in Stage 2. Audio-recorded interviews capture participants’ verbal explanations, enabling analysis of how adolescents articulate, justify, and reason about digitally modified appearance cues. The study contributes methodologically by showing how sequential visual exposure can be used to examine adolescents’ interpretations rather than relying only on scale-based outcomes. Theoretically, it draws on Social Comparison Theory and Online Self-Presentation Theory because evaluating what is considered beautiful and deciding what is suitable to post represent related but distinct processes. Together, these theories explain how filtered and unfiltered appearances are evaluated and how these evaluations inform posting preferences. By foregrounding adolescents’ own interpretations, the research advances understanding of how beauty norms are cognitively constructed within digital marketing environments and highlights the ethical significance of representational authenticity in visual communication targeting young consumers.

items.title: ALGORITHMIC GLOBAL VALUE CHAINS AND HIGHER EDUCATION TRANSFORMATION: RE-ENGINEERING INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS PEDAGOGY IN THE ERA OF AUTONOMOUS INTELLIGENCE

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid emergence of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive supply chain orchestration, and real-time cross-border regulatory analytics is fundamentally transforming how multinational enterprises (MNEs) govern global value chains (GVCs) and enter foreign markets. Yet International Business (IB) higher education remains largely tethered to twentieth-century pedagogical paradigms—relying on static international trade models, retrospective written case studies, and essentialist cultural heuristics that fail to prepare graduates for algorithmically mediated global commerce. Moving beyond surface-level classroom adoption of generative chatbots, this study develops a comprehensive theoretical and operational framework for re-engineering International Business education through the lenses of Global Value Chain Governance Theory, Activity Theory, and Metacognitive Scaffolding. We argue that the defining competency for next-generation IB professionals is Algorithmic Value-Chain Orchestration—the ability to align predictive and generative AI systems with cross-jurisdictional institutional realities, geopolitical risks, and culturally grounded human judgment. To operationalize this capability, the paper introduces a Three-Horizon Curricular Transformation Architecture alongside a Synthetic Global Commerce Laboratory that immerses students in dynamic multi-tier supply chain disruptions, automated customs and rules-of-origin auditing, and cross-cultural digital platform governance. Drawing upon longitudinal pedagogical implementations across undergraduate and postgraduate IB cohorts, we demonstrate significant gains in students' systemic risk reasoning, critical verification of algorithmic outputs, and cross-border strategic adaptability. Finally, the study examines structural challenges—including cognitive atrophy, Western-centric training data biases, and cross-border data compliance—and establishes an institutional governance charter for sustainable business school transformation.

Simple modifications to existing syllabi are not enough as intelligent systems are changing how global companies orchestrate production, regulatory friction, and cross-cultural communication. For IB education tobe relevant, institutions need to redesign their curriculum around a purpose, i.e.,to train boundary spanning global leaders to orchestrate Algorithmic Value-Chains. With the proposed Three Horizon Curricular Transformation and Synthetic Global Commerce Lab, the gap between algorithmic competency and institutional, legal, and cultural judgment can be addressed systematically. Experiences in the classroom with multi-tier GVC wargaming, automated FTA rules of origin auditing, cross-border M&A regulatory panels, and multilingual consumer sentiment forensics show that with AI used as a metacognitive and simulation tool, students are able to have better causal understanding, critical thinking, and cross-cultural understanding. AI in International Business education should not be about automating human intelligence but rather enhancing human agency in a socio-technical system. With first principles understanding, ethical, and cross-cultural understanding, education can enable the next generation of global business leaders to effectively lead an intelligent global economy. items.title: AI-Enabled Digital Twins for Predictive Maintenance: A Case Study

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Scientific Journal of Engineering and Management
items.abstract_text: The increasing use of automation and advanced machinery in modern industries has made equipment reliability and operational efficiency important factors in industrial production. Unexpected machine failures can interrupt production activities, increase maintenance expenses, and affect overall productivity. Traditional maintenance approaches, such as reactive and preventive maintenance, are often unable to identify early signs of equipment failure or accurately determine when maintenance is actually required. To overcome these limitations, this paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin technology for predictive maintenance in industrial environments. A Digital Twin is a virtual representation of a physical machine or industrial system that is continuously updated using data collected from sensors installed on the actual equipment. By combining this technology with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning algorithms, it becomes possible to monitor equipment conditions, analyse operational patterns, detect abnormal behaviour, and predict potential failures before they cause major interruptions. The proposed approach integrates Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, real-time data acquisition, data preprocessing, virtual equipment modelling, and AI-based predictive analysis into a unified maintenance framework. Machine learning techniques such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can be applied for fault detection, condition monitoring, and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation. This paper presents a case-study-based investigation of AI-enabled Digital Twins for industrial equipment monitoring, with particular emphasis on understanding how real-time data and predictive analytics can improve maintenance planning. It also examines the system architecture, working methodology, potential advantages, implementation challenges, and limitations of the proposed approach. The study highlights the potential of integrating AI with Digital Twin technology to transform conventional maintenance practices into more intelligent, data-driven, and condition-based systems, thereby supporting improved equipment reliability, reduced unplanned downtime, and more efficient industrial operations. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Digital Twin, Predictive Maintenance, Machine Learning, Internet of Things (IoT), Industry 4.0, Fault Detection, Condition Monitoring, Remaining Useful Life (RUL).

items.title: Does Generative AI Enhance or Erode Critical Thinking in Music Education?

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Critical thinking has been a cornerstone of education. Some wonder what these technological advancements will do to people’s thinking and, more specifically, to critical thinking. In this chapter, we look at some of the potential affordances and limitations to critical thinking regarding artificial intelligence (AI) and how educators might respond. We address three aspects of critical thinking as outlined by research. First, critical thinking is the capacity to problem-solve. AI has the potential to help solve problems, although it might also erode one’s abilities, what some researchers call “cognitive offloading.” Second, critical thinking is a social process where people come together to think and challenge ideas. AI and newer technologies in general might bring people together; however, they might lead to what we are calling social offloading. Third, critical thinking is dependent on a diversity of ideas. Generative AI has the potential to synthesize a diversity of information and provide greater access; however, its models and algorithms may slowly limit this diversity. We situate these conceptions of critical thinking in concert with AI and provide pedagogical considerations for music educators to move toward a more process-based approach to critical thinking. This includes creating purposeful moments for students to work collaboratively—or to gather—and think critically, while also using AI tools.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.

items.title: Reducing barriers to inclusive tertiary STEM education: opportunities for AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Australia’s growing demand for science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) skills contrasts with stagnant tertiary participation and persistent inequities. This brief review examines barriers to inclusive tertiary STEM education and the potential for artificial intelligence (AI) to support Universal Design for Learning. AI can provide multimodal content, personalised scaffolding, flexible participation and assessment, and support for self-regulated and collaborative learning. Effective adoption therefore requires institutional governance, AI proficiency and sustained educator judgement. Further longitudinal research in Australian tertiary STEM settings is needed to identify which tools reduce barriers, for whom and under what conditions.

items.title: Securing the Foundation of AI: A Deep Dive into Dependency Management and Security in Deep Learning Frameworks

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
items.abstract_text: Deep learning (DL) frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch have powered major AI advancements, yet their reliance on third-party libraries introduces critical, understudied security risks. This article examines dependency management in these frameworks, focusing on dependency characteristics, associated vulnerabilities, and mitigation strategies. We analyze 448 libraries, 8,641 dependency-related commits, and 72 vulnerabilities, using GitHub APIs, official package sites, NVD/CWE databases, and a developer survey. Our findings show that while both frameworks share similar dependency types, PyTorch has more dependencies with less frequent updates. Both exhibit substantial vulnerabilities—42 in TensorFlow and 30 in PyTorch—almost half of which are high or critical severity, many unresolved. Notably, cumulative vulnerability exposure events reach 9,653 for TensorFlow and 627 for PyTorch, largely due to repeated removal and reintroduction of vulnerable dependencies. We also reveal that most security fixes occur incidentally alongside dependency optimization or compatibility improvements. Only 12% of changes explicitly address security, despite 90% of developers acknowledging its importance, reflecting limited experience, over-reliance on dependencies, and unclear accountability. This study sheds light on dependency management practices in DL frameworks, highlighting critical security risks and offering actionable guidance to strengthen DL ecosystem security and resilience.

items.title: Top management team AI attention and carbon emission in manufacturing: the moderating roles of green innovation and industry IT attention

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study draws on the attention-based view (ABV) to examine whether and when the artificial intelligence (AI) attention of top management team (TMT) affects manufacturers' carbon emissions. Building on the idea that attention processes are context-dependent, this study also explores the moderating roles of organizational-level characteristics (green innovation) and industry-level characteristics (industry IT attention). Design/methodology/approach This study collects data on publicly listed manufacturers in North America. This study uses fixed-effect models with endogeneity and selection bias adjustments. Findings This study finds that TMT AI attention is associated with lower carbon emissions in manufacturers. Greater green innovation and industry IT attention can also strengthen the relationship between TMT AI attention and lower carbon emissions. Originality/value This study provides one of the first empirical examinations of the relationship between these factors. This research contributes to extant responsible digital transformation literature by providing evidence that TMTs' attention to AI is associated with lower carbon emissions in manufacturers.

items.title: Beyond access: the evolution of Portugal’s pharmacy-based vaccination strategy and the future role of AI-driven outreach

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Vaccination programmes increasingly face a paradox: expanding access does not necessarily translate into coverage at policy targets. Portugal provides an instructive example. The integration of community pharmacies into seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccination created more than 3,500 vaccination points and approximately 70% of influenza doses were administered in pharmacies in 2023–2024. The pharmacy share then fell to under 46% by 2025–2026, while total influenza doses remained broadly stable (2.41 to 2.56 million per season). This indicates a redistribution of doses across settings rather than a loss of vaccination activity; changes in age eligibility, high-dose vaccination for adults aged ≥85 years in SNS units, and invitation and recall activity may all have contributed. Influenza coverage among adults aged ≥65 years remained below the World Health Organization target of 75%, at 70.5% in 2024–2025 and 73.0% in 2025–2026. This suggests that, residual under-vaccination reflects barriers beyond physical access. The authors use “activation gap” descriptively for potentially addressable interruptions between eligibility and vaccination. Portugal already uses registry-based invitations and reminders, the open question is what a conversational layer, scripted or based on generative AI, could add. Evidence is relatively strong for reminders, growing for scripted conversational interventions and preliminary for generative AI. The authors therefore propose a registry-based randomised comparison of existing recall, existing recall plus a scripted conversational intervention, and existing recall plus a generative-AI conversational intervention, with incremental vaccination, safety, equity, trust and cost per additional vaccinated person as outcomes.

reading.overview: Vaccination programmes increasingly face a paradox: expanding access does not necessarily translate into coverage at policy targets. Portugal provides an instructive example.
reading.interpretation: Portugal’s seasonal vaccination programme illustrates the value of combining community pharmacies and SNS services within a broad delivery network. Changes in the distribution of doses between settings do not, by themselves, demonstrate disengagement or identify the causes of remaining under-vaccination, and they do not suggest that the pharmacy model failed: it expanded the density of vaccination points and was strongly supported by the public ( 7 ). An independently conducted repetition of the survey on public satisfaction with pharmacy involvement in seasonal vaccination would help determine whether this initially high level of support has been sustained across subsequent campaigns. The next policy question is how to improve coverage through this combined infrastructure, building on existing invitations and recall while determining the relative contribution of confidence, motivation, and practical and residual access barriers, and testing interventions accordingly. Conversational systems, including generative AI, merit comparative evaluation as possible additions to these approaches. Their value should be established through incremental vaccination uptake, safety, equity, trust and cost-effectiveness, rather than assumed from technological capability. These conclusions rest on ecological, aggregate data that cannot establish individual-level causality, and the mechanisms discussed will require confirmation through prospective, patient-level research. Such evaluation should be conducted independently of any specific commercial provider, using transparent and predefined criteria.

items.title: Parents’ Perspectives on the Use and Development of Predictive AI in Neonatology: Focus Group Study

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background: Predictive AI models, such as AI-generated early warning systems for detecting critical conditions, are being praised as promising applications in neonatology. Despite technological advancements in predictive AI, the integration of AI at the bedside remains challenging, and few AI technologies are currently integrated into routine neonatal care. A better understanding of the wishes and barriers of patients and, in the case of neonatal patients, their parents, is essential to bridge this gap. Yet, parental perspectives on the use of AI remain underexplored. Objective: This study explored the perspectives of parents whose child had previously been admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit about the development and use of predictive AI in neonatal clinical settings. Methods: We conducted 3 focus groups with 18 Dutch parents of children admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit to explore their views on AI in neonatal care. Participants were purposively recruited via a neonatology parent and patient organization. Discussions focused on predictive AI in acute settings and on AI to predict neurodevelopmental outcomes in later life. A reflexive thematic analysis of the focus group data was performed. Results: Parents generally welcomed predictive AI as a supportive tool for the medical team, anticipating improvements in patient outcomes. AI for short-term predictions was especially appreciated, whereas longer-term predictions were received with some reservations. Overarching concerns regarding predictive AI systems included AI undermining parental intuition, overreliance on AI in decision-making, and undesirable ethical and psychological implications of long-term health predictions. Interestingly, in addition to predictive AI systems that support medical judgment, parents also hoped that other AI tools could be developed to better involve parental input in the decision-making process. Specifically, they envisioned applications that extend beyond clinical decision support to provide parents with information, emotional support, and tailored guidance on the right course of action. Conclusions: Parental perspectives highlight both opportunities and challenges for predictive AI integration in neonatal care. Engaging parents in the design and implementation of AI informs the development of family-centered, ethically responsible AI solutions and may identify opportunities for developing parent-centered AI tools alongside systems designed to support clinicians.

reading.interpretation: Throughout the focus groups, it became evident that parents’ past experiences in the NICU had a significant impact on how they viewed the potential of AI in neonatal care. That is, parents often discussed their perspectives about AI by sharing memories of how they had experienced neonatal care, and reflecting on the potential AI would have had on the ways in which care was provided. In line with parents’ perspectives shaped by their past experiences, integrating predictive AI systems into neonatal clinical care was generally viewed positively. The hypothetical use of AI for short-term predictions was especially appreciated, whereas longer-term predictions were received with some reservation. A dominant theme across the literature on the use of AI in clinical settings was the envisioned role of AI as a supportive tool for the existing medical team, with adequate and continuous human oversight [ 15 , 19 , 20 , 39 - 42 ]. This envisioned role of AI was confirmed as desirable by the parents in our study, who, despite their enthusiasm about AI’s potential for neonatal care, were adamant about the preservation of human expertise, oversight, and contact when AI is used. In contrast to those with a medical background, parents without a medical background more frequently reported feeling insufficiently acknowledged or included by medical staff, sometimes accompanied by uncertainty about which questions were appropriate or necessary to ask. Nonetheless, no clear or consistent differences in perspectives about predictive AI in neonatology emerged from the focus groups, in contrast to earlier findings [ 21 , 24 , 25 ]. On the other hand, it elicited hopes regarding the development of AI systems that could support parents during the period in which their child receives neonatal care

analysis.methods: To explore parents’ perspectives on implementing predictive AI in neonatal clinical care and at the NICU, we conducted a focus group study. Focus groups are semistructured discussions in small groups where participants can share and compare experiences and explore various topics. This is especially valuable when discussing a complex and relatively new topic, such as AI in neonatal care [ 26 , 27 ]. Participants were eligible if they were the parent or caregiver of a child who had been admitted to a NICU in the Netherlands, spoke Dutch, and were available on the date of the focus groups. Participants were purposively recruited via the neonatology parent and patient organization Care4Neo, which reached out to their members and community via newsletter, email, and social media. Interested participants self-selected to participate by providing their contact details through an online form, after which they were contacted by telephone by LS to receive additional information and the written consent form. The data were collected during 3 online focus groups. The focus groups took place in April 2025 and were conducted via Microsoft Teams. Online interviews were chosen to facilitate participation by parents with young children, with previous research indicating that they produce results comparable to those of face-to-face focus groups [ 28 , 29 ]. To facilitate in-depth discussion on the hypothetical integration of predictive AI systems in neonatology, the focus groups initially examined current practices in neonatology and then concentrated on parents’ perspectives on the hypothetical use of AI applications in such contexts. A semistructured topic list was used to facilitate an open discussion of relevant topics ( Multimedia Appendix 1 ). At the start of the focus groups, LS introduced the topic in lay terms using a presentation designed by LS and JD, describing 2 examples of predictive AI models developed for use in the NICU, 1 model for early detection of late-onset sepsis [ 30 ] and 1 electroencephalography (EEG)-based tool for predicting long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes in extremely preterm infants [ 31 ]. The intended function and basic operation of the 2 AI models were described in accessible language, without intentionally or explicitly presenting potential benefits or risks to participants. These concrete examples were provided to give participants a shared and focused understanding of predictive AI in neonatology and to prevent the discussion from becoming overly broad or from referring to different types of AI technologies. LS facilitated the discussion to ensure that all participants had an opportunity to contribute and intervened when necessary to balance participation. Each focus group lasted between 120 and 135 minutes. All focus groups were audio-recorded and then transcribed verbatim. They were coded to ensure confidentiality, and identifying information was removed. The transcripts were then checked for accuracy and completeness by SR. The focus groups were conducted in Dutch, and quotations were translated semantically into English by LS and SR to preserve the meaning and richness of the original quotations [ 32 ]. As we used reflexive thematic analysis, our assessment of data sufficiency was based on the richness and relevance of the data, the depth of discussion, and the extent to which the research question could be meaningfully addressed through the dataset, rather than on a predefined saturation criterion. As such, we did consider information power insofar as we assessed the internal validity of the data and continuously ascertained that the level, quality, and variation of information we received were satisfactory [ 33 ]. The research team consisted of LS, KJ, JD, and SR. LS, KJ, and JD were trained and experienced in qualitative research and ethics of medical technology. SR was a medical student in the final year of her clinical rotations. All researchers were female, and none had clinical experience in neonatal care. None of the researchers had prior relationships with any of the participants. LS, KJ, and JD together developed the focus group design. The focus groups were moderated by LS, while JD took field notes and asked follow-up questions, and SR observed the sessions. The researchers’ backgrounds and perspectives may have shaped the focus group discussions and interpretation of the data. Throughout data collection and analysis, the research team discussed their observations and interpretations while reflecting on the potential influence of their own academic and professional backgrounds and considered alternative interpretations of the data. A reflexive thematic analysis according to Braun and Clarke was performed using NVivo (version 15; Lumivero) [ 34 - 36 ]. Data selection and analysis occurred iteratively and followed a predominantly inductive approach, while also incorporating deductive elements as we followed predetermined study aims and primarily focused on perspectives regarding predictive systems in line with our initial topic list. Nevertheless, although the analysis was informed by the study aims and some anticipated distinctions, such as between short-term and long-term predictions, specific codes and themes initially and primarily emerged from the participants’ perspectives as expressed in the focus group discussions. A first version of the codebook was developed by SR and LS, which was refined in conversation with KJ and JD. All transcripts were then coded independently by SR and LS. Coding and interpretation were then discussed within the research group (SR, LS, KJ, and JD), including differences in coding, with attention to the meaning of the text fragments in the context of the focus group discussions. Through these discussions, alternative perspectives on the emerging findings were considered, while the coding and interpretation of the data were jointly refined within the research group. Throughout the analysis, codes were adapted and additional codes were added when needed, a process that was always discussed with the entire research group. Finally, codes were organized into potential themes, and accompanying quotes were selected for each theme. The coding tree is available in Multimedia Appendix 2 . The data are presented in the form of themes supported by illustrative quotes from participants ( Multimedia Appendix 3 ). The complete dataset is not publicly available due to the sensitive nature of the data, which is protected under Article 9 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The study was performed in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. The research protocol was reviewed by the research quality control committee of the University Medical Center Utrecht and was deemed exempt from the Medical Research Involving Humans Act ( Wet medisch-wetenschappelijk onderzoek met mensen [WMO]). On the other hand, it elicited hopes regarding the development of AI systems that could support parents during the period in which their child receives neonatal care. That is, even though the focus groups were designed to specifically explore parents’ perspectives on the use of predictive AI for clinical decision support, parents—particularly those who did not have a medical background themselves and did not have medical professionals in their social circle to call upon—frequently brought up other potential AI applications that could support them, such as AI-mediated communication tools and emotional support systems for parents. More broadly, they spontaneously suggested a range of functions that they envisioned AI could provide, although some of these would not necessarily require an AI application. For example, one suggestion was that a system could play recordings of parents’ voices to their baby when they were unable to be present. While such a function could potentially be developed as a digital tool, it may not inherently require AI. This broad understanding of what AI could encompass for neonatology suggests that the participants’ expectations may extend beyond applications for which AI is likely the most suitable technology. Overall, this study gave rise to several overarching ethical considerations regarding predictive and general AI development and implementation in neonatal clinical care. These considerations are presented in Table 2 . They include aspects specific to short-term or long-term predictions, as well as general considerations that apply more broadly to AI irrespective of the prediction timeframe or application. Specifically, these encompass ethical considerations regarding (1) the effects on parental intuition and uncertainty about the child’s outcome, (2) actionability of a prediction or outcome, and (3) the need for ongoing parental support and engagement. We urge researchers, developers, clinicians, and other stakeholders to take these into account when they design, adopt, or use AI systems in neonatology. In what follows, we elaborate on and contextualize these essential ethical considerations stemming from the focus groups. In contrast to predictive AI in acute settings, parents expressed reservations about the hypothetical prospect of AI generating long-term predictions about their child’s health. Their concerns centered on the inherent uncertainty underlying such predictions and the burdens these might impose, both presently and in the future, on their child and themselves as parents. Notably, these concerns seem to be related to the broader ethical and psychological issues associated with predictive health information. After all, similar arguments are found in debates surrounding genetic screening for adults, such as genetic screening for a predisposition to breast cancer (eg, “Do I want to be aware of this knowledge when it is uncertain whether I will actually develop the disease?”) [ 43 , 44 ], or for Alzheimer disease (eg, “Do I want to know my risk if no effective treatment exists?”) [ 45 - 47 ]. In these cases, the concerns reflect the same underlying ethical tension between the potential benefits of foreknowledge and the psychological and social burdens that such knowledge may impose. Regarding newborn screening, for instance, screening for rare genetic diseases or prognostic screening for neurodevelopmental conditions, similar concerns have been echoed [ 22 , 48 ]. Although parents may certainly express enthusiasm about the potential of prognostic tests and may strongly desire such prognostic information [ 49 - 51 ], hesitancy when such information concerns their own child is also highlighted [ 22 ]. Consistent with the perspectives of parents in our study, worries about the potential loss of hope or the risk of stigmatization have previously been cited as reasons why predictive health information can be perceived as challenging [ 22 ]. Difficulties in obtaining adequate informed consent, the psychological burden on families, the emotional distress that may arise for young children who are aware of an untreatable condition, and broader ethical considerations such as the child’s right to informational self-determination (eg, the child’s right to an open future) all contribute to this challenge [ 48 , 50 , 52 , 53 ]. Throughout the broader debate on predictive health information, the urgency to continuously assess the psychological and social impact is consistently voiced; especially when it concerns minors, who are assumed to be particularly vulnerable [ 43 , 52 , 54 ]. When contemplating the use of predictive AI, particularly regarding a child’s health later in life, similar concerns should not be overlooked. The provision of information about anything related to the care of their children was one of the most pressing concerns among parents in our study. Interestingly, such a need or desire to be informed is similar to what is known from other studies of parental or patient perspectives on AI in pediatric medicine and radiology [ 15 , 16 , 20 , 42 ]. items.abstract_text: In a global information environment characterised by strong propaganda pressures and a lack of transparency, the demand for independent, high-quality sources is constantly growing. A significant gap is thus emerging between the growing complexity of information flows and users' ability to critically evaluate information. Currently, neither information professionals nor engaged citizens are able to accurately verify every single piece of news, nor do they have access to online platforms capable of selecting, verifying, and aggregating thematic content based on shared quality criteria. The lack of human and technical resources severely hinders the creation of information ecosystems resilient to disinformation. To address this challenge, recent efforts have focused on integrated platforms that combine human expertise with advanced automated analysis tools. Technologies such as machine learning, semantic analysis, and generative artificial intelligence offer innovative solutions for processing large volumes of data and supporting automated fact-checking. Nonetheless, the evolution of these technologies introduces new complexities, reshaping content production and distribution. Algorithms often amplify information polarisation. Traditional media increasingly align with partisan political and economic interests, losing credibility. As a result, citizens align themselves with different news sources in an attempt to reconstruct the truth within a fragmented digital landscape. By bringing together the analysis of manipulative strategies, the evolution of verification methods, hybrid human–AI workflows, and the requirements of explainability within a single survey, the article aims to offer researchers and practitioners a more integrated reference point for the design of effective and accountable verification systems.
