items.abstract_text: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate human-like text, it is becoming an increasingly pressing empirical and societal question: how can AI-generated text be distinguished from human-written text? Through two studies, this paper explored whether and how people judge AI authorship. In Study 1, participants (n = 101) judged the written responses to an inside joke prompt (the prompt chosen based on LLMs' response) and assessed each response on a 7-point scale of −3, definitely AI-written, to +3, definitely human-written, followed by self-reports of justifications. People's classifications were near chance accuracy (51.1%), but their continuous ratings did separate the human-written from the AI-written responses. Multivariate logistic regression showed that accuracy was best predicted by attention to surface-level errors and structural features rather than by deeper experiential cues (for example, interpretations of humor and personal schema matches). In Study 2, a new sample (n = 100) evaluated AI responses deliberately modified with spelling and grammatical errors. Accuracy dropped steeply in participants below chance (39.2%), validating the conclusion of Study 1. Together, the results of these two studies reveal that people's capacity to detect human expression rests less on detecting genuine lived experience than on superficial linguistic cues that are easy to manipulate.

analysis.methods: This research aimed to examine whether human evaluators could distinguish between responses generated by humans and those generated by an LLM and the specific strategies they relied upon. There is no standardized stimulus set for assessing "humanness" in open-ended language production; therefore, all stimuli were developed step by step in several phases to reflect both human intuitions and AI strategies about what makes a text convincingly human. First, in the stimulus development process, three widely used LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek) were told about this research on how well humans can detect AI authorship. Since the aim was to give humans the best chance, the LLMs were asked in which scenarios it would be most difficult for them to "pass" as humans. All three LLMs gave the same two scenarios, that is, childhood memories with sensory experiences and inside jokes (see Appendix A). The meaning of the first one is more intuitive; the second one needs a more specific definition and clarification. In this paper, inside jokes are defined in the same way as they were defined for participants: humorous references that only a small group of people can understand, due to shared context or experience. This definition is consistent with prior work on conversational humor and shared mental models, as well as the modern dictionary [24, 25] . Unlike general trivia or abstract opinion pieces, inside jokes require the author to draw on genuinely idiosyncratic social memory, a specific group of people, a shared moment, and an emotional context that cannot be easily fabricated from statistical patterns alone. The LLMs justified the consensus of the two scenarios by pointing out that these prompts required access to personal experience, shared social context, and subjective sensory memory. However, they neither have authentic experiences nor a group of friends like humans do. Consequently, both domains are ecologically relevant and theoretically motivated as a test bed for authorship detection. On the basis of informal testing, it was found that the AI responses to childhood memory prompt significantly differed from responses by human subjects, in terms of style and detail, whereas AI inside jokes were more plausible. Hence, the inside joke prompt was chosen because it is theoretically demanding but also empirically fair. Once the inside-joke prompt was chosen, a full set of stimuli was built with responses from humans and from ChatGPT 4.0. First, ChatGPT 4.0 received the prompt below and was asked to write 10 inside jokes that would make people believe a human wrote them: "Your task here is to convince other people that you are a human and not an AI. To do that, we would like you to answer a question about an inside joke you have with your friends. An inside joke is something humorous that only a small group of people would understand, because they know the context. As you answer, keep in mind things or ways people say things that AIs wouldn't. There is no minimum or maximum word count. Please take your time and do your best -there are no right or wrong answers." Question: Can you tell us an inside joke you have with your friends and what it means to you? Then, human respondents received the same task in a Qualtrics survey, and each of them gave an example of an inside joke from their own lives (see Appendix B). The respondents also explained the strategy they used to convince others that a human had written their answer. These explanations were then analyzed for strategies that came up often. For this step, the 51 responses were all put into ChatGPT 4.0, and the LLM was instructed to list the different strategies the human respondents had applied. The analysis gave six different strategies: (1) Authenticity: Using a sincere, genuine manner of expression when writing, recounting the reality naturally, rather than deliberately crafted or optimized (2) Avoiding AI "tells": Using deliberate stylistic choices to avoid features commonly associated with AI-generated text, such as overly formal language, generic phrasing, or rigid structure (3) Conversation & informal tone: Using a casual, conversational, or spoken-like tone, such as slang, asides, and rhetorical questions, when composing the response (4) Embracing imperfection: Using intentional or uncorrected imperfections, such as typos, informal grammar, abrupt phrasing, or uneven structure, to reflect natural human writing (5) Emotional appeal: Using expressions of emotion, humor, or affective language to make the response feel more palpable and relatable (6) Unique and personal content: Using specific personal experiences, idiosyncratic details, or unique perspectives to elevate the creativity of the responses Then, each self-reported strategy was coded by the LLM in a binary (0/1) way so that frequencies could be counted. Appeal to authenticity (38%) and reliance on unique personal content (22%) were the two strategies chosen most often. Since these two made up the majority, priority was given to responses in these categories when building the final stimulus set for Study 1. Five responses were randomly picked from each of the two categories, and the ten AI-generated responses from ChatGPT 4.0 were added, so the final set had twenty stimuli. All responses were made anonymous. Importantly, no grammatical errors were corrected at this stage; only minor formatting changes were introduced to make the texts appropriate for subsequent testing. Participants (n = 101; 36 Male, 63 Female, 2 Non-binary/Other) were recruited online through Prolific and voluntarily completed this study. All participants were fluent English speakers and writers. Among the participants, none were under 18 or above 85 years old, 4.95% were between 18-24, 25.74% were between 25-34, 27.72% were between 35-44, 21.78% were between 45-54, 6.93% were between 55-64, 9.90% were between 65-74, and 2.97% were between 75-84. Furthermore, 7.92% of the participants identified as Asian, 69.31% as European, 3.96% as Hispanic/Latino, 0.99% as Pacific Islander, 4.95% as Mixed/Multiple Ethnicity, 7.92% as Other (with the majority being African American), and 4.95% preferred not to disclose. In terms of highest education level, 11.88% earned a secondary/high school diploma, 22.77% had some college/university experience (no degree), 35.64% earned a Bachelor's degree, 19.80% earned a Master's degree, 3.96% earned a Doctorate/PhD, 4.95% reported Other, and 0.99% preferred not to disclose.
analysis.discussion: The first question was whether humans could tell whether the responses to the inside joke prompts were produced by a human or AI. To do this, participants' ratings of each inside joke (the rating from the 7-point scale) were examined. As seen in Figure 1 , participants rated human-created inside jokes as being more likely to be written by a human (M = 0.254, SD = 1.05) and rated AI-generated jokes as more likely to have been written by an AI (M = -0.438, SD = 1.09), t(100) = 4.34, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.43. The average ratings were relatively close to the midpoint of the scale; however, there was a significant difference between them according to the true source of the responses. In Figure 1 , error bars represent standard errors. To assess participants' overall accuracy, each rating was recoded as correct if the subject gave a positive rating to any human-generated response or a negative rating to any AI-generated response, and incorrect if the subject gave a negative rating to any human-generated response or a positive rating to any AI-generated response. Ratings of 0 were considered incorrect, as this neutrality suggests that the subject cannot make a clear distinction. Participants performed only slightly above chance at discriminating human from AI jokes (M = 51.1%), but this difference was not statistically significant, t(100) = 0.581, p = .562, d = 0.06 (Figure 2 ). Participants more accurately identified human-written jokes as human (M = 52.0%, SD = 0.230) than they identified AI-generated jokes as AI (M = 50.0%, SD = 0.258). Next, the strategies participants reported using to discriminate between human and AI-generated responses were examined. Each participant's justification was coded for the presence or absence of eight strategies consistently reported by participants (see above). To examine whether some strategies were more useful than others for discriminating authorship, a multivariate logistic regression model was fitted with all strategy categories entered simultaneously as predictors of accuracy. The overall model was statistically significant, χ²(8) = 66.745, p < .001, indicating that these strategies collectively predicted identification accuracy. However, several strategies emerged as especially good predictors of accuracy. According to Table 1 and Figure 3 , when participants noticed surface-level errors (i.e., misspellings, ungrammatical sentences), they were significantly better at discriminating human-from AI-generated content (OR = 2.57, 95% CI [1.85, 3.56]). Likewise, participants were better when they attended to the structural features of the jokes (i.e., judgments about length, organization; OR = 2.21, 95% CI [1.44, 3.40]), relied on meta-inference about AI behavior (using personal beliefs about how humans vs AI behave; OR = 2.30, 95% CI [1.12, 4.75]), or focused on the emotional cues (evaluating tone, feeling, and/or emotional resonance the response transmits; OR = 1.96, 95% CI [1.07, 3.57]). In contrast, strategies involving stylistic voice, personal schema matching, humor diagnostics, and logical plausibility did not significantly predict accuracy when controlling for other strategies (Table 1 and Figure 3 ). Surface errors produced the largest estimated effect, increasing the odds of an accurate judgment by approximately 2.57 times. In Table 1 To assess whether the eight strategy predictors were excessively collinear, variance inflation factors (VIF) were calculated for the predictor matrix used in the logistic regression model. As seen in Table 2 , all VIF values were close to 1 and well below the commonly used threshold of 5, indicating that multicollinearity was not a concern. The VIF ranged from 1.01 to 1.02 across all eight strategy predictors. Therefore, all eight strategy predictors were retained as separate variables in the model. Lastly, the ROC and the AUC were computed to judge how well the logistic regression model predicted as a whole. The AUC was 0.602; thus, the strategy predictors together separated accurate and inaccurate judgments better than chance, but the predictive strength of the model as a whole was modest (Figure 4 ). Study 1 tested how well people tell human and AI-generated responses apart in a context, inside jokes, chosen to bring out uniquely human experience. Accuracy was nominally higher than chance, but statistical tests did not find this gap significant (Figure 2 ). Human-authored responses were also identified more successfully than AI-generated ones (Figure 2 ). A slight response bias may explain this, that is, a tendency of participants to label responses as human-authored. In everyday life, human communication is the default way of interaction; therefore, participants may have been more ready to assume an ambiguous response came from a human and not from AI. This subtle but significant difference may also come from greater familiarity with human communication patterns, since participants have heard and read humanauthored language all their lives; thus, small cues of human writing may reach their instinct and gut more quickly and be a little easier to recognize than the signs of AI-generated text. The strategies that participants reported are in line with this explanation, and they also show more about how these judgments work. Several strategies did, indeed, matter, including attention to surface errors, structural features of the response, emotion cues, and meta-inference about how AI computers were likely to respond (Table 1 ). In contrast, strategies unique to human experience, such as humor interpretation, personal schema matching (which was expected, given that participants reported having used them in stimulus design), did not reliably predict accuracy. Therefore, this ironic reliance on simple, heuristic and superficial cues is worth noting; it shows that if human judgments are ambiguous, people may turn to cues that are easy to find instead of thinking more carefully about meaning or even about the authenticity of experience, and this fits cognitive load theory [26] . Of all the strategies, surface error has especially strong predictive power. For example, participants took grammatical errors, spelling mistakes and informal slips as signs of human authorship. This shows the schema people now hold for human and AI writing; humans naturally make capitalization, subject-verb and spelling errors in spontaneous communication, so human answers are seen as "imperfect," but AI answers try to have as few such errors as possible and "perfectly" follow the grammar rules. It is likely that the judging heuristic was based on this schema. In addition, grammatical and spelling errors are very prominent and also unambiguous; thus, compared with features like humor or coherence, participants can judge them easily and with confidence. But signaling asymmetry complicates the confidence: their presence strongly signals human authorship, but their absence does not. Yet, even so, because they are informative when present, they retained predictive power. Structural features were also a significant predictor of classification accuracy; this shows that participants judged authorship by easily seen parts of a text and by their schemas for AI-generated text. items.venue: Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science - Economics and Business Administration
items.abstract_text: Consumers can use sustainability information to consume responsibly; however, excessive and complex sustainability claims might confuse consumers and hinder proper evaluations. Based on cognitive appraisal theory, this study empirically investigates the impacts of sustainability information overload (SIO) on green information avoidance (GIA) and green information verification behavior (GIVB) and examines the moderating role of generative AI literacy (GAIL) and the associations of GIA and GIVB with green purchase decision confidence (GPDC). Data from an online cross-sectional survey of 468 adult consumers in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings revealed that SIO positively influenced GIA, and GIA negatively influenced GPDC. However, SIO did not negatively influence GIVB on average. GAIL significantly moderated the SIO-GIVB relationship: SIO was negatively associated with GIVB at low GAIL but not significantly at mean or high GAIL.GIVB positively influenced GPDC. An indirect effect of SIO on GPDC through GIA is significant, but the indirect effect through GIVB is not significant unconditionally. These results suggest that sustainability information overload is associated with distinct coping responses. From a practical perspective, sustainability portals and shopping applications involving GenAI should emphasize evaluability and verifiability rather than enhancing disclosures. Through defining GAIL as a digitally mediated capability from the consumer’s perspective which can serve as a coping tool, this paper builds on cognitive appraisal theory in the context of AI-mediated sustainable consumption and explains the critical engagement of consumers with sustainability information amid overload situations.

items.title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments
items.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Financial Crime Detection: Economic Efficiency, Accountability, and Legal Responsibility
items.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning and Data Analytics

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied to financial crime detection, offering potential efficiency gains over traditional rule-based systems while raising important questions concerning algorithmic accountability and criminal liability. This review examines 25 scholarly and institutional sources across law, criminology, computer science, and regulatory policy. It focuses on three areas: (1) the economic efficiency of AI in anti-money laundering (AML) and fraud detection; (2) criminal liability issues associated with false negatives, algorithmic opacity, and the due diligence responsibilities of system deployers; and (3) governance challenges relating to explainability, human oversight, and cross-jurisdictional regulatory harmonization. The review indicates that machine learning approaches offer potential advantages in identifying complex financial crime patterns and reducing false-positive alerts. However, the available evidence on overall cost-effectiveness and measurable crime reduction remains limited. False negatives represent a particularly significant challenge because undetected suspicious transactions may create regulatory, reputational, and legal risks. The analysis further highlights fragmented liability frameworks and the importance of due diligence in determining responsibility for AI-related failures. The review concludes that effective AI-based financial crime detection requires a human-machine collaborative governance approach supported by explainability, systematic false-negative monitoring, appropriate human oversight, and stronger international regulatory coordination.

items.title: Performance without capability: generative AI and the validity of assessment in higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

items.title: Weather warnings for a multilingual nation: The role of applied linguistics in the National Weather Service’s AI Language Translation Program

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The National Weather Service (NWS) recently developed an AI-powered neural machine translation system to deliver potentially life-saving weather warnings to the 68.8 million Americans who speak a language other than English at home. This forum piece makes the case that applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have a vital and largely untapped role in the continued development of this technology. First, dialect and register variation across multilingual groups demands ongoing sociolinguistic attention, as translation differences affect how people understand and conceptualize risk. Second, the metrics NWS uses to evaluate translation quality leave communicative effectiveness unmeasured, and demographic categories used to identify target audiences miss the breadth of bilingual experience, both of which applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have the tools to address. Third, indigenous, oral-tradition, and signed languages present challenges that corpus-based training cannot resolve alone, and reaching these groups will take community linguistic fieldwork and delivery beyond text. Warnings are only as effective as their comprehension, and applied linguistics can increase understanding and action during extreme weather events across a multilingual nation.

items.title: An Artificial Intelligence-Based Personalized Sports Recommendation Framework for Children with Disabilities: A Narrative Review and Cross-Disability Conceptual Model

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background: Children with disabilities are less physically active than their peers and face personal, social and environmental barriers to sport. Their needs differ across and within diagnostic groups, so uniform activity programs often fit poorly. Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) could support individualized activity recommendations, but their readiness for this purpose is uncertain. Objective: To synthesize evidence on physical activity (PA) and AI- and IoT-enabled technologies across disability groups and to propose a cross-disability framework for personalized sports recommendation. Methods: This narrative review combined a previously completed thematic synthesis of 49 studies (2015–2025) with a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE search (January 2000 to November 2026) using predefined terms and inclusion criteria, plus checks of IEEE Xplore and publisher records. Results: PA interventions show small-to-moderate benefits that vary by disability and outcome; for example, aerobic exercise improved attention in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; standardized mean difference = 0.84), whereas exercise trials in cerebral palsy were at high risk of bias. Technologies follow disability-specific patterns: gesture sensing in autism, activity monitoring in ADHD, gait sensing in cerebral palsy, seizure-detection wearables in epilepsy and sign-language recognition in hearing impairment. Small samples, laboratory validation and weak privacy reporting are common. The proposed framework links six modules: individual profiling, a structured activity catalog, hard safety filtering, transparent ranking, feedback and human governance. Conclusion: AI-supported recommendation may help organize accessible choices, but no health benefit has yet been shown. Staged evaluation is required.

Sources included PubMed and PubMed Central (PMC), IEEE Xplore, the Multidisciplinary Digital Publishing Institute (MDPI), Springer, ScienceDirect, the Journal of Medical Internet Research (JMIR), Nature/Scientific Reports and arXiv. The included studies were grouped into five disability domains: autism spectrum disorder (ASD; 16 studies), ADHD (7 studies), CP and motor impairment (7 studies), epilepsy (5 studies) and hearing impairment (4 studies), with the remaining studies addressing cross-disability or general assistive applications. The source review reported that searches used a general-purpose web search service rather than native database exports, that one reviewer screened and coded studies, that inter- rater reliability was not calculated and that no formal risk-of-bias tool was applied. 2.3 Evidence Source 2: Targeted Search for This Review Because the source review did not address PA or sport, a targeted search was conducted for the present manuscript (Table 1). PubMed/MEDLINE was searched from January 2000 to November 2026. M. Ryan et al., 2017). Second, AIoT technologies follow disability-specific patterns, with movement sensing most mature in CP, physiological sensing most clinically validated in epilepsy and communication technologies most developed for hearing impairment, but nearly all evidence comes from small samples or datasets rather than children in sport settings. It also agrees with reviews of health recommender systems that call for clearer reporting of users, recommendations and evaluation (De Croon et al., 2021). A second implication is that personalization should not mean more surveillance. items.title: What Were You Thinking? An LLM-Driven Large-Scale Study of Refactoring Motivations in Open Source Projects

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
items.abstract_text: Context . Code refactoring improves software quality without changing external behavior. Despite its advantages, its benefits are hindered by the considerable cost of time, resources, and continuous effort it demands. Aim . Understanding why developers refactor, and which metrics capture these motivations, may support wider and more effective use of refactoring in practice. Method . We performed a large-scale empirical study to analyze developers’ refactoring activity, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify underlying motivations from version control data, comparing our findings with previous motivations reported in the literature. Results . LLMs matched human judgment in 80% of cases, but aligned with literature-based motivations in only 47%. They enriched 22% of motivations with more detailed rationale, often highlighting readability, clarity, and structural improvements. Most motivations were pragmatic, focused on simplification and maintainability. While metrics related to developer experience and code readability ranked highest, their correlation with motivation categories was weak. Conclusions . We conclude that LLMs effectively capture surface-level motivations but struggle with architectural reasoning. Their value lies in providing localized explanations, which, when combined with software metrics, can form hybrid approaches. Such integration offers a promising path toward prioritizing refactoring more systematically and balancing short-term improvements with long-term architectural goals.

analysis.methods: This section outlines the empirical study, including the study goal and research questions, the study context, the data collection methodology, and the data analysis approach. Our empirical study follows established guidelines defined by Wohlin et al. [75] . We publish the raw data in the replication package. Figure 1 provides a graphical description of the study design undergone. The goal of this study is to identify the motivations that drive developers to perform refactoring activities, with the purpose of identifying the product and process metrics that can help understand the motivations pushing developers to perform refactoring. The perspective is that of researchers and practitioners seeking additional support to guide developers in performing the refactoring. Therefore, we derived the following research questions (RQs): RQ 1 . Do motivations for refactoring in past studies align with those found in software project change histories? Silva et al. [65] proposed a list of motivations for refactoring efforts provided by professional developers. Pantiuchina et al. [49] built upon Silva et al. 's motivations, focusing on quality metrics and static analysis warnings, extracting information from PRs. However, PRs represent developer interaction but cannot represent the full project change history [55, 78] . Moreover, PRs can be rejected; thus, it is also challenging to discern expert contributions among PRs accepted and not [79] . Hence, we investigate developer motivation, analyzing the single commits from the projects analyzed in the reference study [65] with a broader selection of product and process metrics. No prior studies considered employing the fully established product and process metrics [29, 54] with the refactoring history. Furthermore, developers' commits, PRs, and code comments may not be able to capture all the motivations pushing developers to refactor the codebase; hence, we ask the following: Are there additional motivations driving the developers' willingness to perform refactoring? Refactoring improves source code quality [50] ; yet, quality improvements in readability, performance, safety, and security are only part of the overall picture [48] . For instance, in an industrial context, it is essential to assess refactoring opportunities in situations with limited resources regarding work allocation and time [71] . Silva et al. [65] succeeded in identifying 44 refactoring RMs at the time they ran their study. Therefore, we investigate whether external limitations or additional motivations influence refactoring efforts. Finally, extending Pantiuchina et al., [49] metric assessment, we ask the following: To what extent can product and process metrics reflect the motivations driving the developers' willingness to perform refactoring? Based on Pantiuchina et al. [49] , a relationship exists between specific quality metrics and refactoring operations. However, their metric selection was limited to quality metrics and static analysis warnings. We extended their selection with established product and process metrics [29, 54] , as well as a bigger body of data used in our study, given the time frame between Pantiuchina's work and the present study, thus broadening the candidate for a plausible relationship to RMs. Therefore, we hypothesize that there must already be existing metrics in the commit history of software projects, highly correlated to the ground truth motivations and the hypothetically newly identified ones. The formulated hypotheses are defined as follows: • H 0C . There is no statistically significant correlation between the considered metrics and RMs. Motivation identification (RQ 1 ) -CoT Prompting for RMs -Human validation 4.1 Novel motivation detection (RQ2) -Compare LLM-detected vs. reference study RMs 4.2 Metric-motivation mapping (RQ3) -Open coding into RM categories -Calculate feature importance -Calculate correlations 4.3 RESULTS 5 AI generated RM vs Human RM alignment Catague of new RMs Catague of most informative SMs • H 1C . There is a statistically significant correlation between the considered metrics and RMs. Consequently, considering H 1C as the accepted hypothesis and therefore the evidence of correlation, we expand our hypotheses as follows: • H 1C.1 . The identified correlation is negative. • H 1C.2 . The identified correlation is positive. In this sense, this question aims at identifying the metrics that can explain the existence of the stated motivations and further understand their specific implications. And therefore provide a list of metrics to monitor and guide developers for refactoring recommendations. In this study, we considered as the context dataset the one published by Silva et al. [65] , which consists of a catalogue of 44 distinct motivations for 12 well-known refactoring types (RTs). In their work, they initially selected the top 1000 Java repositories in GitHub, 2 ordered in terms of popularity, and further filtered them, removing the lower quartile based on the number of commits, thus obtaining a list of 748 repositories with consistent maintenance activities. Additionally, they filtered out from the datasets such projects which did not show development activity while conducting their study, thus reducing the number of projects to 471. The final set of considered projects comprised 124 repositories, which featured at least one refactoring during the study period, and answers provided by developers regarding the specific refactoring activity to the author's questions on the refactoring motivation. The final set of projects comprised 222 commits, for which the authors provided answers for a total of 267 RMs, and 44 unique motivations. Within this set of commits, 463 refactorings from 12 RTs were detected using the RMT [72] . Therefore, to validate the motivations provided by developers, our study considers the final set of 124 GitHub-hosted Java projects described in the adopted dataset. 3 In Table 1 , we present the descriptive statistics of the projects that completed all the stages in the data collection (see Section 2.3). analysis.results: This section presents the findings of our investigations and addresses the RQs: To answer RQ 1 we analyzed a total of 758 pairs of RMs, where each pair consisted of two RMs, one from the RMs identified in our study and the other one corresponding to the RM reported by Silva et al. [65] , both related to the same RT. Our findings focus on the alignment with the reference study [65] and the agreement with human experts, followed by an examination of the underlying RMs behind the observed disagreements. Therefore, we needed to assess the alignments based on RM pairs resulting from the same RT. Considering the volume of retrieved RMs, applying a 95% confidence level and a 5% error rate, we sampled a subset of 198 pairs: 136 generated by the LRM, while 62 generated by V3 (see Section 2.4.2). Interestingly, V3 was found to produce more complete and reliable RMs in these fallback cases. As a result, the final composition of our corpus of RMs was composed by 69% LRM-generated and 31% V3-generated. To assess the degree of alignment between these LLM-generated RMs and the ones available in the reference study, we tasked the LLMs and three human experts to evaluate such alignment. In 59 cases out of 198, both the humans and the LLM judged no alignment with the reference study ("No-No", True Negatives), while 97 out of 198 showed agreement with both judging alignment ("Yes-Yes", True Positives). However, there were 42 cases of disagreement: in 8 instances, humans identified alignment that the LLM did not ("Yes-No", False Positives), whereas, in 34 instances, the LLM assumed alignment where humans did not ("No-Yes", False Positives) (see Table 8) . The LLMs generated RMs aligned well with human judgment in most cases, showing agreement in 156 out of 198 cases (∼80%), considering the combination of the true positives and true negatives (see Table 8) . Furthermore, we measured IRA via Cohen's kappa between LLM and humans, resulting in a moderate agreement (𝜅 = 0.567) and it was statistically significant (𝑝 < 0.0001) (see Table 10) . Moreover, according to Bowker's symmetry test, the disagreement was systematic (𝜒 2 = 16.10, 𝑝 < 0.0001), suggesting the LLM consistently identifies different RMs concerning the human ones in terms of interpretation or overlooking. Therefore, we can affirm that there exists a statistically significant, moderate agreement between LLM and human RMs, but systematic differences in interpretation remain. We were also keen to investigate whether specific refactorings were more challenging to motivate and agree upon. The most frequently represented operations were EM (27.77%), MM (17.17%), and MC (13.64%) (see Table 7 ). Less common types included RPack (3.03%), PUA (2.53%), and EI (2.53%). PUM showed the strongest agreement between LLM and human RMs (8 out of 9 pairs aligned), followed by PUA and EI, both with perfect agreement (5 out of 5). In contrast, MM presented the most disagreement, with 28 disagreements out of 34 comparisons. Inline Method (11 out of 16) and MC (15 out of 27) also showed significant disagreement. These results suggest that LLMs struggle more with refactorings involving method or class movement. Based on human annotations, 97 out of 198 RMs (approximately 49%) aligned with those reported in the reference study. Finally, to understand the rationale between humans and the LLMs, we manually analyzed the 42 disagreement cases, categorizing them into five recurring disagreement categories, each reflecting a fundamental difference in how LLMs and humans approach the interpretation of RMs (see Table 11) . All in all, LLMs tend to reason based on localized code context, e.g., method names or syntax-level cues, likely because they lack access to full project information. In contrast, human raters apply a more holistic perspective, considering architectural structures and long-term design goals when assessing RMs. For instance, in the Future vs Present Orientation category, humans often justify changes based on anticipated future needs, such as extensibility or scalability, whereas LLMs focus on immediate benefits, like current testability or readability. Similarly, in the Different Focus of Refactoring Granularity category, LLMs interpret changes at the method level, while humans consider higherlevel structures, such as classes or packages. These patterns suggest that LLMs are proficient in identifying surface-level improvements, but they frequently miss deeper, strategic rationales that require an understanding of broader software design intent. 1. Aligned or not Aligned?: Only 47% of the LLM-generated RMs matched prior reference study according to human evaluation. While there was an 80% agreement between LLMs and humans overall, systematic differences emerged; LLMs rely heavily on local code cues, while humans factor in architectural and strategic goals. Certain refactorings like Pull Up Method saw strong alignment, but Move Method and Move Class revealed persistent LLM struggles, emphasizing the need for deeper context understanding to align fully with past studies. analysis.discussion: We leverage the following section to discuss the key findings of our study by relating the outcomes to every research question and identifying actionable implications for researchers and practitioners. We also address the applicability of our results in favour of refactoring recommendation systems. As shown in RQ 1 , LLMs agreed with human judgments in 80% of the cases but only 47% matched RMs from the reference study. Systematic disagreements emerged, as confirmed by Bowker's test, with LLMs tending to interpret RMs based on local code cues, names, syntax, and immediate readability, rather than broader architectural goals. For instance, RMs for MM and MC saw substantial misalignment, with LLMs overlooking structural intentions behind these changes. In contrast, Pull Up operations had a near-perfect alignment, likely due to their localized semantics. Human raters, instead, often based their evaluations on project-wide consistency, long-term maintainability, and design abstraction, factors that are invisible in the local code snapshot available to the LLM. This gap reveals that while LLMs can mimic reasoning for simple refactorings, they fall short in capturing RMs rooted in architecture or foresight. 1. Local vs Structural Reasoning: LLM-generated RMs should be interpreted as partial approximations. They are effective for routine, localized changes but unreliable for strategic or architectural reasoning. To close this gap, future tools could expand LLM context with project-wide metadata or history-aware embeddings. According to RQ 2 , only 53% of LLM-generated RMs aligned exactly with the prior reference study. However, in 22% of the cases, LLMs enriched the rationale by adding context-specific nuances or detailing effects on testability, naming conventions, or structural clarity. These elaborations were never contradictory; instead, they made tacit developer knowledge explicit. This ability to extend RMs aligns with the finding that LLMs consistently emphasized clarity, maintainability, and readability. For example, when humans described motivation as "renaming, " the LLM often contextualized it in terms of onboarding ease or cognitive load, surfacing deeper reasoning that might otherwise be lost. Our study investigated the motivations behind performing code refactoring by employing LLMs on the version-control history data associated with the refactoring, compared their output to human rationale, as well as to the referenced prior study [65] . Moreover, we studied the extent to which product and process metrics can describe such RMs by analyzing their feature importance and correlation levels. Our results reveal that while LLMs agree with human judgment in most cases, they often diverge in deeper, architectural reasoning, favouring local, surface-level cues over systemic design intent. Still, LLMs demonstrate value in extending and clarifying RMs, surfacing implicit knowledge that is often under-documented. We further showed that most LLM-derived RMs are pragmatic, driven by clarity and simplification, rather than architectural ideals. SMs to depict developer experience and code readability proved informative but insufficient as standalone signals, reinforcing the need for hybrid solutions. Future research should focus on developing context-aware, LLM-guided refactoring recommendation systems that integrate both behavioural signals, such as RMs, and project-level insights. Similarly, future work should exploit the potential of further exploring prompting techniques, e.g., using multi-turn prompts, system-level metadata, or dependency graphs as prompt context. We believe such studies would provide LLMs with a more holistic analysis of the context involving the refactoring operation. LLMs can enhance traceability, documentation, and onboarding when paired with system context and developer interaction data. For researchers, this opens a space to explore enriched prompting, system-aware modeling, and empirical evaluation of hybrid systems. For practitioners, LLMs offer an opportunity to make the "why" behind code changes visible, fostering better collaboration and maintainability. LLMs do not just replicate developer intent; they can help understand, explain, and extend it. The next challenge is building tools that channel this capability with precision, context, and reliability. items.abstract_text: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

items.venue: International Journal of Technology in Teaching and Learning

items.abstract_text: The dominant automation paradigm, which measures artificial intelligence by its capacity to act independently of humans, is increasingly inadequate for complex problem-solving. This article develops the concept of Hybrid Intelligence, defined as an adaptive, self-regulating system arising from the synergistic integration of human and artificial intelligence to enhance cognitive abilities. Revisiting the cognitive-tools tradition through an information-processing lens, it argues that generative AI dissolves the safeguard that once ensured tools amplified rather than supplanted human thinking. It then specifies a layered, multi-agentic architecture in which AI agents and agentic AI are embedded within contextual and collaborative human layers. It applies this architecture to the phases of complex problem-solving. The overriding argument is that sustainable Hybrid Intelligence requires enduring theoretical foundations that outlast individual model releases, ensuring that human–AI collaboration genuinely enhances, rather than inadvertently constrains, human cognitive agency.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Health systems are adding verifiers, AI models that check another AI’s drafted care plans, to reduce errors and omissions. We tested a verifier in two ways. First, three AI models drafted care plans for 447 retrospective test cases; a verifier caught 5 of 17 errors checkable against the patient’s record when counting flags for wrong recommendations, and 10 of 17 when also including flags for missing care. Second, in a prospective trial (NCT07718893), we randomized 240 patients in complex primary care management programs in four states to unassisted physicians, physicians with a guardrailed AI assistant, or physicians with the guardrailed assistant plus a verifier. The verifier raised 11 alerts across 77 encounters; physician adjudicators judged 9 correct, but clinicians in the trial acted on only 1. Safety events were similar across arms. Effective verification may therefore require alerts that clinicians must resolve, despite the risk of alert fatigue.

The registered co-primary outcomes were CITE’s diagnostic accuracy against blinded clinician adjudication, and clinician alert burden and acceptance. The protocol also speciﬁed o ver-escalation with a 5-percentage-point safety margin and a midpoint halt rule, appropriate escalation, and time to decision. We report the trial according to CONSORT 202530 and CONSORT-AI31, and the retrospective testing with reference to TRIPOD-LLM32. Patients and the public were not involved in the design, conduct, or reporting of the trial. The trial took place in Waymark’s multidisciplinary primary care service for Medicaid managed-care members in Ohio, Virginia, Washington, and Illinois. Waymark teams include community health workers, care coordinators, pharmacists, and therapists, supervised by physicians. Waymark enrolls members whom validated risk models identify as rising risk for emergency department visits and hospitalization33,34. Encounters came from the care team’s clinical rounds, which by default discuss patients with multimorbidity or polypharmacy; this enriched enrollment toward these patients, as pre- speciﬁed. Eligible patients wer e Medicaid-enrolled and attributed to a participating primary care site, with English-language documentation and an encounter that required clinical reasoning. We excluded patients with hospice- or palliative-care-exclusive care plans, patients enrolled in a competing AI-safety study within the prior 90 days, administrative-only or pharmacy-only encounters, and encounters in which the supervising clinician was the principal investigator. The sample size of 240 was ﬁx ed in the approved protocol. We randomized patients 1:1:1 with a deterministic HMAC-SHA256 permuted-block scheme (block size 6), stratiﬁed b y site. Allocation was concealed in the trial software. Physicians knew the arm from the drafting interface and were not blinded; outcome adjudicators were blinded. In Arm 1, the supervising physician wrote the assessment and plan without AI assistance. In Arm 2, Gemini 3.1 Pro drafted the assessment and plan under safety guardrails, and the physician reviewed, edited, and signed it. The guardrails had six parts (Supplementary Table 7): a safety system prompt that required a cited source and a conﬁdence le vel for every recommendation and prominent red ﬂags and safety hazards; retrieval of matching summaries from a curated library of society guidelines; a citation check that marked citations outside that library as unveriﬁed; four aut omated veriﬁcation checks (drug interactions, laboratory interpretation, guideline compliance, and a diagnostic safety net); a second- opinion consensus check; and a privacy ﬁlter that r eplaced patient identiﬁers. The model ran at temperature 0.2. These guardrails represent the safety layer that health systems commonly add on top of a language model. In Arm 3, Gemini 3.1 Pro drafted the plan under the same guardrails, and CITE then checked the draft as a further layer before physician review. We chose Gemini 3.1 Pro as the drafting model because it had the highest MedQA accuracy (97.4%) among frontier models in a comparison of general-purpose models and clinical AI tools35. analysis.discussion: We tested a veriﬁer for AI-dr afted care plans in two ways and report two ﬁndings. First, in plans for authored test cases, CITE caught 5 of 17 checkable errors at its primary threshold and 10 of 17 at its broader threshold, with speciﬁcities of 97.3% and 93.9%. In the trial, it r aised no false alarms at its primary threshold, and physicians judged 9 of its 11 ﬂags v alid. Checkable errors were much rarer in live care than in the test cases: 1 of 161 live drafts (0.6%) had one, compared with 16 of 447 test-case plans (3.6%) from the same model. That one error was in an Arm 2 draft, which CITE did not check, so the trial could not estimate how many live errors CITE catches. CITE’s 9 valid ﬂags wer e missed workups and unsupported statements, which are real problems outside the ﬁv e checkable types. We also found a key challenge for use in real-world care. Even when CITE found real problems, clinicians seldom carried its ﬂags int o the signed care plan. Future research needs to examine why ﬂags ar e or are not incorporated into care plans, including the design of the tool’s user interface and the balance between alert fatigue The comparison of the guardrailed assistant with unassisted physicians answers the ﬁrst question that health systems ask: can a guardrailed AI model draft plans for physician review without adding safety events? We did not ﬁnd a lar ger randomized comparison of this kind in live care; the closest prospective study was a single-arm study of 98 patients12. Guardrailed drafts were similar to unassisted physicians on safety events (4.9% vs 5.1%), escalation, and time to decision, and emergency visits and hospitalizations were numerically lower with guardrails. This is the local evidence that governance groups ask for4. The conﬁdence inter vals do not exclude differences of several points in either direction. Two explanations could account for the gap between valid ﬂags and signed notes. All 5 ﬂagged unsupported statements stayed in the signed notes, and 1 of 4 valid ﬂags for missing car e led to a change. One explanation is automation bias19,20. In a randomized trial of 44 physicians trained in AI literacy, wrong AI suggestions lowered diagnostic accuracy by 14.0 percentage points (95% CI − 18.9 to − 9.1)21. In the randomized substudy of NOHARM, physicians with AI help often left out useful AI recommendations1, and other randomized studies of AI decision support found similar gaps13,25. Another explanation, which the trial could not test, is that clinicians judged some ﬂagged items not t o need a change. Two designs could close this gap: a ﬂag that the clinician must r esolve before signing, and a ﬂag sent t o the care team member who acts on it, such as the pharmacist for a medication The lower error rate in live drafts held even in rising-risk patients with many conditions and medications. The drafting model, chosen for its benchmark accuracy, also had the most clinically consequential errors of the three models in the test cases (15.0% of plans). The test cases over-represented risky scenarios and used a different rating process, so the two rates are not directly comparable. The direction agrees with reports that benchmark results do not carry over directly to care9,26,27. CITE raised few ﬂags, and this matters for any design that mak es clinicians resolve them. Clinicians override most decision-support alerts17, acceptance falls with repeated alerts18, and a trial of alerts for acute kidney injury found harm at some hospitals28. CITE ﬂagged 9.1% of liv e encounters and 14.4% of plans for authored test cases, did not increase over-escalation, and did not detectably lengthen time to This study has limitations. In the retrospective test, Claude Opus 4.8 drafted the ratings and was also the veriﬁer ’s model and one of the rated models, which may favor its own plans and its own detections. One model drafted all live care plans, in one organization in four states. In plans for authored test cases, CITE caught 5 of 17 checkable errors at its primary threshold and 10 of 17 at its broader threshold. In the trial, CITE raised 11 ﬂags acr oss 77 encounters, physicians judged 9 valid, and clinicians acted on 1; safety events were similar across arms. Effective veriﬁcation ma y therefore require ﬂags that clinicians must r esolve, designed to limit alert fatigue, and trials that select encounters with more checkable steps, such as visits for anticoagulation or chronic kidney disease.

items.abstract_text: While AI is rapidly reshaping higher education by offering greater accessibility, personalized learning, and enhanced student engagement, its adoption often surpasses institutional capacity to adapt governance, pedagogy, and knowledge practices. This study, part of an ongoing collaboration between the University of North Carolina Wilmington (USA) and the University of Hertfordshire (UK), explores the practical integration of AI in higher education and proposes an Artificial Intelligence Readiness Framework to support curriculum design, assessment, governance, and knowledge management. The paper presents an exploratory case study of guided AI use in a large postgraduate taught module involving over 300+ international students at the University of Hertfordshire Business School. Drawing on module-level secondary data and instructor reflections, the study examines student engagement with AI, challenges encountered, and implications for teaching and assessment practice. Preliminary findings suggest that structured AI integration within active learning activities supported idea generation, writing development, and student engagement. However, instructor observations also indicated that some students relied on AI-generated content without sufficient critical evaluation, resulting in weaker alignment with assessment expectations. While students generally disclosed their use of AI, concerns remained regarding overreliance and the development of critical thinking skills. The study offers preliminary practitioner insights and introduces an AI Readiness Framework to support the responsible and pedagogically informed integration of AI into higher education curricula.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is associated with changes in entrepreneurship education in emerging economies, focusing on entrepreneurial competencies, student cognition, venture originality and early graduate behavior. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a multisource, multicohort quasi-experimental design. Principal analyses draw on an approximately 900-student longitudinal survey and a preliminary 18-month graduate follow-up. Published evidence on educator perspectives and on 150 business plans with 45 interviews across three Chinese universities is used only for contextual triangulation and is not pooled with the study-specific statistical analyses. Findings In the principal student analyses, generative AI was associated with stronger opportunity recognition but lower divergent thinking and higher confirmation bias. Predictive analytics was associated with more evidence-based evaluation, while structured intelligent tutoring was associated with stronger metacognitive reflection. Published business-plan evidence is used only to contextualize homogenization. The 18-month venture-creation differences were not statistically significant and remain exploratory. Research limitations/implications The nonrandomized design, incomplete wave-specific attrition information, unavailable matching diagnostics, reliance on published contextual evidence for homogenization and educator perspectives and short follow-up period limit causal claims and cross-context generalization. Future studies should use controlled designs, complete longitudinal reporting, longer graduate tracking and cross-country comparisons. Practical implications Educators should require prompt logs, independent evidence checks, revision rationales and originality rubrics that reward local validation, assumption testing, judgment and distinctive venture logic. Social implications In emerging economies, AI can broaden access to entrepreneurial feedback and market knowledge, but inadequate guidance may yield generic ventures detached from local needs. items.title: Cross-Attention or Concatenation? A Multi-Seed Empirical Study of Code-Comment Fusion for Pull Request Outcome Prediction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Predicting whether a pull request (PR) will be merged, rejected, or left unre solved is a recurring problem in empirical software engineering, yet it remains unclear how much explicit fusion of code changes and reviewer comments adds over simpler designs, and conclusions drawn from a single training run can be misleading. We report a multi-seed comparison of encoder-based fusion strategies on a retrospective dataset of 33,955 PRs from 155 projects, three platforms, and 12 programming languages. A CodeBERT–RoBERTa hybrid with bidirectional cross-modal attention is compared with concatenation and late-fusion variants, four alternative code encoders (GraphCodeBERT, UniXcoder, CodeT5, CodeReviewer), unimodal baselines, and two re-implemented prior systems, using five random seeds per model. The cross-attention hybrid reaches 88.11% mean accuracy (sample SD 0.39 percentage points, pp) and outperforms its code-only counterpart in every seed (+1.85 pp; Holm-adjusted paired p = 0.008). How-ever, the seven best models lie within a 0.42 pp band, and cross-attention exceeds concatenation by only 0.34 pp on average across five encoders (positive for four of five, not significant for any single encoder); at one seed (42) the ordering of the two reversed. Review comments alone are about as informative as code alone, and combining them adds roughly 1.6–1.9 pp. Project identity is strongly associated with the outcome (Cram´er’s V = 0.60), so the random split used here probably overstates generalisation. All analyses are retrospective, use features that become available only after review, and exclude LLM-based baselines.

reading.interpretation: Our results suggest three practical lessons for work on PR outcome prediction. First, the main gain comes from modelling both modalities: adding comments to code, or code to comments, is worth about 1.6-1.9 pp, whereas the choice among cross-attention, concatenation, and several code encoders matters by tenths of a point. Practitioners with limited compute can therefore start with concatenation of pooled encoder outputs, which is simpler than cross-attention and statistically indistinguishable from it in most of our configurations. Second, fusion comparisons need multiple seeds: for CodeBERT+RoBERTa, the per-seed gap between cross-attention and concatenation ranges from -0.06 pp to +1.83 pp around a pooled mean of +0.88 pp, so a single seed can report anything from a near tie to a two-point cross-attention win. One of our seeds (42) happens to favour concatenation by a hair, while four favour cross-attention; the pooled comparison itself does not reach significance after Holm correction. Third, evaluation design may matter more than architecture. The strong association between project and outcome, nearduplicate texts across splits, and post-hoc features such as review duration can all inflate scores, and none of the architectural choices we compare addresses them. Whether the observed ordering of models survives project-held-out or chronological evaluation is an open question that this paper cannot answer.

items.title: From policy to pedagogy: a thinking-centered framework for epistemic agency in AI-enabled higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has challenged longstanding assumptions about the relationship between academic performance and student learning. When AI can generate essays, analyses, explanations and solutions, final products may no longer provide sufficient evidence that students engaged in the reasoning processes those products are intended to represent. This conceptual and theoretical paper proposes the IDEA framework as a thinking-centered approach to AI-enabled pedagogy. Drawing on scholarship in learning theory, reasoning, assessment and generative AI, the framework distinguishes among critical, systematic and creative thinking and connects these capacities to deductive, inductive and abductive reasoning. It further incorporates epistemic offloading and epistemic agency to examine how cognitive responsibility is distributed between learners and AI. The framework considers assignment structure, disciplinary context and learner development to determine when AI should be restricted, guided, or integrated. It also emphasizes making student reasoning, judgment, reflection and intellectual ownership visible. By shifting the focus from regulating AI use to identifying the cognitive and epistemic work that must remain meaningfully with the learner, IDEA provides a concept-to-application model for aligning generative AI with the purposes of teaching, assessment and curriculum in higher education.

items.title: AI-ASSISTED ACOUSTIC ANALYSIS OF LEGAL DISCOURSE PROSODY: OPPORTUNITIES AND LIMITATIONS

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The article examines the methodological potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted acoustic analysis for investigating prosody in legal discourse. Prosody is viewed as an essential component of spoken legal communication, shaping the expression of epistemic stance, interpersonal relations, discourse organisation, and persuasive strategies through variations in pitch, intensity, rhythm, pausing, speech rate, and voice quality. The study addresses the limited attention paid to the acoustic dimension of legal discourse and evaluates the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI technologies into prosodic research. The object of the study is the prosodic organisation of spoken legal discourse; the subject is the methodological potential and limitations of AI-assisted acoustic analysis of legal speech. The aim of the study is to provide a criteria-based evaluation of AI-assisted acoustic analysis as a methodological framework for research on legal prosody. The research is theoretical and methodological, drawing on studies in acoustic phonetics, computational paralinguistics, forensic phonetics, legal linguistics, and speech processing. Descriptive, comparative, and criticalevaluative methods are applied to assess AI-assisted acoustic analysis according to six methodological criteria: validity, reliability, scalability, interpretability, ecological validity, and legal and ethical admissibility. The findings demonstrate that AI significantly improves the efficiency, reproducibility, and scalability of acoustic analysis by automating speech preprocessing, feature extraction, and computational modelling, enabling large-scale investigation of authentic legal speech. At the same time, important limitations remain, including reduced ecological validity, limited model transparency, algorithmic bias, risks of overinterpreting acoustic evidence, and legal and ethical concerns. The study argues that AI should complement rather than replace expert phonetic interpretation. It concludes that a human-in-the-loop approach integrating computational technologies with linguistic expertise provides the most reliable framework for future research on legal prosody while ensuring methodological transparency, scientific validity, and legal accountability.

items.title: When AI Performs, What Remains? An Integrative Review of Generative AI and Cognitive Capital in Individuals and Organizations

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

The relevant question is not only whether a tool improves productivity, but which human capacities it exercises, which it replaces and which it leaves unpracticed. This reframing connects three literatures that are rarely read together: learning science, which separates performance from learning [18] ; organizational research, which treats absorptive capacity and routines as collective assets [20] ; and extended-mind theory, which treats tools as potential components of cognition [5] . Cognitive capital offers a common unit for these perspectives because it asks what remains available to people and organizations when systems change, fail or are replaced. It also makes visible a tension in the evidence: the more capable and fluent an assistant becomes, the easier it is to accept its outputs without the effort through which competence is built and judgment is calibrated. Managing this tension requires deliberate choices about when AI should support, challenge or step back. This tension will become more pressing as AI systems move from answering requests to executing multistep tasks with less human involvement. As agents take on more of the work, the gap between what a human-AI system can do and what people can still do without it may widen, and the capacities needed to supervise, correct or replace those systems may be among the first to erode. Treating cognitive capital as an organizational asset to be measured, renewed and protected, alongside financial and human capital, is one way to keep that gap visible and governable. These concepts are organized into four mechanisms, seven principles and testable propositions that remain hypotheses rather than a validated theory. Their value lies in turning a broad concern about AI and human capability into measurable questions that organizations and researchers can address together.

items.title: The limits of declarative authorship: the structural vulnerability of intellectual property in the age of generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

The real problem is that some humans incentivized by the IP system use AI to produce work and claim it as their own. The IP system is not designed to detect or resist this conduct. The declarative human provenance relied on by IP law would thus appear to be subsidizing such appropriation. If this is true, then the path forward is not simply detection, but an adjustment of the incentive structure. Some readers may remember the Inkasso case and the "above average talent" controversy from 1980s German copyright law. In Inkasso-Programm, the German Federal Court of Justice required a computer program to clearly exceed an average programmer's skill. EU software harmonization later replaced that test with the author's own intellectual creation standard and excluded other criteria (BGH, 1985; European Commission, 2000 ; Directive 2009/24/EC, art. 1(3)). Why should we stay away from that particular temptation? Raising a threshold of protection would arguably be a heightened threshold for originality, and it failed back then for several reasons. Elitism and subjectivity (who judges talent?) are two of its problems. Also, its punitive character toward a lot of genuine human effort would be another. It was only displaced by harmonization under Directive 91/250/EEC after it became clear that it would leave most programs unprotected and create divergence with other Member States (European Commission, 2000) . Raising originality requirements to exclude AI level output would repeat that test and fail for the same reasons. Another way may be to shift frameworks for IP away from protecting what AI commoditizes (execution) and toward supporting what AI makes more valuable (verification, curation, contextual expertise). Legal liability could enforce a narrow right in the certificate and verification mark, rather than the underlying output itself. The IP system should acknowledge that private contracts and restrictive technical protection measures will increasingly function as a substitute for public IP law, regardless of whether academia and policymakers think that is a good idea. More fundamentally, it calls into question the 300 year old premise of IP: that granting temporary monopolies over creative expression is the best way to incentivize production. In markets where production costs approach zero, the binding constraint is judgment rather than effort, and that premise may need revision.
