items.title: Generative AI and Cognitive Autonomy in Cameroonian Higher Education: A Conditional Amplification Framework for Learning

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly entering higher education, yet its implications for learner autonomy remain unsettled, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined how pedagogical GAI use relates to self-regulated learning, cognitive engagement, augmented cognitive autonomy (ACA), and deep learning in six Cameroonian higher education institutions. Quantitative data from 812 students and faculty members were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, followed by 24 semi-structured interviews. GAI use was positively associated with self-regulation, while self-regulation and cognitive engagement sequentially mediated its relationship with ACA. ACA was strongly associated with deep learning. AI literacy and institutional governance strengthened the relationship between GAI use and ACA. Qualitative findings revealed both reflective, dialogic uses and cognitive delegation. The findings support an emerging Augmented Cognitive Autonomy framework in which GAI amplifies learning conditionally, depending on users' regulatory capacities and institutional support, with implications for equity and human capability development.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: EPRA International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research (IJMR)
items.abstract_text: This study examined how internal control systems and ethical oversight shape corporate governance effectiveness in AI-driven organisations, using listed deposit money banks in Nigeria as the focus. The increasing use of artificial intelligence in banking operations has introduced governance risks that traditional control systems may no longer fully address. Previous studies mostly considered internal controls, ethics, and governance as separate issues, with limited evidence on how they work together in emerging economies. The study therefore assessed the effects of Risk Assessment, Control Activities, Information and Communication, and Monitoring Activities on Tobin’s Q, and also examined the moderating role of Ethical Oversight. A correlational and panel data research design was adopted. Secondary data were sourced from the audited annual reports and accounts of 13 listed deposit money banks in Nigeria for the period 2015 to 2024. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, Hausman specification test, and random effects regression were used for the analysis. The findings showed that all the internal control variables had positive and significant effects on Tobin’s Q, while Information and Communication had the strongest influence. Ethical Oversight also showed a positive direct effect and significantly strengthened the relationship between internal control systems and firm value. The study concludes that effective internal controls, when supported by credible ethical governance, improve market performance and broaden the traditional view of corporate governance in technology-driven institutions. It therefore recommends that deposit money banks strengthen risk management systems, widen internal audits to cover AI systems, establish active ethics committees, invest in secure digital reporting platforms, and provide continuous governance training for directors and compliance officers.

items.title: Longitudinal association between AI dependence and pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition: the role of AI self-efficacy and perceived stress

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into teacher education has brought both opportunities and challenges. While AI tools are increasingly accessible to pre-service teachers, excessive dependence on AI may inadvertently undermine their critical thinking disposition—a key competency in professional development. Based on social cognitive theory, this study investigates the influence of AI dependence on pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition, with a particular focus on the mediating role of AI self-efficacy and the moderating role of perceived stress. A three-phase longitudinal design was employed. The study tracked 461 pre-service teachers from Jiangxi Province, China. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the hypothesized relationships, including the mediation effect of AI self-efficacy and the first-stage moderating effect of perceived stress. Results showed that AI dependence significantly and negatively predicted pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition. AI self-efficacy partially mediated this negative association. Furthermore, perceived stress significantly moderated the first stage of the mediation process, such that the negative association between AI dependence and AI self-efficacy was stronger among pre-service teachers with higher levels of perceived stress. The conditional indirect effect was stronger at higher levels of perceived stress, and the index of moderated mediation was significant. The second-stage moderation was not significant. These findings highlight the potential risks associated with excessive AI dependence in teacher education: over-reliance on AI may undermine pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition partly through reduced AI self-efficacy. Moreover, perceived stress amplifies the negative indirect effect by moderating the first stage of the mediation process. This study extends social cognitive theory to the context of AI use and provides practical implications for promoting balanced AI engagement and critical thinking development in teacher training programs.

items.abstract_text: Purpose: This review synthesizes evidence from recent studies of human–AI collaboration in service and digital ecosystems to build and test a multi-level conceptual framework. Design/methodology/approach: Thirteen studies (Tier A) from 2024 to 2026 were analyzed in full text and compared with 25 qualitative and mixed-methods studies (Tier B). In total, 38 service and digital ecosystem studies were analyzed within this review. Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and the Affect–Behavior–Cognition (ABC) model was used as the underlying theoretical framework. Narrative and thematic analysis were employed to synthesize the results from the included studies. Findings: Transparency, process control and outcome control have significant effects on employees in terms of cognitive and behavioral effects, while system-initiated engagement has little effect. Human–AI interaction does not, on average, perform better than the best human in each task (g = ?0.23, p < .001), but does perform better than a single human in a variety of tasks (g = 0.64). Value is created through the integration of systems and not through technology itself. User experience, digital maturity, interoperable IT, and AI-induced technostress condition value realization. Originality/value: The study provides a three-stage framework, seven testable hypotheses, seven gaps in current research and an operational measurement for value creation at the employee level and for firm- and network-level value co-creation.

analysis.discussion: This systematic review contributes to solving several unclear issues of human–AI collaboration. Value co-creation through human–AI collaboration is enabled by the integration of socio-technical resources rather than by technology. An integrated multi-level framework that connects Service-Dominant Logic (S-D Logic) and the ABC model through Intelligence Augmentation is provided. 38 peer-reviewed studies (13 Tier A studies = 13 primary full-text studies and 25 Tier B studies = 25 studies for triangulation) were synthesized. The design parameters of transparency, process control and outcome control are the most reliable ones. Calibrated reliance rather than maximum adherence is crucial for decision quality. The materialization of benefits of collaboration is dependent on AI literacy, digital maturity, interoperable infrastructures and technostress. This paper provides seven formal hypotheses, seven research gaps, and an operational measurement agenda. To the scholar, this provides a platform for cumulative research in business, service management, HRM, and information systems. To the practitioner, human- AI collaboration should be designed, governed, and measured as an integrated system. The key issue is not if AI is deployed, but the extent to which humans and AI are integrated; the level of reliance that has been calibrated between humans and AI; and the extent to which organizations are equipped to deal with the resulting HR and service processes as AI becomes more and more autonomous. The key differentiator between those organizations that create value through human-AI collaboration and those that simply deploy technology through HRM and service processes, is their capacity to calibrate human reliance on AI; to govern and manage risk; and to ensure that the employee and service provider’s well-being is sustained. This review shifts the discussion from whether human-AI collaboration creates value to the issues of how, for whom, and under what conditions human-AI collaboration can create value. By mapping design features to employees’ perceptions, reliance calibration to decision- making quality, and organization readiness to network outcomes, the review presents a framework that helps guide research while providing practitioners and policymakers with a structural framework that can be used to implement human-AI collaboration in organizations. Theoretical and Contextual Contributions of the Study Our theoretical contributions to Service-Dominant Logic, the ABC model, Intelligence Augmentation, and the Reliance Calibration mechanism are as follows: Firstly, by integrating four different theoretical viewpoints into one holistic framework and thus adding value to the current knowledge in this field. Secondly, by clearly positioning Service-Dominant Logic as the underlying macro-logic for creating value through the integration of different resources, the ABC model as the micro-level response to any given input, Intelligence Augmentation as the mechanism to catalyze value at both the individual as well as the firm and network level, and Reliance Calibration as the underlying driver that explains how positive design features impact employee perceptions while average hybrid synergy is actually below that of the best single party (g = −0.23). Thirdly, by extending the logic of how value is co-destroyed by AI as an operant resource and how different employee, firm and network level boundary conditions such as AI literacy, digital maturity, interoperability and technostress impact the value created through hybrid AI systems. Finally, these theoretical contributions are translated into seven testable hypotheses, seven research gaps and a comprehensive measurement agenda. INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ACADEMIC RESEARCH IN BUSINESS AND SOCIAL SCIENCES Vol. 16, No. 11, 2026, E-ISSN: 2222-6990 © 2026 Value because of the application of AI is created by its integration into business, by the way it is governed, and by the calibration of employees’ use of AI. While deployment of AI is necessary, the main challenge for management relates to creation of value through these other dimensions. Therefore, key practical implications relate to transparency and overriding into AI systems, employees’ calibration of their use of AI as opposed to strict compliance with processes, and matching of processes to tasks between creation and decision making. The implications also extend to the typical challenges of establishment of adequate infrastructure and satisfactory cybersecurity as well as to specific AI stressors. Above all, AI literacy and sufficient redesigning employees’ roles to utilize AI effectively in their work are required. In terms of implementation, a phased rollout is suggested to be followed by measurement of employees’ reliance on AI and decision quality. Benefits for policy makers. The main implication of the findings for policy makers is to make meaningful human oversight possible and to understand that within the scope of the EU AI Act oversight by humans only works if they can test and challenge AI outputs. Therefore, there is a need for AI literacy, for process control and for outcome control. A risk-based approach for different tasks, the funding of shared interoperable infrastructure and standards, in particular for the public sector but also for countries in the Gulf region and other emerging economies, the protection of workers and their well-being and last but not least a longitudinal evaluation and shared measurement instruments are required.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the conclusions. First, the review is restricted to English-language, peer-reviewed publications from January 2024 to October 2026; it therefore omits earlier foundational empirical work (which is used here only for theoretical grounding) and non- English evidence. Second, the Tier B studies were verified at abstract or bibliographic level and are used for triangulation, so the strength of evidence behind each theme varies by tier. Third, the heterogeneity of designs and outcomes precluded pooled meta-analysis, and the effect sizes reported derive from a single primary meta-analysis, which itself shows very high heterogeneity (I² = 97.7%). Fourth, the 38-study corpus, while theoretically focused, is smaller than those of broad bibliometric reviews, and publication bias toward positive findings cannot be excluded. Finally, the framework and hypotheses are derived from the evidence rather than tested; they should be treated as propositions for empirical validation. The generalizability of the conclusions is also bounded by the sectors represented in the corpus, which, as Gap 5 notes, under-represent public administration and emerging economies, and by the pace of change in generative AI, which means that findings on specific tools may date quickly even if the underlying mechanisms of integration, reliance and strain prove durable. Future updates of this review should therefore revisit the corpus periodically and extend the search to additional languages and databases. items.title: Generative AI adoption and governance in universities: impacts on perceived research excellence and technology commercialization success in Southeast Asia

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: The International Journal of Information and Learning Technology
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transformed into research value within Southeast Asian universities by investigating the institutional and adaptive mechanisms linking technological capability to perceived research excellence and technology commercialization success. Design/methodology/approach Drawing upon institutional theory and dynamic capability theory, the study develops the Institutionally Regulated Research Adaptability framework and tests it using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 2,371 respondents across 170 universities in eleven Southeast Asian countries, with institutional-level aggregation supported through within-group agreement and interclass correlation diagnostics. Findings The results demonstrate that institutional AI regulatory capacity exerts stronger effects on adaptive academic reconfiguration than foundational technological capability conditions. Dynamic research agility emerged as the strongest predictor of perceived research value realization. The proposed negative moderating effect of excessive regulatory readiness was not supported; instead, regulatory structures reinforced adaptive responsiveness. Importance–performance map analysis further identified dynamic research agility and regulatory-ethical framework readiness as the most critical strategic intervention priorities. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, while institutional aggregation may mask within-university variation. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and comparative multi-group analyses to examine national-level institutional heterogeneity across higher education systems. Practical implications Universities should prioritize institutional AI governance maturity, strengthen adaptive research agility, and strategically align faculty capability development with regulatory frameworks to translate AI capability into sustainable research and commercialization outcomes. Social implications The study highlights how institutionally coordinated AI integration can strengthen regional research ecosystems, support responsible digital transformation, and enhance Southeast Asia's academic innovation capacity within emerging knowledge economies. Originality/value This study advances AI-in-higher-education scholarship by shifting analytical focus from technology adoption to institutionally coordinated value transformation. It introduces institutionally regulated research adaptability as a novel explanatory mechanism and provides one of the first large-scale multilevel empirical examinations of GenAI-enabled research transformation across Southeast Asian higher education systems.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines strategic content licensing between a generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform and a digital news publisher in digital news markets, an important issue for understanding where AI platforms rely on publisher content while competing for user attention. It analyzes how citation intensity shapes licensing incentives, pricing, user diversion and welfare. Design/methodology/approach We develop a game-theoretic model of two-dimensional horizontal differentiation in which the AI platform has a comparative advantage in content integration and the publisher has a comparative advantage in factual accuracy. The model examines how citation intensity, hallucination risk, user preference correlation and per-use royalty jointly determine equilibrium outcomes. Findings Licensing between AI platforms and publishers arises from a trade-off between two countervailing forces: entry displacement and engagement expansion. Content licensing requires sufficiently high citation intensity; mutual gains additionally require low preference correlation. The pricing effects of citation intensity are nonmonotonic. Subscription prices can rise or fall depending on the strength of citation relative to royalty costs. User diversion is shaped by the balance between referral traffic expansion and direct substitution. Welfare improves only when engagement expansion dominates entry displacement. Originality/value This study models AI–publisher licensing in a two-dimensional Hotelling framework of asymmetric comparative advantages, conceptualizing citation intensity as a content-composition variable that shapes output quality, user traffic and royalty payments beyond existing display-level constructs.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. Semantic patterns revealed overlapping orientations towards questioning, improvement, examples, feedback, and concepts, spanning clarification, answer checking, revision, application, and task-focused support. These findings distinguish interaction persistence from cognitive engagement and suggest that conversation design should support students to articulate their reasoning and co-construct knowledge with AI, rather than prioritising continued interaction alone.

items.abstract_text: Purpose As sustainable considerations increasingly influence real estate finance, traditional property valuation methods face limitations in capturing environmental, social and governance value. This paper aims to critically evaluate the role and potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven appraisal techniques in supporting informed and effective sustainable property investment decisions. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review was conducted, analyzing contemporary research sourced from major academic databases. The review focused on identifying AI applications (including machine learning and deep learning) used for valuing sustainable property attributes, assessing green real estate financial performance and integrating ESG factors into investment frameworks. Identified benefits, challenges and future trends were synthesized. Findings AI-driven appraisal demonstrates significant potential to enhance sustainable investment through improved accuracy in valuing green features, increased efficiency in data analysis and portfolio management and greater objectivity compared to traditional methods. Explainable AI techniques are emerging as crucial for ensuring transparency. However, key challenges remain, including the availability and quality of standardized ESG data, mitigating algorithmic bias, ensuring model interpretability for complex sustainability metrics and the need for skilled human oversight. Originality/value This paper provides a focused synthesis of the current state-of-the-art regarding AI appraisal specifically for sustainable real estate investment. items.title: Designing transparency in AI influencer marketing: a consumer–agency architecture

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose The purpose of this study is to develop an understanding of AI influencer transparency and its effects on affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a conceptual synthesis of influencer marketing, consumer psychology and human–algorithm interaction research. Findings This paper introduces the Consumer–Agency Architecture (CAA) framework, distinguishing between information, control and provenance transparency. CAA posits that effects of transparency on consumer outcomes are driven by reductions in reactance, whether affective or cognitive. Information transparency primarily mitigates affective reactance; control transparency reduces cognitive reactance; and provenance transparency can attenuate both. Lower reactance, in turn, can support the formation of affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. The framework further identifies boundary conditions that either strengthen or weaken the relationship between transparency and reactance. Research limitations/implications This paper proposes a conceptual framework that remains to be empirically tested. It also posits that transparency effects in AI influencer marketing are primarily driven by reactance, not gains in perceived authenticity. The developed model also assumes that transparency forms have distinct rather than additive or even nonlinear effects on cognitive and affective reactance. Such assumptions could be tested in future work. Practical implications Brands and platforms should treat transparency as a portfolio of design levers rather than a single disclosure: match the specific type of transparency to the focal objective, anticipate trade-offs and avoid one-size-fits-all transparency that can erode trust. Social implications CAA provides a consumer-welfare lens for governing AI-influencer ecosystems by clarifying how transparency can support consumer agency. Originality/value CAA frames transparency in AI-influencer marketing as a means of respecting and protecting consumer agency, offering a mechanism-based foundation for designing ethically grounded, trust-sustaining AI-mediated brand relationships.

items.title: From multitasker to procrastinator: multitasking entitles employees with high work identity to procrastinate

items.abstract_text: Purpose Although multitasking has traditionally been associated with unintentional efficiency losses, it may also generate intentional efficiency losses by fostering procrastination. Drawing on moral licensing theory, this study examines whether, how and when multitasking is positively associated with procrastination. Design/methodology/approach We conducted a survey of 362 employees across three time points to examine the relationship between multitasking and procrastination and explore the mediating role of psychological entitlement and the moderating role of work identity. Findings Multitasking was positively related to procrastination through psychological entitlement. Work identity further strengthened this indirect relationship by amplifying the positive relationship between multitasking and psychological entitlement. Practical implications This study offers actionable guidance for mitigating procrastination by reducing unnecessary multitasking, addressing psychological entitlement, and limiting the licensing risk of multitasking among employees with high work identity. Originality/value This study extends the understanding of multitasking's consequences by uncovering its potential link to intentional inefficiency and identifies psychological entitlement as a key mechanism linking multitasking to procrastination.

items.title: Large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.

For clarity, a single puzzle represents one complete Parsons problem task. Each puzzle contains all the foundational elements a student would need: a problem description, the correct lines of code (which would eventually be scrambled), the expected program output, and associated Comma Separated Values (CSV) data where applicable. These 315 puzzles served as the consistent baseline across all three stages of the study. By feeding the exact same 315 puzzles to the LLM in Stage 1 and Stage 3, we were able to conduct a direct comparison of the AI’s distractor-generation performance before and after refinement. This study used a GenAI-assisted methodology and did not involve human participants, student data, personal data, or identifiable information. Human involvement was limited to the authors evaluating the generated outputs. In accordance with the institutional requirements for human research, formal ethics approval was not Stage 1: Initial generation of distractors To address RQ1, a prompt containing the topic, context (e.g., Traffic Flow Analysis), question description, correct code, detailed distractor generation instructions, output constraints, and a predefined JSON output format for each puzzle was provided to Gemini-2.5-flash. A temperature of 0.7 was used to allow sufficient variation in the generated distractors while maintaining reasonable output consistency. The prompt incorporated zero-shot CoT prompting which required the AI model to specify its pedagogical reasoning behind each task before producing the final output. For each puzzle, the model was instructed to generate two logic - based distractors and two method-based distractors. A logic-based distractor changes the reasoning within a computational step while preserving the overall procedure. For example, the target procedure is mean error – specifically, Mean Absolute Error (MAE) – but a distractor used Mean Squared Error – a similar procedure but logically incorrect. In contrast, a method-based distractor replaces the computational method with a different one, such as instead of calculating sum, median is used. In total, 315 puzzles with four distractors each resulted in 1,260 initial distractors. The model was also prompted to generate a corresponding pedagogical rationale for each distractor, articulating the specific student misconception it intended to assess. Stage 2: Evaluation of generated distractors Stage 2 evaluated the functional plausibility of the generated distractors. First, each puzzle was verified whether it contained four semantically plausible distractors: two logic-based distractors and two method- based distractors. Second, distractors of the same type had to target the exact same line of correct code. For example, if the AI generated two logic distractors, both distractors should offer incorrect variations of the same correct line, instead of entirely different parts of the program. To evaluate each distractor, we replaced the corresponding correct line with one generated distractor, producing a modified version of the original program. Then, it was further assessed through two program-level checks: compilability and output divergence. The first examined whether the modified program could still be compiled in a Python environment without any errors. The second assessed output divergence by comparing the modified program’s output against the output of the correct solution. A distractor was considered output- divergent when the modified program produced a different result, indicating a notable change in the behaviour of the program, rather than a surface-level change. These checks ensure distractors were not superficially created but introduce a meaningful change in program behaviour that mirrors a genuine student error. items.title: AI-enabled reshaping paths of manufacturing firm innovation ecosystems: a dynamic capability perspective

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose Current research on AI-enabled manufacturing transformation largely focuses on the firm-level dimensions of R&D, production or marketing, with few studies examining how AI drives manufacturing transformation at the ecosystem level. This study addresses this gap by investigating the AI-enabled reshaping paths of manufacturing firm innovation ecosystems (MFIE) from a dynamic capability perspective. Design/methodology/approach This multi-case study adopts a dynamic capability perspective to conduct comparative analysis of four typical manufacturing firms, with data triangulated from in-depth interviews, corporate archives and industry reports, thereby identifying both common patterns and differentiated paths of AI-enabled MFIE reshaping. Findings The reshaping path comprises three components: differentiated reshaping pressures as the trigger, AI-enabled dynamic capability construction as the mediator and inter-ecosystem coopetitive replacement as the outcome. At different reshaping stages, focal firms build AI-enabled opportunity identification, solution diffusion and standard locking capabilities to resolve corresponding pressures. Four distinct paths are identified: technology efficiency enhancement, emerging market expansion, independent R&D technology breakthrough and ecosystem platform dominance. Different AI application strategy combinations lead to heterogeneous dynamic capability effects, influencing reshaping outcomes. Originality/value Departing from the single-ecosystem evolution perspective, this study conceptualizes MFIE reshaping as coopetitive replacement between old and new ecosystems and constructs a dynamic capability-based path framework and classification matrix. The study provides actionable guidance for managers to select and implement reshaping paths and offers implications for industrial policy formulation.

items.title: Can Grief Remain Slow in a Fast Digital World? Digital Cemeteries, Algorithmic Memory, and Slow Living

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: OMEGA - Journal of Death and Dying
items.abstract_text: Digital platforms have become sites of mourning, remembrance, and continuing bonds with the dead. Yet the temporal consequences of platformed commemoration remain insufficiently theorised. This conceptual article asks whether grief can retain a self-determined rhythm within digital environments organised by notifications, automated resurfacing, metrics, and circulation. It brings grief theory, digital mourning research, algorithmic memory, Slow Living, and Slow Memory into dialogue. The article argues that grief has no universally correct speed: it is discontinuous, relational, and marked by oscillation between loss-oriented and restorative activity. The problem is therefore not digital speed alone, but the transfer of temporal agency from mourners to platforms. To address this problem, the article proposes “slow digital mourning” as an ethical framework centred on temporal autonomy, contextual remembrance, reversible consent, non-metricised commemoration, plural rhythms, and the right to silence or forgetting. It concludes with implications for platform design, digital cemetery governance, and future empirical research.

items.title: AI-Driven Reliable SFC Deployment: Challenges, Opportunities, and Perspectives

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques are driving increasing volumes of reliability-sensitive Service Function Chain (SFC) requests from applications such as autonomous driving, smart manufacturing, and intelligent healthcare. These applications require not only feasible deployment but also continuous service availability under failures, disruptions, and uncertainty. Existing reliable SFC deployment studies have largely relied on rule-based approaches, which provide explicit formulations and interpretable decision rules but often struggle with dynamic, large-scale, and multi-objective requirements involving reliability, latency, cost, and security. AI-driven solutions therefore offer a promising direction for enabling adaptive and data-driven deployment decisions. This survey first clarifies the workflow of SFC deployment and the distinction between conventional and reliable SFC deployment. We then review rule-based reliable SFC deployment, analyzing its major design rationales, representative solution paradigms, and limitations. Building on this analysis, we examine AI-driven methodologies for reliable SFC deployment, with a particular focus on deep reinforcement learning approaches, which dominate the existing literature. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions toward adaptive, robust, and scalable reliable SFC deployment.

items.abstract_text: Practice-oriented cybersecurity education often requires novice learners to build target web systems by hand before security analysis begins, imposing extraneous cognitive load. An earlier study introduced a Red/Blue teaming model in which a large language model (LLM) agent builds the target systems (vibe coding) under Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) control, so that learners audit, attack, and defend. This single-cohort study examines learner-level evidence from the 2026 cohort (n = 34) of a university web-security course, set against institutional Course-Quality-Improvement (CQI) satisfaction records for nine of the ten academic years 2017–2026. Evidence comprised self-reported coding-effort logs (n = 25), single-item final-course survey measures (n = 27), and peer cross-evaluation scores (71 ratings). Logged total coding effort had a median of 3.8 h. In the final-course survey, 96% agreed implementation burden had decreased and 93% that deeper engagement in vulnerability analysis and defense design was possible (raw means 4.67 and 4.44 of 5; Wilcoxon p < 0.001). The 2026 CQI score (91.55) ranked second among the nine records (descriptive). In this single-institution context, delegating system construction to an LLM agent was associated with lower perceived implementation burden, greater reported security-analysis engagement, and high satisfaction; multi-site replication is required.

items.title: A Survey of Robotic Navigation and Manipulation with Physics Simulators in the Era of Embodied AI

items.abstract_text: Navigation and manipulation are core capabilities in Embodied AI, but training agents to perform them directly in the real-world is costly, time-consuming, and unsafe. Therefore, sim-to-real transfer has emerged as a key approach, yet the sim-to-real gap persists. This survey examines how physics simulators address this gap by analyzing properties that have received limited attention in prior surveys. We also analyze their features for navigation and manipulation tasks, as well as their hardware requirements. Additionally, we offer a resource with benchmark datasets, metrics, simulation platforms, and methods to help researchers select suitable tools while accounting for hardware constraints.

analysis.methods: As illustrated in Figure 3 , navigation agents must overcome partial observability by building memory of historical observations and actions to guide their decisions. Memory can be categorized into Explicit and Implicit Memory. Explicit memory methods construct structured representations of the environment for planning. They are divided into Metric Map-Based and Graph-Based approaches, which trade off between spatial precision and scalability. Metric Map-Based Methods. These methods discretize the environment into representations like grids, point clouds, or voxels to build a map, as shown in the 3D metric map in Figure 3(a) . Such maps are effective for fine-grained spatial reasoning and precise path-finding. For instance, many approaches use 2D occupancy grid maps to compute shortest paths [24, 51] . To enhance environmental understanding, maps can also be augmented with semantic information, such as object labels or language-grounded features extracted by models such as CLIP [29, 73, 146] . While metric maps excel at capturing detailed spatial information for low-level control, their significant computational and memory requirements for maintenance and updates limit their scalability in large-scale environments. More recent methods, including VLFM [207] and BeliefMapNav [231], combine occupancy or frontier maps with language-grounded value or belief maps for zero-shot semantic navigation. These methods improve interpretability and open-vocabulary generalization but remain sensitive to dense memory costs, perceptual noise, and accumulated mapping errors. Graph-Based Methods. To address the scalability limitations of metric maps, graph-based methods abstract the environment into a topological structure, where nodes represent key locations or landmarks and edges denote traversable paths, as seen in the hierarchical graph in Figure 3(b) . This abstraction is highly effective for efficient, long-range planning in large environments. Topological graphs are commonly used in tasks like Image-Goal Navigation, where nodes can represent panoramic views or image embeddings [11, 153, 162] . Additionally, knowledge graphs can model spatial and functional relationships between objects, enabling agents to infer object locations for semantic navigation tasks [201] . Path planning is then performed using classical algorithms like Dijkstra's or learned planners based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Implicit memory methods rely on learned representations, pre-trained knowledge, or predictive models to infer actions from a history of observations. This approach comprises three categories: Latent Representation-Based, Foundation Model-Based, and World Model-Based. Latent Representation-Based Methods. These methods encode sequences of observations and actions into latent vectors, which serve as the agent's memory state, as depicted in Figure 3(c ). Architectures such as LSTMs and Transformers are used to process sequential inputs (e.g., images, text) and maintain internal state, thereby integrating temporal information to mitigate partial observability [65, 234] . While effective for short-horizon tasks, these methods compress historical information, potentially leading to the loss of fine-grained spatial details. This makes them prone to accumulating errors over long trajectories in complex environments. Foundation Model-Based Methods. Foundation model-based navigation leverages LLMs and VLMs primarily as semantic priors and high-level decision modules to interpret free-form goals into actionable subgoals (Figure 3(d) ). An early paradigm converts perception into textual descriptions, enabling an LLM to perform stepwise reasoning and action selection [225, 228] ; newer approaches use VLM embeddings for open-vocabulary goal specification and scene understanding. For example, OpenFMNav [98] combines LLM-based parsing of user demands with VLM-based open-set perception to construct a semantic score map for exploration and exploitation, while OVExp [183] projects VLM features into top-down maps to support open-vocabulary, goal-conditioned exploration across unseen objects and goal modalities. To reduce partial-observability errors and hallucinations, recent works have coupled VLMs with structured memories (e.g., semantic maps or retrieval history buffers) or adapted them to incorporate past experience via fine-tuning [206, 220, 221] . More recently, several works have treated navigation itself as a primary pre-training objective and built navigation-specific foundation models. InternVLA-N1 [172, 182] uses a dual-system design with waypoint planning and low-latency control, while NavA 3 [219] pairs a global Reasoning VLM with a local point generation VLM for open-vocabulary, spatially grounded localization. Additionally, NavFoM [218] targets scalability across tasks and embodiments by unifying multi-view histories with viewpoint/time tokens and history selection. Meanwhile, NavRAG [180] scales supervision by using retrieval-augmented LLM generation to produce user-style VLN instructions from hierarchical scene descriptions. World Model-Based Methods. World model-based methods learn a predictive dynamics model to forecast future observations (or latent states) conditioned on candidate actions, enabling look-ahead planning, trajectory ranking, and synthetic data generation (Figure 3(e) ). For example, Navigation World Models [9] use controllable video generation to simulate egocentric rollouts for planning and scoring, while latent-dynamics approaches such as X-Mobility [114] predict in a latent space and decouple world modeling from policy learning to improve generalization capability. Other efforts in autonomous driving, including the GAIA series [68, 152, 181] and NVIDIA Cosmos [1, 2] , likewise emphasize controllable future generation and offline "what-if" evaluation of action predictions over observations. Robust manipulation in Embodied AI is shaped by both the learning algorithm and the sensing modalities available to the robot. In practice, system design often begins by selecting task-relevant variables to observe and the bandwidth at which to observe them. For example, global object geometry and free space can often be captured by vision, whereas contact onset, slip, normal/shear force, and local compliance require force or tactile sensing. This sensing choice constrains the downstream representation, controller interface, simulator requirements, and the policy architecture itself. We therefore organize manipulation methods along two perspectives: (i) Sensing Modalities, which determine what information is observable and how quickly it can be fed back during execution, and (ii) Policy Learning, which determines how the resulting observations are mapped to actions. We categorize sensing modalities by the information they provide to the policy. Vision-based sensing captures global scene and object information, contact-based sensing captures local interaction states after contact, and vision-contact fusion combines both for contact-rich manipulation. Vision-only (RGB / RGB-D / point cloud, etc.). Vision provides rich global context-including object identity, pose, geometry-and is therefore effective for geometry-dominant tasks such as reaching, pre-grasp planning, pick-and-place, and structured assembly when contact conditions are mild. analysis.discussion: In this section, we discuss (1) the unification of navigation and manipulation, (2) common simulator-induced failure cases, and (3) future directions of Embodied AI. The separation between navigation and manipulation is useful for organizing algorithms. However, many realworld robotic tasks require an agent to possess both capabilities simultaneously. In household rearrangement, open-vocabulary mobile manipulation, and long-horizon activity benchmarks, an agent must both search through partially observed space, identify objects and receptacles, move its body to feasible interaction poses, grasp or push objects, transport them, and verify the final state [10, 102, 159, 170, 205] . In this view, navigation changes what can be perceived and reached, while manipulation changes the environment that later navigation and planning must reason over. A first line of work treats unification as hierarchical system integration. These systems typically maintain an explicit spatial or semantic state, use a language model, vision-language model, symbolic planner, or valuemap representation to decompose an instruction into subgoals, and then call specialized skills for exploration, navigation, grasping, placing, or articulated-object interaction [75, 77, 225, 228] . This design is practical because each module can use mature tools. For example, such systems can combine path planning for navigation, perception and grasp synthesis for manipulation, and low-level controllers for execution. However, the main limitation is the interface between modules. A high-level planner may produce a semantically correct subgoal that is unreachable, dynamically infeasible, or unsafe under the current contact and embodiment constraints. Conversely, a low-level skill may succeed locally but leave the scene in a state that violates the assumptions of the next skill [170, 205] . A second line of work tries to reduce hand-designed interfaces by learning more shared action and representation spaces. Large robot datasets and VLA models, such as RT-1 [18] /RT-2 [235] , RT-X [38] , OpenVLA [92] , and 𝜋 0 [15] , show that vision-language pretraining and multi-robot demonstration data can improve generalization for language-conditioned robot control. More recent latent-action approaches make the unification problem more explicit. For example, UniVLA [19] learns task-centric latent actions from videos and then decodes them into embodiment-specific controls, allowing manipulation, navigation, and egocentric human videos to contribute to a common policy representation. Cross-domain embodied VLMs, such as MiMo-Embodied [62] , similarly suggest that spatial reasoning, affordance prediction, and task planning can share a common multimodal backbone across domains, although these models remain closer to high-level reasoning modules than to complete closed-loop controllers. The important trend is therefore not only about scaling model size, but also about separating task intent from embodiment-specific execution. For example, language and vision specify what should change, latent actions or action tokens represent how progress should be made, and robot-specific controllers realize the motion under physical constraints. Humanoid and legged mobile manipulation make these constraints especially clear. Whole-body tasks require the robot to coordinate base motion, balance, arm motion, hand contact, body posture, and sometimes foot-ground interaction. Recent systems such as WholeBodyVLA [84] , Ψ 0 [184] , HuMI [127] , and unified legged-manipulator policies [66] therefore combine high-level visual-language or latent-action representations with embodimentspecific data collection, retargeting, RL controllers, or whole-body control interfaces. From the simulator-property perspective of this survey, this trend raises more fidelity requirements. For example, a simulator for unified agents must model not only traversability and visual semantics, but also object contacts, articulated objects, base-arm coupling, foot contacts, actuation limits, controller timing, sensor latency, and failure recovery. [21] : policies that are stable during simulated training can fail or drift during sim-to-real deployment because of actuation, timing, balance, contact, terrain, or whole-body dynamics mismatch. (c) Deformation-physics failure case: for cloth, garments, and other deformable objects, turning off or simplifying physics can produce visually plausible but physically inconsistent behavior, including incorrect drape, stretching, frictional interaction, and self-contact. The deformable-object example is adapted from SynReal/Style3D demos [165, 169] . Although simulators enable scalable training and repeatable evaluation, deployment failures often arise from mismatches in the simulator properties on which an embodied policy relies. Figure 9 provides three examples of failure. The first is a perception failure case in which visual corruptions, sensing artifacts, field-of-view changes, or transition perturbations alter what the agent observes and how it updates its state [25] . The second is a locomotion failure case, where a policy that is stable in simulation may fail or drift on hardware because of actuation limits, controller timing, latency, balance constraints, terrain response, foot-ground contact mismatch, or unmodeled whole-body dynamics [21] . The third is a deformation-physics failure case, where a visually plausible simulation is insufficient because cloth, garments, ropes, bags, and other soft objects depend on material properties, friction, self-contact, multi-layer contact, and deformation dynamics. Disabling or simplifying such physics can change drape, stretching, contact evolution, and object-state transitions, making the resulting data or evaluation unreliable for physical interaction [165, 169] . In practice, failures in navigation can arise from perception, geometry, and collision mismatches; legged or humanoid systems additionally introduce locomotion and whole-body control mismatches; and manipulation depends on robot dynamics, contact modeling, material properties, and, in deformable-object settings, soft-body physics. Moreover, the same high-level metric can hide different simulator errors. For example, two navigation agents may have similar SPL but different collision responses or clearance margins, two locomotion policies may have similar simulated return but different hardware drift or fall rates, and two manipulation policies may have similar simulated success but differ in contact force, slip margin, deformation behavior, or robustness to material variation. items.abstract_text: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is a common and disabling consequence of stroke, arising from the complex interplay of vascular injury, cerebral small vessel disease, network disruption, neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and individual susceptibility factors. Advances in neuroimaging have improved understanding of PSCI pathophysiology and enabled the identification of imaging biomarkers associated with cognitive outcomes. This narrative review provides a comprehensive overview of current neuroimaging markers relevant to PSCI, including conventional magnetic resonance imaging, diffusion tensor imaging, resting-state functional MRI, arterial spin labeling, positron emission tomography, and connectome-based approaches. Particular attention is devoted to radiomics and artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI, multimodal AI, and foundation models, which are increasingly investigated approaches for biomarker discovery, biological phenotyping, and prediction of cognitive outcomes. The review further examines multimodal frameworks that integrate neuroimaging, radiomic features, blood-based biomarkers, digital biomarkers, and AI-driven analytics to support risk assessment and prognostic stratification. Despite considerable progress, important challenges remain, including methodological heterogeneity, limited standardization, insufficient external validation, concerns regarding model interpretability, and regulatory barriers to clinical implementation. Emerging technologies, such as federated learning, foundation models, digital twins, and large language models, may further contribute to the advancement of precision neurology. The convergence of multimodal biomarkers, advanced analytical approaches, and digital-health technologies may improve prognostic assessment, support individualized management strategies, and facilitate the translation of precision-medicine approaches into routine clinical care for individuals with PSCI.

items.title: Effect of Teledermatologist Supervision in AI Skin Cancer Apps on Patients’ Trust and Adherence Intentions: Randomized Controlled Trial

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Skin cancer incidence is rising globally, increasing pressure on dermatology services and making efficient triage increasingly important. AI-driven skin cancer mobile health apps may help address this need, but their usefulness depends on whether users trust the advice and intend to follow it. Teledermatologist supervision has been proposed to combine AI efficiency with human clinical oversight, but dermatologist shortages make it critical to understand whether such supervision improves patient trust and adherence at the population level, or whether AI-only advice suffices for most users. Objective This study tests whether teledermatologist supervision in an AI-driven skin cancer app affects patient trust and adherence intentions, compared with AI-only advice, and whether these effects differ by motivational context and risk assessment level. Methods The randomized controlled, online vignette experiment with repeated measures was conducted from May to June 2025 as a single-center study among Dutch adults via an academic hospital-based patient panel. Eligible participants were adult members of the Erasmus MC Digital Patient Panel invited by email; those not completing all 4 vignette trials were excluded from the analysis. Participants completed 4 simulated mobile app scenarios varying in advice source (AI-only vs hybrid teledermatologist and AI) and risk assessment level (high vs low). The primary outcomes were trust in the advice (0‐100 scale) and adherence intention (recoded 3-level ordinal scale). Mixed-effects models were used to analyze the data. Results Of the 2707 patient panel members, 879 participated (response rate: 32.5%). Participants were aged 18 to 93 (mean 62.5, SD 12.64) years; 50.4% (n=443) were female, and 21.4% (n=188) had a history of skin cancer. Participants were randomly allocated to motivation conditions (concern: n=438 vs curiosity: n=441). Trust was higher for hybrid advice than AI-only advice (mean 76.9, SE 0.73 vs mean 65.7, SE 0.73; estimated difference 11.98; partial η ²=0.22; P <.001). The odds of adherence were 1.7 times greater with hybrid vs AI-only (odds ratio 1/0.59=1.7, 95% CI 1.28-2.22; P <.001). High-risk assessments increased adherence (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 2.2-3.8; P <.001), with a moderated effect by motivation ( P =.03), showing stronger adherence with concern vs curiosity. The effect of advice source on adherence was fully mediated by trust. Conclusions Teledermatologist supervision of AI-based advice robustly increased patient trust and adherence intentions, particularly for high-risk assessments and concerned users. Our experiment is innovative in testing teledermatologist supervision in a population-level AI skin cancer app and in examining how motivational context shapes responses to advice. Unlike studies focused on postreferral teledermatology or chatbot-based advice, this study isolates the effect of hybrid AI-human advice in a store-and-forward screening context. These findings suggest that developers and health care implementers may consider integrating teledermatologist supervision to maximize patient trust of and adherence to advice, potentially improving triaging efficiency and safety.

reading.interpretation: This randomized controlled, vignette experiment aimed to answer the question “How do advice source (AI alone or Hybrid) and user motivation (curiosity vs concern) shape patient trust and adherence intentions to the provided advice within the context of AI-supported teledermatology?” The 879 participating adults reported trusting risk assessments from a hybrid source (AI plus a teledermatologist) more than AI-only assessments and reported higher intentions to follow the advice. Mediation analysis showed that trust fully explained this effect, meaning that hybrid advice increased adherence intentions by increasing the participants’ trust. A high risk of a malignancy (rather than a low risk) further strengthened the intention to follow the advice, particularly among participants who use the app out of concern rather than out of curiosity. Notably, the sensitivity analysis revealed that the interaction between motivational context and risk assessment level was specific to the disengagement threshold: concern-motivated participants were significantly less likely to neglect a high-risk assessment compared to curiosity-motivated participants, while the 2 groups did not differ substantially in rates of high adherence intentions. This suggests that users motivated by curiosity are more likely to neglect when receiving high-risk assessments, compared to users who are already concerned. From a health behavior perspective, this is consistent with protection motivation theory [ 55 ], which posits that threat appraisal motivates protective behavior most strongly when perceived vulnerability is high and personally relevant. Participants received no financial or material compensation for participation. No harms were posed on participants as it was an online study, and no concomitant care was provided. All efforts have been made to ensure that individual participants cannot be identified in any images of the manuscript or supplementary material. As this study involved a hypothetical vignette-based experiment assessing patient-reported trust and adherence intentions rather than a health-related intervention delivered to patients or a health-related outcome, prospective trial registration was not required under International Committee of Medical Journal Editors guidelines [ 44 ]. The study was nonetheless preregistered on the Open Science Framework [ 45 ] to enhance transparency of our research on May 26, 2025, after recruitment had begun but before any data inspection, cleaning, or analysis. The experiment was emailed to 2707 panel members between May 22 and June 10, 2025, with the first response being on May 22. The data collection period was defined by the panel administrators. After demographics and an AI attitudes scale, participants were randomly assigned by Qualtrics to motivation conditions (concern or curiosity; see Multimedia Appendix 2 ). They completed 4 trials in 2 randomized blocks, varying advice source (AI-only vs hybrid) and risk assessment (high vs. low). Each trial presented 1 advice output, followed by trust and adherence intention measures. Consequently, each participant saw 4 assessment outputs, 1 high-risk and 1 low-risk per advice source. After each assessment, participants answered 1 item measuring trust and another measuring their intention to adhere to the advice. Finally, participants were debriefed about the aim of the study. In a preexperiment questionnaire, participants answered questions on demographic data (age, gender, and skin cancer history) and their attitudes toward AI in health care, measured using a Dutch version of the validated 4-item AI Attitude Scale (AIAS-4) [ 46 ], with participants indicating their level of agreement on scales from 1 (“Not at all”) to 10 (“Completely agree”). After each trial, trust was rated on a continuous slider (0=no trust, 100=full trust) with the question “How much trust do you have in this result?” This single-item format was chosen to minimize respondent burden across 4 repeated trials. While single-item measures cannot capture all dimensions of trust, they can provide reliable and valid indicators of overall trust judgments [ 47 ]. Adherence was assessed by asking “What would you do next regarding your mole?” Participants selected 1 of 5 response options ( Table 1 ), which were recoded, with input from a clinician, into a 3-level ordinal adherence variable for both risk assessment levels. The recoding scheme was designed to reflect medically meaningful levels of adherence. Because the clinical implications of the same response differ depending on whether the AI advice indicated high or low risk, the classification of the responses varied by risk condition. Analyses were conducted using both SPSS (version: 28.0.1.0(142); IBM Statistics) and RStudio (2025.05.1 Build 513). For H1, a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) was used with trust as the continuous outcome, advice source and risk assessment as within-participants factors, motivation as a between-participants covariate, and participant as a random intercept. Although the Shapiro-Wilk test was significant, the residuals appeared normally distributed and no other assumptions were violated, and we proceeded with the LMM. Effect size was calculated using the following equation: η p 2 = F × d f e f f e c t F × d f e f f e c t + d f e r r o r . For H1b and H2, a cumulative link mixed model (CLMM) [ 48 , 49 ] was used given the ordinal nature of adherence intentions. Category counts were sufficient. Logit plots supported proportional odds assumption for advice source and motivation, but risk assessment violated it. To address this, 2 binary generalized linear mixed model sensitivity analyses were conducted: 1 contrasting high adherence vs moderate adherence/neglect combined and 1 contrasting neglect vs high/moderate adherence combined. The latter reflects the theoretically motivated distinction between engagement (high and moderate adherence) and complete disengagement (neglect). The results of both sensitivity analyses are reported alongside the primary CLMM findings. A CLMM was conducted with adherence intentions, predicted by the independent variables: advice source, risk assessment, motivation, and their interactions, with a random intercept for participant ID. analysis.results: The study received 1040 responses in total. Of the 2707 patient panel members, there were 879 full completions, resulting in a response rate of 32.5% ( Figure 3 ). Excluded participants were slightly older than included participants (mean 64.9, SD 12.31 y vs mean 62.5, SD 12.62 y; t 1030 =2.19, d =0.19; P =.03). There were no statistically significant differences in baseline AI attitudes (mean 5.95, SD 2.33 vs mean 6.17, SD 2.08; P =.30), gender distribution ( P =.22), personal skin cancer history ( P =.82), or motivation assignment ( P =.95). The median completion time was 4 minutes 56 seconds (IQR 2:55-3:45; range 1:28-175:26). Participants had a mean age of 62.5 (SD 12.64, range 18‐93) years with balanced gender distribution (female: n=443, 50.4%; male: n=433, 49.3%). A total of 188 (21%) reported a prior skin cancer diagnosis. The average AIAS-4 score was 6.17 (SD 2.08; n=879), indicating a slightly positive attitude toward AI. The LMM revealed a significant main effect of advice source on trust ( F 1,2643 =758.50; P <.001); trust was higher for hybrid (estimated marginal mean 76.88, SE 0.73) than AI-only (estimated marginal mean 65.68, SE 0.73), with an estimated difference of 11.98 (95% CI 10.39-13.58). This relatively narrow interval indicates a precise estimate of the source effect on trust. Advice source’s effect size was large (partial η ²=0.22), supporting hypothesis H1a that participants trust hybrid-based assessments more than AI-only assessments. Table S1 in Multimedia Appendix 5 shows the tests of fixed effects, while Table S2 in Multimedia Appendix 5 shows the estimates of fixed effects. In all CLMMs, odds ratios (ORs) reflect the cumulative odds of being in a higher adherence intention category, with values greater than 1 indicating increased odds of stronger adherence intentions. The CLMM found a significant main effect of advice source ( b =–0.52, SE 0.14; z =–3.84; P <.001) on adherence intentions (see the full table in Multimedia Appendix 6 ). The OR for hybrid compared to AI was approximately 0.59 (OR 1/0.59=1.7, 95% CI 1.28-2.22; P <.001), indicating that participants were about 1.7 times more likely to be in a higher adherence intention category under the hybrid advice source condition compared to the AI-only advice, supporting hypothesis H1b. The CI suggests a reasonably precise estimate of this effect. The CLMM also found a significant main effect of risk assessment on adherence intentions ( b =–1.07, SE =0.14; z =–7.86; P <.001). Because lower scores indicate stronger adherence intentions, this means that participants who received a high-risk assessment were about 3 times more likely (OR 2.9, 95% CI 2.2-3.8) to report higher adherence intentions compared to those with low-risk diagnoses. The relatively narrow CI indicates a precise estimate of the risk effect. Importantly, a significant interaction between risk and motivation was found ( riskHigh × motivationCuriosity; b =0.40, SE =0.19; z =2.13; P =.03). This indicates that the boost in adherence intentions associated with high risk was weaker among curiosity-motivated participants compared to those motivated by concern, which can also be seen in Table 2 . In practical terms, individuals driven by concern showed a larger increase in adherence intentions when receiving a high-risk assessment than those driven by curiosity. To address the proportional odds assumption violation for risk assessment, 2 binary generalized linear mixed model sensitivity analyses were conducted with the same predictors and participant random intercepts. The first contrasted high adherence intentions vs moderate/neglect; the second contrasted neglect vs high/moderate adherence, reflecting the theoretically motivated distinction between engagement (high and moderate) and disengagement (neglect). Main effects replicated across both models: hybrid source increased odds of high adherence intentions (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.08-1.94; P =.01), and high-risk assessment strongly reduced odds of neglect (OR 9.40, 95% CI 6.04-14.63; P <.001). Critically, the risk × motivation interaction replicated in the neglect model (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.25-0.78; P =.005), confirming that concern-motivated participants were significantly less likely to neglect a high-risk assessment compared to curiosity-motivated participants—consistent with the CLMM finding that the boost in adherence intentions from high risk was larger for concern than curiosity. The interaction did not reach significance in the high adherence intentions model ( P =.11), indicating that the effect is specifically concentrated at the disengagement threshold rather than the high engagement threshold. These analyses confirm that the CLMM findings are robust to the proportional odds violation. The relatively narrow CIs indicate that these effects were estimated with good precision. The CLMM—with participant as a random intercept—showed that greater trust significantly increased odds of stronger adherence intentions. Advice source had no main ( P =.29) or interaction effect ( P =.17), indicating trust’s influence on adherence intentions was consistent across sources (see Multimedia Appendix 7 ). These results suggest that trust mediates advice source’s effect on adherence intentions, supporting hypothesis H3, contrasting with H1b where advice source affected adherence when trust was not accounted for. The indirect effect of advice source on adherence intentions via trust was estimated as the product of 2 paths: source → trust and trust → adherence intentions, assessed through a Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 draws. To obtain unbiased estimates, both CLMM for trust’s effect on adherence (path b) and LMM for source’s effect on trust (path a) were rerun without any interaction terms. The CLMM showed a statistically significant negative effect of trust on adherence intentions (estimate=–0.030, SE =0.002; P <.001), indicating that higher trust predicted better adherence. The LMM revealed a highly significant and negative effect of AI source compared to the reference hybrid source (estimate=–11.20, SE =0.41; P <.001), indicating lower trust under AI-only advice. Combining these path coefficients, the indirect effect was estimated as 0.34 with a 95% CI (0.29-0.39), excluding zero and indicating good precision as well as full mediation (H3). The relatively narrow CI indicates that this mediated effect was estimated with good precision. This positive indirect effect suggests that hybrid advice sources increase adherence intentions by enhancing trust. Figure 4 provides an overview of the results of the main hypothesis tests.
analysis.discussion: This randomized controlled, vignette experiment aimed to answer the question “How do advice source (AI alone or Hybrid) and user motivation (curiosity vs concern) shape patient trust and adherence intentions to the provided advice within the context of AI-supported teledermatology?” The 879 participating adults reported trusting risk assessments from a hybrid source (AI plus a teledermatologist) more than AI-only assessments and reported higher intentions to follow the advice. Mediation analysis showed that trust fully explained this effect, meaning that hybrid advice increased adherence intentions by increasing the participants’ trust. A high risk of a malignancy (rather than a low risk) further strengthened the intention to follow the advice, particularly among participants who use the app out of concern rather than out of curiosity. Notably, the sensitivity analysis revealed that the interaction between motivational context and risk assessment level was specific to the disengagement threshold: concern-motivated participants were significantly less likely to neglect a high-risk assessment compared to curiosity-motivated participants, while the 2 groups did not differ substantially in rates of high adherence intentions. This suggests that users motivated by curiosity are more likely to neglect when receiving high-risk assessments, compared to users who are already concerned. From a health behavior perspective, this is consistent with protection motivation theory [ 55 ], which posits that threat appraisal motivates protective behavior most strongly when perceived vulnerability is high and personally relevant. Curiosity-driven users—who may perceive themselves as less personally at risk—may be more prone to dismissing unexpected high-risk findings as a false alarm. The results also identified trust as the central mechanism through which hybrid advice improves adherence intentions, highlighting the value of integrating teledermatologist supervision into AI-driven skin cancer apps to maximize triaging efficiency. An overview of the main results can be found in Figure 4 . Our findings differ slightly from those of Soellner and Koenigstorfer [ 56 ], who found that the mediators between increased patient compliance and human physician supplementing AI were perceived social presence and innovativeness, suggesting multiple mediating factors are induced by human clinician presence. Similarly, Reis et al [ 57 ] found patients preferred human-only chat responses for reliability, empathy, and willingness to follow advice, compared with an AI chatbot or a hybrid chat. Soellner and Koenigstorfer [ 56 ] presented AI in a positive manner and communicated a clear purpose, mentioning AI’s capability in diagnosing skin lesion photos. In contrast, Reis et al [ 57 ] used chatbot transcripts without clarifying AI’s role, possibly explaining the preference for human-only advice rather than hybrid. These findings suggest hybrid advice works best when users understand the AI’s purpose, not as a full substitute for human care [ 58 ]. Therefore, it is recommended to ensure patients understand the purpose of AI’s involvement, alleviating patients’ concerns about losing human involvement in health care [ 59 ], and for making human-AI collaboration more effective. Although including a human teledermatologist was found to increase the likelihood of higher adherence intentions by a factor of 1.7, and users’ trust in the assessment from 66% to 77%, always including human teledermatologist supervision may be increasing workload too much [ 26 ]. Both AI-alone and hybrid models are more cost-effective postreferral than face-to-face assessments without AI [ 26 ], but only offering teledermatology to cases where the AI assessment is high risk, or shifting the usage of AI to postreferral by a primary health care provider, may be an effective compromise, depending on the intervention requirements and goals. This is particularly relevant given that Smak Gregoor et al [ 30 ] found that low-risk app assessments failed to prevent unnecessary appointments, tripling benign lesion claims. Offering teledermatology review to concerned users with low-risk assessments may be a strategy to prevent in-person appointments, depending on the health care system. To avoid users neglecting high-risk assessments, strategies are required to ensure that those who use the app out of curiosity take the assessment seriously. High-risk assessments may require tailored messaging for users who do not present with preexisting concern, to prevent disengagement in precisely the cases where action is most warranted. Our study provides insights on intended adherence to low-risk/benign assessments—reflecting most real-world cases—rather than comparing stage 0 skin cancer with stage 2 as did Soellner and Koenigstorfer [ 56 ], which represents the minority of cases. Thus, our results provide insights into drivers of patients’ adherence intentions prior to triaging, which is crucial for avoiding overdiagnosis [ 9 , 30 ]. It is worthy of noting that the vignettes in our study altered the motivation (curiosity vs concern), which is intertwined with perceived lesion risk. This was done intentionally to create credible vignettes. However, it is plausible that a user of an app has low perceived lesion risk and is not curious but is using the app for other reasons. Further research could investigate whether using the app because it was encouraged by a family doctor, or family member, or for any other reason influences adherence to the app’s advice. Our study did not consider costs of teledermatology integration, so AI-only solutions may be more cost-effective despite lower adherence intentions and trust although hybrid solutions appear to be most effective postreferral [ 26 ]. The study sample was drawn from the Erasmus MC Patient Panel, representing highly engaged health care users with typically higher digital literacy and education levels than in the general population, which may limit generalizability. The vignette-based experiment involved participants experiencing hypothetical scenarios, and stated trust and adherence intentions may not fully reflect behavior during actual app use. The use of predetermined simulated app outputs rather than participant-uploaded images prioritizes internal validity by isolating the effects of advice source and risk level, though it may reduce perceived personal relevance compared to a real app scenario. However, vignette responses have been shown to correspond closely with real clinical behavior [ 60 ], and relative comparisons between conditions are generally robust to hypothetical bias [ 61 , 62 ]. The mixed design—with motivational context as a between-participants factor and advice source and risk level as within-participants factors—allowed for controlled manipulation of key variables while accounting for individual differences.
