items.abstract_text: Background As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increasingly becomes a source of health information for patients, some patients and family members have already obtained relevant explanations or recommendations from AI and brought this information into clinical communication. This change may create new communication demands for nurses. This study aimed to explore clinical nurses’ communication experiences and response strategies when patients or family members introduced AI-generated health information into nurse–patient communication. Methods A qualitative descriptive design was adopted. Using purposive sampling combined with a maximum variation strategy, 18 clinical nurses with relevant communication experience were recruited from three tertiary hospitals in Sichuan Province and Shanghai, China. One-to-one semi-structured interviews were conducted between May and August 2026. The interviews focused on specific nurse–patient communication events personally experienced by the participants. Data were analyzed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Results Two themes and six subthemes were identified. The first theme, changes in nurse–patient communication in the context of AI, included seeking confirmation from or questioning nurses using AI-generated health information, increased explanatory work, and increased communication opportunities. The second theme, nurses’ responses to AI-generated health information, included identifying patients’ actual concerns, explaining information differences in relation to the patient’s specific situation, and maintaining communication while seeking professional support. Conclusion The introduction of AI-generated health information into nurse–patient communication may both increase nurses’ explanatory work and create new opportunities for communication. Nurses may need to consider patients’ existing understanding and actual concerns, explain discrepancies between AI-generated health information and clinical arrangements in relation to the patient’s specific situation, and seek professional support when necessary. These findings may inform efforts to support nurses’ communication skills, although their applicability across different clinical settings requires further exploration.

The reporting of this study followed the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) ( 19 ). In China, tertiary hospitals represent the highest level in the three-tier hospital classification system and provide comprehensive medical and specialist services. Participants were recruited from a range of clinical departments. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) registered nurses who were engaged in direct patient care and health-related communication at the participating hospitals; (2) at least 1 year of clinical nursing experience; (3) experience within the previous 12 months of communicating with patients or family members who explicitly mentioned, showed, or referred to AI-generated health information obtained from tools such as DeepSeek or Doubao; and (4) the ability to recall and describe at least one relevant nurse–patient communication event. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) relevant experiences involved only general internet searches or conventional health information seeking, without the use of AI by patients or family members; (2) the experience was based only on second-hand information or reports from others, without direct involvement in the relevant nurse–patient communication; and (3) inability to participate fully in the interview or unwillingness to have the interview audio-recorded. Purposive sampling was used to recruit nurses who met the inclusion criteria, together with a maximum variation strategy to capture a range of experiences across different care contexts. Variation was sought primarily in clinical department, years of nursing experience, and the types of AI-related nurse–patient communication events experienced by participants. Recruitment information was distributed through hospital nursing administration departments or designated departmental contacts, and interested nurses contacted the research team directly. The researchers conducted a brief screening to confirm participants’ relevant experiences. Eligible nurses were then informed about the study purpose, interview procedures, and intended use of the data and were free to decide whether to participate. A total of 21 nurses volunteered for the study. To maintain variation across clinical departments, three volunteers (two from internal medicine and one from surgery) were not selected for the final sample because these departments were already represented among the selected participants. A total of 18 nurses were included in the study. Sample adequacy was assessed with reference to the concept of information power, taking into account the specificity of the research question, the relevance of participants’ experiences to the research question, the richness of the interview data, and the degree of experiential variation required for the analysis ( 20 ). Data richness was assessed based on the specificity of communication events, the contextual details provided, and nurses’ descriptions of their judgments and responses. Data collection and preliminary analysis proceeded concurrently, allowing the research team to assess whether the accounts provided sufficient depth and variation to address the research question. Sample adequacy was therefore considered in relation to the depth and diversity of the accounts rather than a predetermined numerical threshold. The 18 interviews provided detailed accounts of specific nurse–patient communication events and variation in participants’ clinical backgrounds and experiences. Based on the depth and diversity of these accounts, the research team considered the sample adequate to address the research question and concluded recruitment. Although recruitment information was distributed through nursing administration channels, nurses voluntarily contacted the research team to express their interest in participation. This approach was intended to reduce potential pressure to participate, although the possibility of self-selection bias could not be entirely excluded. analysis.discussion: After patients obtain health information through AI, nurse–patient communication may extend beyond nurses simply providing explanations and guidance to include confirming patients’ existing understanding and comparing information from different sources. Nurses may need to address discrepancies between AI-generated health information and actual clinical arrangements, while also making use of patients’ prior knowledge and proactively raised questions to facilitate communication. Understanding patients’ underlying concerns, assessing the applicability of AI-generated health information to the individual clinical situation, and seeking additional professional support when uncertainty arises emerged as important components of nurse–patient communication in this context. Patients’ use of AI to obtain health information before communicating with nurses allows them to enter clinical conversations with pre-existing understanding, seek confirmation from nurses, or compare AI-generated recommendations with actual clinical arrangements. Tan et al. ( 7 ) reported that patients may bring health information obtained from the internet into clinical encounters and verify their existing understanding by asking questions or discussing the information with healthcare professionals. Similarly, a survey of respondents in the United States by Ayo-Ajibola et al. ( 1 ) found that some patients considered treatment options based on information generated by ChatGPT while also seeking further confirmation from physicians. Previous studies have examined the influence of AI-generated health information on patient education and the professional role of nurses. The present study extends this work by focusing specifically on situations in which patients or family members actively introduce AI-generated health information into everyday nurse–patient communication. It illustrates how nurses respond to patients’ existing understanding, explain discrepancies between AI-generated health information and actual clinical arrangements, and experience changes in their communication work during this process. However, patients’ prior access to health information does not necessarily mean that nurses will always face a greater explanatory burden. Some nurses in this study noted that when patients had already acquired relevant basic knowledge or used AI to organize the questions they wanted to ask, the discussion could move directly to issues related to the patient’s specific situation. Liu et al. ( 10 ) similarly found that AI chatbots may facilitate patients’ access to health knowledge, while the generated content may also increase the explanatory work required of nurses. In a study of patient interactions with a GPT-4 chatbot, Carl et al. ( 21 ) found that most patients perceived the information provided as useful, comprehensive, and easy to understand, although they still placed greater value on clinicians’ explanations of medical issues. The authors also suggested that if AI can provide some preliminary explanations, it may allow healthcare professionals to devote more time to more complex concerns ( 21 ). These findings suggest that the influence of AI-generated health information on nurse–patient communication is not unidirectional, but may depend on the content of the information patients obtain, how they understand it, and how they express their concerns. When the information patients bring is complex or differs from actual clinical arrangements, nurses may need to spend additional time explaining these discrepancies. In contrast, when patients are able to articulate their concerns clearly, AI-generated health information may provide a useful basis for further discussion. Therefore, rather than focusing solely on whether patients use AI, it may be useful to examine how patients interpret and use AI-generated health information and how this information may shape the process of nurse–patient communication. From a precision health perspective, these findings suggest that the value of digital health information depends not only on its accessibility but also on how it is interpreted in relation to individual patients’ concerns and circumstances. Although AI-generated health information may not contain obvious errors, this does not mean that it can be directly applied to an individual patient. In this study, some nurses felt that explaining why generally correct information was not applicable to a particular patient was more difficult than correcting information that was clearly inaccurate. For example, patients might attribute their current discomfort to a medication after reading AI-generated health information about possible adverse effects and then ask whether the medication could be discontinued. In such situations, the key issue lies not only in whether the information provided by AI is factually correct, but also in how patients relate that information to their own symptoms and current treatment. Previous studies have also highlighted the limitations of AI-generated medical information. Wang et al. ( 22 ) noted that AI shows potential in providing general medical knowledge, but its reliability remains limited in more complex healthcare tasks. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Wei et al. ( 23 ) found substantial heterogeneity in the accuracy of ChatGPT responses to medical questions, with evaluation outcomes influenced by factors such as question type and assessment methods. While these studies have primarily focused on the accuracy of AI-generated health information, the present study further suggests, from the perspective of nurse–patient communication, that whether information is correct and whether it is applicable to a particular patient are two distinct issues that nurses need to consider separately. Participants noted that even when AI-generated content had a reasonable medical basis, patients could still develop inappropriate interpretations of their symptoms or clinical care arrangements if they overlooked the conditions under which the information was applicable. Therefore, when responding to AI-generated health information provided by patients, nurses may need to consider more than whether the information is correct or incorrect. They may also need to consider the patient’s condition, medication use, and stage of treatment, and explain the conditions under which the relevant recommendations may apply and how they differ from actual clinical arrangements. analysis.limitations: This study has several limitations. First, all participants were female nurses recruited from three tertiary hospitals in Sichuan Province and Shanghai, China, which may limit the transferability of the findings to other healthcare settings and regions. Second, the findings were based on nurses’ retrospective accounts and may have been affected by recall and social desirability bias. Third, organizational factors, including workload, staffing levels, time pressure, and hospital policies on AI use, were not examined. In addition, the versions and interfaces of AI tools were not recorded, and patients’ health and digital literacy and nurses’ AI literacy were not assessed. Finally, online interviews may have provided fewer observable nonverbal cues than face-to-face interviews, potentially affecting data richness. items.abstract_text: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.

items.title: Explainable AI for tail-risk forecasting in cryptocurrencies: evidence from green and energy-intensive assets for risk-aware investment decisions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to develop an explainable deep learning framework for forecasting tail risk and volatility in cryptocurrency markets, with a particular focus on differences between energy-intensive and ESG-oriented digital assets. It aims to assess how volatility dynamics and downside risk exposure vary across environmental profiles and market regimes and how these differences can inform risk-aware investment decisions. Design/methodology/approach The proposed framework uses a quantile long short-term memory model to estimate predictive quantiles and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), enabling the modeling of asymmetric, fat-tailed and regime-dependent risks. The analysis focuses on four cryptocurrencies – Bitcoin and Litecoin (energy-intensive) and Algorand and Chia (lower-energy alternatives). The model integrates SHapley Additive exPlanations-based explainability and a regime classification (calm vs stress). Robustness is assessed using 20-, 40- and 60-day rolling evaluation windows, while predictive performance is evaluated through coverage rates, hit ratios and Kupiec and Christoffersen back testing procedures. Findings The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across the four cryptocurrencies rather than a uniform green-versus-energy-intensive ranking. Chia records the lowest Q50 root mean squared error (0.00149) and mean absolute error (MAE) (0.00119), whereas Algorand has the lowest full-sample CVaR (0.0293) and Litecoin the highest (0.0411). Regime results are also asymmetric: Bitcoin’s Q10 violation rate rises from 8.74% in calm periods to 11.74% in stress periods, while Litecoin and Algorand record more Q10 violations in calm than in stress regimes. Chia combines the lowest global Q10 violation frequency (2.98%) with the highest mean CVaR violation loss (0.127419), showing that infrequent breaches can still be severe. These findings support asset-specific tail-risk monitoring and cautious use of energy-profile information in risk-aware investment decisions. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by integrating quantile-based deep learning, explainable artificial intelligence, regime-specific diagnostics and sustainability considerations into a unified risk-forecasting framework. Its main value lies in complementing connectedness and spillover studies with interpretable, asset-level distributional forecasts and formal tail-risk backtesting. The results provide decision-support information for risk monitoring and portfolio analysis, but do not imply that lower-energy cryptocurrencies are universally safer or that the observed differences are causal.

items.title: Generative AI adoption in organizations: A conceptual model of job crafting, employee productivity, creativity and work engagement

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping organizational work, yet its behavioural consequences for employees remain unevenly understood. Existing research on productivity, creativity and engagement is fragmented and rarely examined within a single theoretical framework. Drawing on Job Demands Resources theory, Conservation of Resources theory and Self Determination Theory, this conceptual paper develops an integrative model of how organizational GenAI adoption affects employee productivity, creativity and work engagement. Job crafting is proposed as the central behavioural mechanism. The model treats GenAI as both a job resource and a job demand. It therefore recognizes a double edged pathway in which technology insecurity and passive over reliance can offset the benefits of adoption. AI literacy, ethical use clarity and organizational readiness are identified as boundary conditions that determine which pathway prevails. Four hypotheses are developed, covering the mediating role of job crafting for productivity and engagement, its moderating role for creativity, and the conditioning effect of AI literacy and ethical guidance. A time lagged, multi source survey design, supplemented by supervisor ratings and an optional field experiment, is proposed for future empirical testing. The paper offers a resource based account of human and AI collaboration. It also provides managerial guidance for organizations that want GenAI adoption to deliver sustainable gains in performance and well being rather than short lived efficiency gains that erode over time.

items.title: Strategic futures of B2B marketing: a Delphi-based foresight study on AI and interconnected drivers of transformation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to investigate the strategic futures of business-to-business (B2B) marketing by identifying the interlinked themes shaping its transformation, with particular attention to artificial intelligence (AI) as a cross-cutting force embedded in sociotechnical and institutional developments. Design/methodology/approach A two-round Delphi study with 29C-level industry experts was conducted. Responses were coded into 192 thematic mentions across 16 themes, analyzed through co-occurrence mapping and classified in a dual-axis typology by perceived nature (opportunity vs challenge) and origin (sociotechnical vs institutional). Findings AI is central but rarely operates in isolation: it co-occurs with every other theme, functioning as the connective node between internal capabilities and external demands in interorganizational relationships. The typology reveals a statistically significant attribution asymmetry (χ2(1) = 40.23, p &lt; 0.001): internally buildable themes are framed as opportunities, externally imposed demands as challenges. Originality/value The paper theorizes AI not as a tool within the firm but as a boundary-spanning coordination mechanism coupling sociotechnical and institutional domains. The dual-axis typology, tested attribution asymmetry and three propositions provide a foresight-driven framework for understanding strategic readiness in B2B transformation.

analysis.methods: To explore how B2B marketing leaders envision the strategic role of AI within future marketing configurations and its interdependencies with other transformation drivers, we used a Delphi methodology. The Delphi approach is particularly suitable for investigating complex, uncertain and emergent phenomena where empirical generalizations and longitudinal evidence remain limited, but where expert-based anticipatory knowledge can provide valuable strategic insight (Linstone and Turoff, 1975; Skulmoski et al., 2007) . While prior AI and marketing research has frequently relied on conceptual frameworks, experimental designs or case-based analyses (Haenlein and Kaplan, 2019; Mikalef et al., 2021) , such approaches are less suited to capturing forward-looking, system-level expectations regarding the evolving role of AI in B2B environments. Our study contributes methodologically by offering a foresight-oriented, empirically grounded perspective on how experts conceptualize the interconnected drivers shaping future B2B marketing transformation. he study consisted of two iterative rounds of data collection and analysis. In round 1, we gathered qualitative insights through open-ended questions focused on perceived opportunities, challenges, significant changes and long-term impacts in B2B marketing. Responses were thematically coded to identify emerging concepts and underlying assumptions. This design follows recent B2B research that relies on open-ended questions to capture the breadth of executives' perspectives on emerging technologies (Asamoah et al., 2024) . In round 2, participants were provided with a synthesized summary of key themes and illustrative quotes derived from the first round. They were then asked to evaluate, refine or contest these findings and to provide additional elaboration where necessary. This iterative process enhanced the robustness of the insights by validating thematic salience and clarifying ambiguities. Our design prioritized qualitative depth, allowing us to explore how experts construct meaning around AI and its systemic role, aligning with methodological recommendations in marketing foresight research (Rowe and Wright, 1999) . Source(s): Authors' own work The Delphi panel comprised 29 senior experts from diverse backgrounds, including B2B marketing executives, digital transformation leaders and international consultants. Participants were recruited purposively against explicit inclusion criteria: • a minimum of 10 years of professional experience in B2B marketing, strategy or digital transformation; • current seniority at director or C-level with decision authority over technology or marketing strategy; and • demonstrable, active involvement in AI-related or digitaltransformation initiatives within their organization. Candidates were identified through professional networks and screened against these criteria before invitation. Of 34 experts invited, 29 met all criteria and completed both rounds (5 declined or did not complete Round 2). To limit selection bias, we sampled deliberately across industries and regions rather than from a single sector or network. The panel included participants from various sectors, such as manufacturing, logistics, IT and services, with most holding C-level or directorlevel positions (e.g. Chief Marketing Officer, Chief Executive Officer, Director of Strategy). Geographically, the panel comprised experts based in Europe, North America and the Middle East, including Germany, Switzerland, the UAE, Canada, Belgium, Italy, the Czech Republic and The Netherlands (an anonymized overview of the respondents is provided in Appendix 1). This composition, diverse in role, industry and region, enabled a multi-perspective understanding of the strategic and systemic dynamics surrounding AI adoption in B2B marketing. The responses from Round 1 were analyzed using an abductive coding approach (Tavory and Timmermans, 2019; Vila-Henninger et al., 2024) , combining inductive theme development with sensitizing concepts drawn from organizational theory. We developed a two-dimensional typology to classify the foresight inputs across two axes: the nature of the foresight content (opportunity vs challenge) and the type of transformation implied (sociotechnical vs institutional). This approach allowed us to distinguish whether responses described: • internal organizational or technological changes (sociotechnical); • externally imposed pressures from norms, regulations or market expectations (institutional); or • a combination of both (hybrid). Responses were coded line by line to identify core foresight themes (e.g. AI, sustainability, customer relationships). Each quote was then assessed for its underlying driver and a structured table was created linking each coded theme to its classification and rationale. Following this, themes were grouped under the five predefined themes, and a visual mapping (Figure 2 ) was created, representing each theme by its dominant classification and sizing it by frequency. Each theme was positioned horizontally by an orientation index, calculated as (opportunity mentions -challenge mentions)/total mentions and ranging from -1 (framed exclusively as a challenge) to + 1 (exclusively as an opportunity), and vertically by its dominant transformation logic, with bubble area proportional to the number of coded mentions. This analytical approach enables a nuanced understanding of how experts anticipate transformations in terms of both content and the logic of change shaping the field. Each coded mention served as the unit of analysis. A mention is one theme referenced by one participant within one of the five open questions; repeated references to the same theme by the same participant within a question were counted once, while distinct drivers within a single response were coded separately. This yielded 192 coded mentions across the 29 participants, of which 92 carried opportunity valence and 100 challenge valence. Mentions were grouped into 16 themes and assigned to the five predefined overarching theme categories that structured the round 1 rating task: digital transformation; strategic & sustainable management; market & customer interaction; organizational dynamics; and innovation & product strategy. Themes were classified as hybrid only where responses explicitly linked an internal capability to an external demand, not where coders were uncertain. analysis.discussion: The typology reveals more than a distribution of themes; it reveals a consistent attributional logic. Drivers over which firms hold design authority are read as sources of possibility, whereas drivers imposed from outside are more often interpreted as constraints to be absorbed. The internal domain is where managers locate agency, and perceived agency is what makes a driver register as an opportunity. This attribution may be potentially dysfunctional. If institutional demands are pre-classified as burdens, firms may focus on complying with them rather than on building capabilities that allow them to derive value from them. The distribution supports this interpretation: of the 61 institutional mentions, only 12 carry opportunity valence. Moreover, two institutional themes, price sensitivity and competitive pressure (T12) and talent shortage and workforce demographics (T16), attract no opportunity framing at all. The exception is sustainability and ESG expectations (T10), the only institutional theme with a substantial opportunity share. This is also the theme in which firms have begun to build internal capabilities, with AI-enabled sustainability tracking and ethical sourcing verification appearing among the strategic use cases reported by the panel (Table 3 ). Where an external demand has been internalized as a capability, its valence can therefore shift. Sustainability is not an anomaly in the pattern but an illustration of how the pattern can be disrupted. The hybrid themes reinforce this interpretation from the opposite direction. Capabilities, skills and change management (T5), innovation speed and time-to-market (T9) and trust, ethics and transparency of AI (T15) are the three themes whose coding required both logics simultaneously, and all three carry challenge valence. In the panel's foresight, friction is concentrated at the interface between these domains: these themes require firms to develop internal capabilities in response to external expectations, making the coupling between the two particularly difficult to manage. AI occupies this interface more than any other theme, making its position analytically decisive rather than merely prominent. Although classified as sociotechnical, AI carries the lowest orientation index of the large sociotechnical themes, and its strongest co-occurrences tie it simultaneously to internalcapability themes (T2, T5, T6) and to the external-legitimacy theme of regulation, data protection and policy stability (T11). AI is thus internal in classification, connected across the foresight structure, yet less unambiguously positive than its sociotechnical neighbors. This pattern points to a boundaryspanning role rather than to AI as a discrete technology. The duality reported in Section 4.1 follows directly from this position: AI is not only a means of developing internal capabilities but also an instrument through which those capabilities are made responsive to external demands. Paschen et al. (2020) captured one facet of this dynamic through their notion of collaborative intelligence, in which machine problemsolving is balanced against human judgment. The present findings suggest that this balancing act extends beyond the human-machine relationship to the relationship between internal capability and institutional expectations. This attributional pattern extends technology-oriented perspectives by highlighting that emerging transformation drivers are evaluated not only according to their technological characteristics but also according to the agency managers perceive over them. Rather than treating technology adoption as a primarily technical or organizational decision, this perspective draws attention to the interpretive processes through which firms assign strategic meaning to transformation drivers. The findings further suggest that AI's theoretical significance lies in its capacity to connect technological development with institutional legitimacy. Rather than functioning as an isolated technological innovation, AI-driven transformation involves coordinating technological capabilities with demands relating to regulation, data protection, ethics, stakeholder expectations and organizational adaptability. AI transformation can therefore be understood as a process of sociotechnical and institutional alignment rather than technology implementation alone. More broadly, the typology indicates that B2B marketing transformation emerges from the interaction of internally buildable capabilities, externally imposed demands and evolving stakeholder expectations. This suggests a broader theoretical shift from examining transformation drivers in isolation toward examining how firms construct their strategic meaning and translate external demands into internal capabilities. This attributional perspective therefore shifts attention from the presence of transformation drivers to the way firms construct their strategic meaning. The preceding interpretation can be condensed into three propositions. Each is grounded in a specific pattern in the present data, yet each states a relationship that extends beyond the panel studied here and can therefore be examined in other business-to-business settings. The first proposition formalizes the relationship between perceived origin and evaluation. P1. The more a transformation driver is perceived as originating outside the firm's sphere of control, the more likely it is to be framed as a challenge rather than an opportunity, regardless of its technological content or its objective tractability. Examining this proposition across firms that differ in regulatory exposure, or across buyers and suppliers within the same relationship, could establish whether the asymmetry is a general feature of managerial foresight or a property of particular institutional environments. The second concerns the position that boundary-spanning technologies occupy within managerial thinking. P2. Technologies that mediate between internally buildable capability and externally imposed legitimacy demands occupy more central positions in actors' foresight structures than technologies whose application is confined to either domain. Comparative work on technologies with a similar mediating function, such as traceability systems or sustainability reporting platforms, could indicate whether the centrality observed here for AI reflects a general interface function or a characteristic of this technology alone. The third proposition concerns how these perceptions develop as applications mature. Strategic applications increase firms' exposure to customers, regulators and other stakeholders, potentially changing the basis on which those applications are evaluated. P3. As AI applications move from operational to strategic levels of use, the considerations managers associate with them shift from capability and efficiency toward legitimacy and compliance, because strategic applications require greater external justification than operational ones. Longitudinal case research following applications as their scope widens is best suited to this proposition, which concerns change over time within firms rather than variation between them. items.title: Personalized AI-Supported Sport and Physical Activity for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Sports Science and Human Performance
items.abstract_text: Background: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) show frequent motor difficulties, lower physical activity (PA) and fewer opportunities for sport participation than their peers. Individualized programs are therefore needed. Artificial intelligence (AI), wearable sensors and the Internet of Things (IoT) could support such personalization, but the evidence base has not been examined from a sport-science perspective. Objective: To synthesize evidence on PA interventions and AI- and IoT-enabled technologies relevant to children with ASD and to propose a framework for personalized, AI-supported sport and PA programs. Methods: A narrative review, guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA), combined a previously completed thematic synthesis of 49 studies of AI- and IoT-enabled assistive systems for children with disabilities (16 ASD-related) with targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and publisher databases up to November 2026. Results: Meta-analyses indicate moderate benefits of PA interventions for motor skills, skill-related fitness and social functioning (e.g., Hedges' g = 0.62), although study quality is generally low. ASD-focused AI research mainly addresses gesture recognition, emotion analysis and socially assistive robotics in small samples (about 10–24 children), and none has tested fitness outcomes. The proposed artificial intelligence of things (AIoT)-CARE framework (Capability, Applicability, Robustness, and Ethics and Safety) links five stages: co-designed profiling, an accessible activity catalog, consent-based sensing, explainable recommendations with human override, and family-involved review. Conclusion: AI-supported personalization is a promising design direction, not a proven intervention. Phased evaluation using participant-level validation, real-world testing and AI-specific reporting guidelines is required.

analysis.methods: This article is a narrative review with a conceptual framework. A narrative design was chosen because the relevant evidence spans sport science, developmental disability research, computer science and ethics, and differs too widely in designs, populations and outcomes for pooled quantitative analysis. To strengthen transparency, the review was planned and reported with reference to the six criteria of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA): justification of importance, statement of aims, description of the literature search, referencing, scientific reasoning and presentation of data (Baethge et al., 2019) . The review drew on two sources. The first was a previously completed qualitative systematic review and thematic synthesis of AI-and IoT-enabled assistive systems for children with disabilities, entitled "AI and IoT-Enabled Assistive Systems for Children with Disabilities: A Qualitative Systematic Review and Thematic Synthesis" (unpublished thesis). That review followed a workflow informed by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Page et al., 2021) and thematic synthesis methods (Thomas & Harden, 2008) . Across 28 structured searches, approximately 260 records were screened, 81 reports were assessed for eligibility and 49 English-language studies published from 2015 to 2025 were included; 16 formed an ASD-related cluster. Sources included PubMed/PMC, IEEE Xplore, MDPI, Springer, ScienceDirect, JMIR, Nature/Scientific Reports and arXiv. The source review acknowledged several limitations: searches relied on a general-purpose web search service rather than direct database exports, a single reviewer screened and coded studies, inter-reviewer agreement was not measured and no formal risk-of-bias tool was applied. The second source was a targeted search conducted for the present manuscript to cover the sport and PA literature that the source review did not address. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched up to November 2026 using combinations of the terms autism OR autistic OR "autism spectrum disorder"; "physical activity" OR exercise OR sport OR "motor skills" OR fitness; and accelerometer OR wearable OR exergaming OR "virtual reality" OR robot OR "machine learning" OR "artificial intelligence". Publisher platforms (IEEE Xplore, MDPI) and reference lists of included reviews were checked for key engineering papers. Authoritative policy documents and reporting guidelines were identified from the issuing organizations. Priority was given to systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), large cohort or surveillance studies, consensus statements and reporting guidelines. Primary technical studies were included when they illustrated a function relevant to activity support, such as gesture recognition or movement monitoring, or when they reported limitations relevant to children. Every bibliographic record was checked against PubMed or the publisher record, and DOIs were confirmed where available. Retracted or unverifiable items were excluded. Evidence was synthesized thematically under four headings: motor development and PA in ASD; PA and sport interventions; AI-and IoT-enabled technologies; and ethics and evaluation methodology. The framework was developed in four linked steps. First, sensing and interaction technologies relevant to ASD were identified. Second, their potential functions were mapped onto the requirements of PA programs identified in the sport-science literature. Third, the AIoT-CARE dimensions (Capability, Applicability, Robustness, and Ethics and Safety), first used in the source review to appraise AIoT systems, were adapted to PA settings. Fourth, candidate outcomes, validation criteria and safeguards for future empirical testing were specified. This manuscript is an interpretive narrative review. It is not a new systematic review or meta-analysis, and no participants were recruited, no intervention was delivered and no statistical testing was performed. Effect sizes are reported as stated in the cited sources and should not be read as estimates for the proposed framework.
analysis.discussion: This review brought together three literatures that are usually considered separately: PA and sport interventions for children with ASD, AI-and IoT-enabled sensing and interaction, and the ethics and methodology of AI evaluation. Three findings stand out. First, PA interventions show moderate average benefits for motor skills, skill-related fitness and social functioning (Healy et al., 2018; Howells et al., 2019) , but heterogeneous effects and low-quality evidence (Ruggeri et al., 2020; Xing & Wu, 2025) leave the question of what works for whom largely open. Second, AI technologies for autistic children can recognize gestures and some movement patterns in small samples (Siddiqui et al., 2021; Ullah et al., 2023) , yet emotion recognition is unreliable (Kalantarian et al., 2020) and no study has linked AI-personalized activity to fitness or well-being. Third, individualization is rare even in AI-based pediatric rehabilitation (Kaelin et al., 2021) , indicating that personalization remains an aspiration rather than an established feature. These findings agree with broader analyses of AI in health, which report that technical performance often fails to translate into clinical impact because of dataset shift, weak generalization and inadequate evaluation (Kelly et al., 2019) . They also agree with digital PA research in intellectual disability and autism, where mixed results and weak designs limit inference (Van Biesen et al., 2024) . The network meta-analysis showing that exergaming lost its advantage for executive function in ASD when analyzed separately (Tao et al., 2025) illustrates why technology should not be assumed superior to well-designed conventional activity. At the same time, the evidence that therapists can use wearable data to tailor rehabilitation (Iosa et al., 2018) and that adaptive designs can be tested rigorously in autistic children (Kasari et al., 2014) suggests a credible route forward. The framework's contribution is to make personalization visible and testable. It specifies what information is collected and why, how recommendations are generated and overridden, and how outcomes should be judged. It separates generating a recommendation from demonstrating benefit. It also embeds participation-focused theory (Imms et al., 2017; Ryan & Deci, 2000) so that the aim is not simply more recorded movement but sustained, meaningful and enjoyable participation. Context also shapes how the framework can be applied. Most PA and AI studies reviewed here were conducted in high-income countries with access to specialist staff and devices. In low-and middle-income settings, schools may have large classes, few adapted physical education specialists and limited budgets. In such contexts, the non-technical elements of the framework, namely co-designed profiles, a structured activity catalog and regular family review, may offer most of the benefit at low cost, while optional sensing can be introduced later if validated, affordable tools become available. Strengths include the integration of sport-science, engineering and ethics evidence, verification of every reference against PubMed or publisher records, explicit separation of evidence from inference and alignment with current AI reporting guidelines. The review also has limitations. As a narrative review, it did not use duplicate screening or formal risk-of-bias appraisal for the targeted search, so selection bias cannot be excluded. The source review carried its own limitations, described in Section 2.2, including single-reviewer screening, web-based searching, no risk-of-bias tool and an English-language restriction. The included technical studies varied widely in methods and outcomes, preventing a common effect measure. The source review covered AI and IoT assistive technologies for children with disabilities in general rather than sport interventions for ASD, so links between movement monitoring and activity recommendations are design implications rather than findings of the included studies. Much of the PA evidence comes from highincome countries, and its transfer to low-and middle-income settings is uncertain. This review proposes the AIoT-CARE personalized activity framework, a child-centered model for tailoring AI-supported sport and PA programs to children with ASD. It integrates evidence that PA interventions offer moderate but heterogeneous benefits, that AI and wearable technologies can describe some movements but have not been tested against fitness or well-being outcomes, and that robust validation, privacy protection and human oversight are essential. The framework combines co-designed profiling, an accessible activity catalog, optional minimal sensing, explainable recommendations with human override and family-involved review. Whether it improves fitness, participation or well-being must be determined through phased, ethically approved research in real-world settings. The overarching aim should be to use technology to widen children's choices and safe participation, not to automate decisions about them.

items.venue: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Insights
items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) digital humans, developed to mimic humans, have emerged as promoters in marketing. Although existing studies have identified that AI digital humans' anthropomorphism shapes marketing outcomes, the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism remains underexplored. Focusing on historical figure-inspired AI digital humans in tourism destination marketing, this study examines how their multiple anthropomorphic features influence consumers' responses under the Computers are Social Actors and Media are Social Actors paradigms. Design/methodology/approach An online survey (N = 435) was conducted in 2026. Respondents completed a questionnaire after watching a typical travel vlog featuring a historical figure-based AI digital human. Findings We revealed that voice, behavior and mental anthropomorphism influence consumers' parasocial interactions with AI digital humans, which subsequently affect consumers' attitudes toward tourism destinations. Mental anthropomorphism mediates appearance, voice and behavior anthropomorphism's effects on parasocial interactions. Furthermore, mental anthropomorphism's effect is conditioned by consumers' familiarity with the AI digital human's historical figure prototype. Research limitations/implications This study extends existing research by demonstrating that AI digital humans' multiple anthropomorphic features shape consumers' parasocial interactions, with historical figure familiarity serving as a moderator. However, nonprobability sampling and a single cultural context restrict generalizability, warranting cross-cultural research with probability sampling in the future. Practical implications This study provides practical insight into developing AI digital humans in tourism marketing. Marketers should systematically optimize their human-likeness across voice, behavioral and mental traits, while considering consumers' individual differences. Originality/value This study fills the research gap in AI digital humans by unpacking the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism and showing that its effects are contingent on consumers' traits.

items.abstract_text: While large language models (LLMs) have captured global attention for their linguistic abilities, our work harnesses their power to overcome traditional barriers in querying Linked Data (LD) and Resource Description Framework (RDF) triplestores. This article presents an innovative framework that integrates LLMs into conversational user interfaces (UIs), enabling the dynamic generation of precise SPARQL queries without the necessity for constant retraining. Most conversational UI models struggle with adaptability as they require frequent retraining whenever datasets are updated or expanded. This limitation impedes their effectiveness as general-purpose extraction tools. To address this challenge, our approach 1 seamlessly incorporates LLMs into the conversational UI process, fostering a more sophisticated understanding and interpretation of user queries and enhancing overall responsiveness. By leveraging the advanced natural language processing capabilities of LLMs, our method improves RDF entity extraction in web systems that utilise conventional chatbots. Furthermore, it extends the functionality of these chatbots, allowing them to respond directly to queries based on the RDF schema while providing an assistive interface that deepens understanding of the dataset and its underlying domain. This facilitates the extraction of more meaningful information. By adopting this approach, interactions become more refined and context-sensitive, a crucial advancement for managing the intricate query structures commonly found in RDF datasets and Linked Open Data (LOD) endpoints. We have evaluated our approach in practical settings by assessing the tool’s ability to address complex queries and to answer general ecological queries, with the outputs evaluated by human experts. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in system expressiveness and response accuracy, showcasing the potential of LLMs to transform information retrieval. The findings not only confirm their adaptability in enhancing existing systems but also open up exciting possibilities for their deployment in specialised web information domains, paving the way for future research in this evolving field.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images. However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation. Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports. Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support. By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation. This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation. Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.

items.venue: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers - Engineering Sustainability
items.abstract_text: Although artificial intelligence (AI)-driven digital twins (DTs) are increasingly promoted for sustainable built asset management, there is limited empirical evidence of their full lifecycle application – particularly in emerging economy contexts that combine technical, environmental, and human-centric performance indicators. This study examines the integration of an AI-enabled DT system across the design, construction, and operational stages of ‘Nirmitee Tower’, a green-certified commercial complex developed by a mid-sized construction firm in Central India. Adopting a mixed-methods case study approach, the research collected triangulated evidence from system analytics, environmental performance metrics, semi-structured interviews, and post-occupancy surveys. Operational definitions were applied for key measures such as material waste, comfort score, and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning energy use, with baselines drawn from comparable pre-DT projects. Key findings include: a 21% reduction in project delivery time, a 35.9% decrease in material waste, a 28.3% reduction in annual energy use, a 21.1% reduction in water consumption, and a 32% improvement in occupant comfort scores. This study contributes by providing a validated, multi-dimensional assessment framework for AI–DT performance, by demonstrating a rare emerging market case of full lifecycle DT integration in a small- and medium-scale enterprise context, and by aligning technical results with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 13).

items.abstract_text: This study examines the extent to which AACSB-accredited accounting programs in the United States are integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into their curricula in response to evolving professional and technological demands. Using data from 184 AACSB-accredited institutions, we examine the presence of AI-focused degree programs and dedicated courses at both undergraduate and graduate levels. Our results indicate that, overall, AI adoption remains limited, with only 23.91% of programs offering specialized AI accounting degrees, 18.47% providing undergraduate AI accounting courses, and 22.28% including graduate-level AI accounting courses. Specialized degree programs lead slightly among adopters than graduate courses. AI integration typically occurs in isolated offerings rather than being embedded across curricula. Private institutions, although fewer in number, demonstrate proportionally higher adoption rates than public institutions. These findings highlight a potential gap between industry expectations for accounting graduates in terms of their level of readiness to utilize AI in their roles. These results suggest that accounting programs should strategically plan and integrate AI into their education to enhance student preparedness and professional relevance.

That notwithstanding, full AI-specialized Accounting degree programs are still emerging and will require further investment in curriculum design, faculty recruitment, and industry alignment. We also find that 34 institutions (18.47%) offer an undergraduate course in AI accounting, underscoring the slow pace of AI adoption at the undergraduate level. Many undergraduate programs remain focused on foundational accounting concepts and may lack the curricular space or faculty expertise to incorporate AI content. This suggests a modest but meaningful start at the graduate level, likely reflecting growing awareness of AI's impact on advanced financial reporting, auditing, and analytics. Graduate-level AI initiatives may benefit from the flexibility of elective-based curricula and stronger alignment with professional upskilling demands. items.abstract_text: Background Emergency medicine is characterized by urgency, criticality, severity, and diversity, which places high demands on undergraduate medical education. Traditional lecture-based teaching has limitations in developing students' advanced clinical competence and clinical transfer ability. Although virtual simulation and case-based learning (CBL) have demonstrated benefits in medical education, their combined application in emergency medicine teaching has not been systematically evaluated, especially based on artificial intelligence (AI). This study primarily aimed to investigate whether the integrated AI-powered virtual simulation combined with CBL could improve students' higher-order clinical competencies and clinical transfer ability, and secondarily to obtain empirical evidence to support the optimization of undergraduate emergency medicine teaching. Methods Third-year undergraduate students majoring in clinical medicine were selected as the research subjects and randomly divided into the control group and the experimental group. The control group adopted the traditional teaching method, while the experimental group adopted the AI-enabled virtual simulation combined with real emergency case teaching method. The learning situation of the virtual simulation platform was automatically recorded by the platform, and the teaching effect was evaluated through theoretical scores, objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) scores, clinical practice tracking evaluation (including advanced clinical ability and clinical transfer effect evaluation), comprehensive evaluation of learning psychology, and teaching satisfaction questionnaire. Results Compared with the control group, the students in the experimental group demonstrated significant advantages in all assessment dimensions, including theoretical test, various practical skills in OSCE, disease assessment, emergency management, clinical decision-making, as well as learning confidence, autonomous learning ability and teaching satisfaction ( P &lt; 0.001). Further analysis indicated that within the experimental group, greater investment in study time was significantly associated with better clinical performance and diagnostic accuracy. Crucially, Cox regression analysis confirmed that diagnostic accuracy was an independent protective factor for the weakness of clinical transfer ability (HR = 0.6469, P &lt; 0.00001), meaning that students with higher diagnostic accuracy had a significantly superior clinical competence. Conclusions In conclusion, this study demonstrates that the teaching model combining AI-powered virtual simulation with real cases can comprehensively and significantly enhance the comprehensive clinical skills and learning experience of medical students. The teaching effect can effectively transfer to the real clinical environment, and the diagnostic accuracy cultivated during the teaching process has important predictive value for the long-term clinical prognosis. This provides empirical evidence for the reform of emergency medicine education and emphasizes the importance of linking educational process evaluation with clinical outcomes.

analysis.methods: This study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in Clinical Medicine (five-year program) at China Three Gorges University. The research subjects were third-year undergraduate students who had completed the study of basic medical courses and voluntarily participated in this study. Exclusion criteria included: those with previous emergency clinical practice experience; those who could not complete the entire teaching and evaluation process due to special reasons. A total of 91 students were screened in the study, among which 83 met the inclusion criteria and were divided into a control group (n = 39) and an experimental group (n = 44) using a random number table method. Detailed information is presented in Figure 1 . The teaching content of both groups was formulated in accordance with the undergraduate emergency medicine teaching syllabus, focusing on common acute and critical diseases such as cardiac arrest, acute stroke, and acute coronary syndrome. The total teaching duration was 8 weeks, with 2 class hours per week. The traditional teaching method was adopted, which was teacher-centered. Teachers gave lectures combined with PPT demonstrations, supplemented by oral explanations of classic cases, and no virtual diagnosis and treatment platform operation was performed. The "Zhiqu" virtual clinical training platform (17) combined with CBL was adopted. The specific teaching process was as follows: (1) Pre-class preparation: The research team screened real emergency cases, which were entered into the Curefun platform after review by senior emergency physicians. Students previewed the case background through the platform before class, requiring a preview duration of no less than 30 min per case. (2) In-class teaching: Teachers guided students to discuss cases in groups. Students completed simulated operations such as medical history collection, auxiliary examination selection, diagnosis, and treatment plan formulation through the platform. The in-class platform operation duration was about 40 min per class hour, and teachers gave real-time comments and explanations on students' operation processes and results. (3) Post-class review: Students reviewed cases and completed extended case exercises through the platform, requiring a postclass platform usage duration of no less than 20 min per case. Meanwhile, the platform automatically recorded the cumulative usage duration of each student, the sub-item usage durations of pre-class preview, in-class operation, and post-class review, as well as the number of completed cases and the accuracy of diagnosis and treatment, which served as the core data for subsequent correlation analysis. Demographic data including gender, age, and place of origin (rural/urban) were collected via questionnaire. Before the initiation of the educational intervention, a baseline knowledge test (total score 100) consisting of multiple-choice questions, true/false questions, and short-answer questions was administered, and the scores were recorded. A unified final examination was conducted after course completion, consisting of objective items (multiple-choice and true/false questions, 40%) and case-analysis questions (60%), with a total score of 100. An objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) (18) assessment using standardized patients (SP) was organized at the end of the course. Assessment domains included history taking, physical examination, emergency skills, and doctorpatient communication. Scores were independently rated by two senior emergency physicians, and the mean score was adopted (total score 100). This domain included assessments of advanced clinical competence and clinical transfer effect. During the clinical internship in the emergency department, students' performance was evaluated by their supervising attending physicians. Advanced clinical competence was assessed across five subdomains: disease assessment (0-20 points), emergency management capability (0-30 points), clinical decision-making ability (0-20 points), interdisciplinary integration ability (0-20 points), and communication and teamwork (0-10 points), with a total score of 100. Clinical transfer effect was evaluated using the Mini-Clinical Evaluation Exercise (Mini-CEX) instrument (19). This included academic self-efficacy and self-directed learning ability. • The Academic Self-Efficacy Scale (ASES) was used to measure students' confidence in learning (20) . • The Self-Directed Learning Readiness Scale (SDLRS) was used to assess autonomous learning ability (21, 22) . A self-designed questionnaire was used, covering six dimensions: satisfaction with the teaching model, improvement in clinical thinking ability, improvement in decision-making ability, improvement in emergency management ability, improvement in learning motivation, and improvement in knowledge mastery. A 5-point Likert scale was adopted (1 = strongly dissatisfied, 5 = strongly satisfied). Data were extracted from the platform's backend system, including six indicators: total usage duration, pre-class preparation duration, duration of in-class practice, post-class review duration, number of completed cases, and diagnostic accuracy, allowing precise recording of platform usage for each student. Statistical analyses were performed using R software (R version 4.3.1) and GraphPad Prism 9 software. Continuous data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (� x + s), and between-group comparisons were conducted using the independent-samples t-test. Categorical data were presented as number (percentage), and between-group differences were analyzed using the χ 2 -test. Statistical analyses were performed using appropriate parametric or nonparametric tests to compare baseline characteristics, academic performance, clinical competence, psychological scales, and questionnaire scores between the experimental and control groups. Stratified analyses were conducted in the experimental group according to Mini-CEX scores and diagnostic accuracy to explore differences in clinical performance and learning engagement among subgroups. Pearson or Spearman correlation analyses were used to evaluate the relationships among learning engagement, diagnostic accuracy, and clinical performance. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression models were applied to identify predictors and independent protective factors for the study outcome, with hazard ratios (HR), 95% confidence intervals (CI), and P-values reported. Subgroup analyses and interaction tests stratified by gender, region, baseline scores, and age were further performed to assess the robustness of the association between diagnostic accuracy and clinical outcomes. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

analysis.discussion: Emergency medicine poses unique pedagogical challenges for undergraduate medical students. Learners are required to rapidly integrate fragmented pre-clinical theoretical knowledge into practical clinical reasoning (23) . However, traditional teaching methods, such as theoretical lectures and limited clinical internships, have significant deficiencies in the dynamics and complexity of simulated emergency environments, making it difficult to effectively cultivate the high-level competencies of medical students, such as clinical decision-making, emergency handling, and teamwork (24, 25) . This weakness in ability cultivation directly affects the quality of the future medical workforce and may potentially increase the risk of medical errors. This study designed and implemented a randomized controlled trial to evaluate a new teaching model that integrates AI-powered virtual simulation technology with real emergency cases. Medical students were randomly divided into a control group receiving traditional teaching and an experimental group receiving the new teaching method. A multi-dimensional evaluation system was adopted, including theoretical assessment, OSCE, and clinical internship tracking assessment (such as Mini-CEX). Preliminary results suggest that the experimental group appears to demonstrate advantages in multiple evaluation dimensions. Compared with previous studies, the advantages of this study lie in its attempt to be among the first to integrate AI-driven virtual simulation platforms with structured real emergency cases and the use of a longitudinal, multi-dimensional evaluation system. This may help illustrate the potential superiority of this model in improving teaching effectiveness, more importantly, this study provides an early attempt, within emergency medicine education intervention research, to link objective skills assessment indicators (such as diagnostic accuracy) collected during teaching with long-term clinical internship performance and outcome risks. Although previous studies have explored the application of virtual simulation in nursing or specialized skills training (11, 13) and have focused on the development of specific courses for emergency resident physicians (23, 26) , there remains relatively limited evidence systematically assessing the impact of AI-powered virtual simulation combined with real cases on the full chain of medical students' theoretical knowledge, practical skills, and advanced clinical ability. Our results, that the experimental group outperformed the traditional teaching group in theoretical test, OSCE practical operation, advanced clinical abilities (such as emergency management, interdisciplinary integration), and learning satisfaction, offer preliminary empirical support for the potential effectiveness of this integration model. The findings of this study may yield several tentative practical implications for undergraduate emergency-medicine teaching. Firstly, the study suggests that the "AI-driven virtual simulation combined with real cases" teaching model can potentially compensate for the deficiencies of traditional teaching in the dynamics, complexity, and high-risk nature of simulated emergency environments. Differed from conventional lecturecentred teaching, which relies heavily on static textual and pictorial descriptions, the AI-driven virtual-simulation platform reconstructs dynamically-evolving emergency scenarios. It permits students to repeatedly practise under simulated time pressure, obtain immediate feedback on their diagnostic and therapeutic decisions, and conduct personalised repeated training. When combined with real-case-based learning, this approach reproduces the complex, high-risk decision-making context of emergency medicine within a safe pre-clinical setting, thereby potentially compensating for key deficiencies of traditional classroom-based teaching before students enter formal clinical rotations. These observations may provide preliminary evidence for medical schools and teaching hospitals to reform emergency medicine courses and introduce intelligent simulation teaching tools. Secondly, the study revealed that objective clinical skills, especially diagnostic accuracy, appeared to be independent protective factors for students' future clinical competence. This finding suggested that the medical education evaluation system may warrant consideration for reform, shifting from excessive emphasis on theoretical knowledge assessment to more emphasis and effective assessment of core clinical abilities closely related to patient safety and prognosis, such as through objective structured clinical examinations (OSCE) and diagnostic accuracy assessment to quantify students' practical competence (27) . Finally, according to students' selfreported questionnaire responses (subjective measurements), this teaching model appears to have improved students' learning interest, learning-related confidence and satisfaction with teaching. Complementary objective evidence for teaching effectiveness was obtained from examination results, clinical internship ratings and platform-usage records. Therefore, educational administrators may consider supporting the promotion and application of such student-centered, technology-enabled innovative teaching methods in course design and resource allocation. It is worth noting that, despite the educational merits of AIenhanced virtual simulation, gains in learning efficiency may come with notable potential costs for medical education: overreliance on standardised AI-generated scenarios could induce stereotyped clinical thinking and greater cognitive load, uneven access to AI educational resources risks widening the digital divide across institutions; and face-to-face faculty mentoring and interpersonal-skill training remain irreplaceable. Importantly, these pitfalls are not inherent to AI itself. In this study we mitigated these concerns by treating AI simulation only as a supplementary rather than replacement tool, integrating it with authentic case-based learning and emergency clinical rotations, capping task workload to reduce time burdens for learners and educators, and having all AI-generated cases manually checked by senior emergency physicians for clinical accuracy. While no adverse outcomes emerged in our short-term intervention, longer-term follow-up is still needed to uncover latent drawbacks and lasting effects of AI-integrated medical teaching. Of course, this study also has several limitations that need to be considered when interpreting the results and planning future research. First, the sample was derived from medical students in a single center and a single grade, and the sample size was relatively limited, which may restrict the generalizability of the research results to other institutions, students of different grades, or the resident physician group. Second, although clinical internship tracking and evaluation were conducted, the follow-up period might still not be sufficient to fully assess the long-term sustainability of the teaching effect and its ultimate impact on the career. Third, the study did not set up a control group of "only virtual simulation" or "only case teaching", so it was difficult to completely separate the respective contributions of the two teaching components. Future research can adopt factorial design to further clarify this. To overcome these limitations, future research should be conducted on a multicenter and larger samp

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence dependence and academic performance: serial mediation through attentional control and physical fitness and moderation by grade level
items.abstract_text: Objective This study examined the association between generative artificial intelligence dependence (GenAID) and academic performance (AP) among adolescents, whether attentional control (AC) and physical fitness (PF) mediated this association individually and in sequence, and whether grade level moderated these pathways. Methods Participants were 1,461 Chinese adolescents. PF was assessed using standardized fitness tests; GenAID and AC were measured by questionnaires; and standardized scores in Chinese language, mathematics, and English served as indicators of AP. Structural equation modeling and related analyses were conducted using AMOS 24.0 and SPSS 26.0. Results GenAID was negatively correlated with AC, PF, and AP ( p &lt; 0.01), whereas all other pairwise correlations were positive ( p &lt; 0.01). All direct predictive paths among the variables in the serial mediation model and the predictive paths from the interaction terms to AP were statistically significant ( p &lt; 0.01). GenAID significantly predicted lower AP through three indirect pathways: AC (95% CI [−0.067, −0.031]), PF (95% CI [−0.190, −0.003]), and AC followed by PF (95% CI [−0.009, −0.002]). Grade level significantly moderated the AC–AP and PF–AP paths: the standardized coefficients for Grade_AC_inter and Grade_PF_inter were −0.101 ( p &lt; 0.001) and −0.164 ( p &lt; 0.05), respectively. Conclusion GenAID directly predicted lower AP and also predicted lower AP indirectly through AC, PF, and AC followed by PF. The findings indicate interrelationships among GenAID, AC, PF, and AP. Grade level moderated the serial mediation model, with a weaker negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP at higher grade levels.
