analysis.methods: The final sample comprised 1,461 Chinese adolescents aged 12–17 years, including 735 boys and 726 girls. Of the 2,000 questionnaires distributed, 1,638 were returned; after invalid responses were excluded, the usable-response rate among returned questionnaires was 89.19%. According to the grade-level categories specified in the Education Law of the People’s Republic of China, the sample included 361 students in Grade 7, 350 in Grade 8, 410 in Grade 10, and 340 in Grade 11. Students in Grades 9 and 12 were excluded because these graduating cohorts may differ substantially in psychological stress, emotional fluctuations, and academic pressure, thereby increasing sample heterogeneity. Participation was voluntary, and legal guardians were informed about the study and provided written informed consent. The Ethics Committee of Sichuan Normal University approved the study (2026LSTY01). Questionnaires were classified as invalid if they contained substantial item-level missingness, could not be linked to standardized academic examination scores, or could not be linked to valid PF scores. PF records were treated as invalid when indicator scores were markedly inconsistent with the participant’s actual physical condition. The inclusion criteria were adequate proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing in Chinese and written informed consent from a parent or legal guardian. The exclusion criteria were a psychological disorder, physical disability, intellectual disability, developmental impairment, sports injury, or a similar condition. GenAID was measured using the 17-item Student Generative Artificial Intelligence Dependence Questionnaire developed by Yu and Yan (2026) . The instrument comprises three dimensions: cognitive and behavioral dependence, functional dependence, and emotional dependence. Cognitive and behavioral dependence comprises six items (e.g., “When completing learning tasks, I first consider using generative AI to help me complete them”); functional dependence comprises six items (e.g., “I believe that generative AI can meet my learning needs”); and emotional dependence comprises five items (e.g., “I believe that generative AI can understand my emotions and needs”). Items are rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) on a five-point Likert scale. All items are positively keyed and summed, with higher total scores indicating greater GenAID. Cronbach’s alpha was 0.898 in the present sample. AC was measured using the Chinese version of the 21-item Attentional Control Scale revised by Yu (2017) . The instrument comprises five dimensions: inhibitory control (five items), attentional shifting (four items), task persistence (five items), attentional focusing (four items), and divided attention (three items). Items are rated on a four-point scale (1 = never, 2 = sometimes, 3 = often, and 4 = always). Seven items are positively keyed (e.g., “I can concentrate well even when music is playing in the room”), and 14 are reverse-scored (e.g., “When I am studying, I am easily distracted if someone is talking in the same room”). Item scores are summed, with higher total scores indicating better AC. Cronbach’s alpha was 0.862 in the present sample. PF was assessed in accordance with the National Student Physical Health Standard (2014 Revision) across three weighted dimensions: body morphology (15%), physiological function (15%), and physical performance (70%). The indicators were body mass index (BMI), vital capacity, the 50-m sprint, sit-and-reach, standing long jump, the 1,000-m run for boys, the 800-m run for girls, pull-ups for boys, and one-minute sit-ups for girls. The total PF score comprised a standard score and bonus points. The standard score, calculated as the weighted sum of the individual indicator scores, had a maximum of 100 points. Bonus points were awarded for eligible indicators when performance exceeded the 100-point standard, yielding a maximum total score of 120 points. Scores were classified as excellent (≥90.0), good (80.0–89.9), passing (60.0–79.9), or failing (≤59.9). AP was derived from total scores in Chinese, mathematics, and English on large-scale, standardized, in-person examinations administered by the participating schools. Because test difficulty and scoring rules varied across schools and grade levels, raw scores were converted to standardized scores. At both the junior and senior secondary levels, the maximum score for each subject was 150 points. Scores were transformed as follows: standardized score = (raw score / total possible raw score) × 100, producing AP values from 0 to 100 ( Li and Jiang, 2023 ). After obtaining approval and support from the administrators of the sampled schools, the research team distributed informed-consent forms to all eligible students who participated in the questionnaire survey. Students completed the questionnaire only after a legal guardian had signed the form. Data collection was completed within 6 months. PF data were obtained from the test records that each school submitted to the National Student Physical Health Network. School physical education teachers administered the tests and entered and reviewed the records using standardized procedures. Testing protocols, equipment specifications, and operating procedures followed the regulations of the Ministry of Education of the People’s Republic of China and the General Administration of Sport of China. Scores were classified as excellent, good, passing, or failing according to the official criteria. At the junior secondary level, PF results contributed 1 point to the physical education component of the senior high school entrance examination. At the senior secondary level, failure to meet the standard affected eligibility for high school graduation. The questionnaire was administered online, either collectively during information technology classes or outside class time under parental supervision. Completion took approximately 10 min. AP data were drawn from large-scale, standardized, in-person examinations administered by each school and were based on combined scores in Chinese, mathematics, and English. Analyses were conducted in AMOS 24.0 and SPSS 26.0. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, and overall model fit was evaluated using structural-model fit indices. Harman’s single-factor test was used to assess common method bias. Descriptive statistics summarized the study variables, and Pearson correlations quantified their bivariate associations. Path coefficients and direct effects were estimated in AMOS by maximum likelihood. Indirect effects were evaluated using a bias-corrected nonparametric percentile bootstrap proc

For Path 2, the indirect effect through PF (GenAID → PF → AP) was −0.010 and accounted for 15.87%. For Path 3, the serial indirect effect through AC and PF (GenAID → AC → PF → AP) was −0.005 and accounted for 7.94%. These results supported H2, H3, and H4. Figure 3 presents the structural equation model for GenAID → AC → PF → AP and the estimated direct and indirect paths. Both interaction terms had significant negative paths to AP: Grade_AC_inter (standardized coefficient = −0.101, p < 0.001) and Grade_PF_inter (standardized coefficient = −0.164, p < 0.05). These coefficients indicated grade-level moderation. Conditional effects were evaluated using 5,000 bootstrap resamples, and simple slopes were used to depict the interactions. Conditional effects were estimated at grade levels 1 SD below (M − 1 SD) and 1 SD above (M + 1 SD) the mean ( Niu et al., 2025 ). At the lower grade level, AC was a significant positive predictor of AP (effect = 0.429, p < 0.001), whereas its predictive association with AP was not significant at the higher grade level ( Table 5 ). Correspondingly, the indirect predictive association between GenAID and AP through AC (GenAID → AC → AP) was significant and negative at the lower grade level (effect = −0.101, p < 0.001) but not significant at the higher grade level. The confidence intervals for the lower-grade conditional paths excluded 0, and Figure 4 presents the simple slopes. These results supported H5. Conditional direct and indirect effects by grade level. Moderation plots. The positive AC–AP and PF–AP slopes were statistically significant at the lower grade level ( M − 1 SD) but not at the higher grade level ( M + 1 SD). At the lower grade level (M − 1 SD), PF had a significant positive effect on AP (effect = 0.367, p < 0.001), whereas the effect was not significant at the higher grade level (M + 1 SD). At the lower grade level, the indirect predictive associations along GenAID → PF → AP and GenAID → AC → PF → AP were both significant and negative (effect = −0.030, p < 0.001; effect = −0.016, p < 0.001, respectively); neither pathway was significant at the higher grade level ( Table 5 ). The confidence intervals for the lower-grade conditional paths excluded 0, and Figure 4 presents the corresponding simple slopes. These results supported H6.
analysis.discussion: This study tested a moderated serial mediation model. GenAID was a significant negative direct predictor of adolescents’ AP and also negatively predicted AP indirectly through AC and PF. Grade level also moderated the serial mediation model: the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP weakened as grade level increased. The correlation and prediction analyses indicated interrelationships among GenAID, AC, PF, and AP. The association between GenAID and AP is thus part of a broader pattern of relationships involving cognitive functioning and PF indicators. The findings supported H1: GenAID significantly and negatively predicted AP directly, with higher GenAID scores corresponding to lower adolescent AP. GenAID can have contrasting implications for adolescent AP. Cognitive offloading theory holds that sustained overreliance on external tools may diminish deep processing and independent thought ( Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ). Once cognitive outsourcing becomes routine, the apparent reduction in cognitive load provided by external tools becomes a maladaptive transfer of that load, compromising deep processing and disrupting the allocation of cognitive resources. Adolescents may outsource complex thinking processes, including independent thought, decision-making, and information processing, to GenAI. Although this may reduce cognitive load in the short term, the development of dependence can lead to the continued depletion and impairment of cognitive functioning. Previous research suggests that GenAI’s capacity to generate text, images, video, and audio can substantially improve adolescents’ learning efficiency ( Kasneci et al., 2023 ), whereas excessive dependence can reduce independent thinking and impair cognitive functioning ( Zhang et al., 2024 ). Academic emotions and anxiety also shape adolescent AP. Persistent dependence on AI can heighten academic anxiety, prompt doubts about one’s abilities, and reduce academic self-efficacy, adversely affecting AP ( Li et al., 2026 ). A 30-month longitudinal study of 26,811 Chinese students in Grades 7–12 across nine subjects found that AI assistance increased homework scores by approximately 18% and reduced completion time by 30%, while examination scores decreased by 18%–24%. Learning losses were concentrated among approximately 80% of AI users whose behavior was consistent with homework outsourcing, as indicated by exceptionally short homework completion times combined with high homework scores. AI users whose homework completion times were similar to those of nonusers experienced small learning losses ( Strömberg and Lei, 2026 ). These findings support the interpretation that GenAID is negatively correlated with academic performance. GenAID negatively predicted adolescent AP through AC, consistent with H2. The negative indirect estimate through AC was lower than the direct estimate for GenAID predicting AP, suggesting that stronger AC can reduce the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP. Previous research has linked excessive AI use in adolescence to neurobiological changes, including reduced prefrontal-cortex activation and lower hippocampal gray-matter density; these changes may contribute to cognitive-overload symptoms such as distractibility and impaired decision-making ( de Sousa et al., 2026 ). Excessive dependence on AI has also been associated with poorer long-term memory retention and AC ( Deckker and Sumanasekara, 2025 ). AC, in turn, is consistently associated with adolescent AP: impaired AC is related to poorer AP ( Bruce et al., 2016 ), whereas stronger AC is related to better AP ( Ma and Li, 2023 ; Song et al., 2018 ). AI’s predictive relationships with adolescent cognitive functioning and AP differ substantially according to how individuals use it. Research suggests that the learning benefits of AI depend on students’ AI literacy and how they prompt AI and verify its output. Higher AI literacy can positively predict AP through prompting practices, information verification, AI-assisted calibration accuracy, and perceived task cognitive load ( Shen, 2026 ). AI also has the potential to provide students with personalized, efficient learning experiences ( Xuan, 2025 ). In the present study, the negative indirect effect via AC was the largest, indicating that AC constitutes an important correlational pathway in the negative association between GenAID and poorer AP. The observed correlational pattern suggests that AI literacy, cognitive load and AC may co-vary with this association. A parallel pattern emerged for PF. GenAID was negatively associated with PF, whereas PF was positively associated with AP, yielding the negative indirect effect proposed in H3. The negative indirect estimate through PF was lower than the direct estimate for GenAID predicting AP, suggesting that higher PF can reduce the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP. Prior research suggests that excessive AI dependence among adolescents may involve substantial out-of-school time devoted to human–AI interaction, thereby increasing sedentary behavior, reducing time available for exercise, and lowering PF ( Liu et al., 2026 ). Higher PF, by contrast, has been associated with better AP ( Wen et al., 2018 ; Liang and Li, 2020 ). These findings offer a plausible account of the observed indirect effect: by displacing time otherwise available for exercise, GenAID may gradually compromise PF, with downstream implications for AP. Cognitive behavioral therapy interventions can alleviate negative emotions, stress, anxiety, and related psychological problems. Health-risk behaviors in adolescence tend to cluster, and the occurrence of one such behavior often increases the likelihood of others. These interventions can therefore target co-occurring unhealthy behaviors and psychological and behavioral problems in adolescents ( Zhang et al., 2026 ). This pattern raises the possibility that combined cognitive and exercise interventions may be associated with lower digital dependence. The model also yielded the negative serial indirect effect through AC and PF proposed in H4. GenAID negatively predicted adolescent AP through the combined pathway involving AC and PF. The negative estimate for this serial indirect pathway was lower than both the direct estimate for GenAID predicting AP and the estimates for the separate indirect pathways through AC and PF, suggesting that stronger AC and higher PF can jointly reduce the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP. verified_article_review.methods: Researchers linked questionnaires from 1,461 students aged 12–17 at urban Chinese schools to fitness tests and standardized scores in Chinese, mathematics and English. The questionnaires measured reliance on generative AI and students' reported ability to direct their attention.
verified_article_review.results: Students who reported greater dependence on AI also reported poorer attentional control and had lower academic scores. Statistical models linked dependence to scores through attentional control and fitness, separately and in combination.
verified_article_review.discussion: The survey connects students' accounts of attention to an outcome the schools recorded independently. Students already struggling to concentrate or to keep up with schoolwork might also seek more assistance.
verified_article_review.limitations: The measures came from one period. Students rated their own attention. The study did not track when they sought AI help or control for family socioeconomic circumstances.
verified_article_review.review_scope: Checked the participants, measures, associations and limits in the publisher's full HTML.

editorial_digest.idea: How do students describe their attention when they rely on AI?
editorial_digest.explain: Teenagers' answers were linked with school records and fitness tests.
editorial_digest.approach: Researchers linked 1,461 Chinese adolescents’ ratings of AI dependence and attention to their fitness tests and their scores in Chinese, mathematics and English.
editorial_digest.finding: Students reporting greater dependence also reported more trouble directing their attention and earned lower school exam scores.
editorial_digest.interpretation: The data leave open whether struggling students turn more often to AI.
editorial_digest.limitation: The measurements came from one period. Students rated their own attention, so the study cannot establish whether concentration problems preceded their reliance on AI.

reading.overview: Objective This study examined the association between generative artificial intelligence dependence (GenAID) and academic performance (AP) among adolescents, whether attentional control (AC) and physical fitness (PF) mediated this association individually and in sequence, and whether grade level moderated these pathways. Methods Participants were 1,461 Chinese adolescents.
